title: traversable1Laws' list-applicative property does not terminate on a 110-cell grid
description:
In the uncommitted Foldable1/Traversable1 work (sized-grid-g4xz), tests/Test/Utils.hs's traversable1Laws includes:

  agreesWithList :: Fun Int [Int] -> f Int -> Property
  agreesWithList (applyFun -> h) g =
    traverse1 (\x -> 0 : h x) g === traverse (\x -> 0 : h x) g

and tests/Main.hs instantiates it at Grid '[Periodic 10, Periodic 11].

That is 110 cells traversed in the list applicative, where every per-cell list has length at least 1 and typically more. The result is the cartesian product across all 110 cells -- at an average branching factor of 2 that is 2^110 grids. The property never terminates.

Observed: 'cabal test all' hangs indefinitely at

  Traversable1
    traverse1 Identity == Identity:                OK
    traverse1 agrees with traverse (Maybe):        OK
    traverse1 agrees with traverse ([]):           <hangs>

with the test binary spinning until killed. Two separate 'cabal test all' runs and one direct run of the test binary were killed at 550s-2400s without it completing. With the three files of that work stashed, the same suite runs 839 tests in 23 seconds.

The intent of the property is right -- the list applicative is what exercises (<.>)'s association, which Maybe does not -- so it is the instantiation that is wrong, not the law. Fixes to weigh:

  * State it at a small grid: Grid '[Ordinal 2] or Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2] keeps the product to 4-16 branches and still associates (<.>) non-trivially.
  * Or keep the big grid and use a generator whose images are all singletons, which makes the product trivial and defeats the point.

The first is the real fix. Note the same hazard is already documented on zipLowerDim/mapLowerDim in Internal.Grid.Shape -- 'mapLowerDim @gridTiles@ on a 9x9 board gives 387,420,489 grids' -- so the library has met this before.

Found while verifying sized-grid-mbh0: the work was already in the tree uncommitted and blocked the suite. It is stashed as 'Foldable1/Traversable1 WIP (sized-grid-g4xz), parked to verify mbh0'.
close_reason: Closed

title: ../aoc/src/2018/18.hs still hand-rolls the neighbourhood sized-grid-7gs was built to replace
description:
The design note docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-11-safe-neighbour-offset-design.md lists four ../aoc call sites under 'Consumers after the change'. Three moved: 2015/18.hs:40 and 2025/04.hs:53 both call experiment neighbours, and 2024/04.hs:76 calls offsetCoord. The fourth did not.

../aoc/src/2018/18.hs:70-80 is still the 11-line hand-roll the note quotes:

  neighborsOf :: forall n. (KnownNat n, 1 <= n) => Coord '[Clamped n, Clamped n] -> [Coord '[Clamped n, Clamped n]]
  neighborsOf (r :| c :| _) =
    [ toEnum nr :| toEnum nc :| EmptyCoord
    | dr <- [-1 .. 1], dc <- [-1 .. 1], (dr, dc) /= (0, 0),
      let nr = fromEnum r + dr, let nc = fromEnum c + dc,
      nr >= 0 && nr < nVal && nc >= 0 && nc < nVal ]
    where nVal = fromIntegral $ natVal (Proxy @n)

Line 59 even carries the old call commented out above it:

  -- neighs = experiment (filter (/= pos fg) . nubOrd . moorePoints 1) fg
  neighs = experiment neighborsOf fg

sized-grid-7gs's close reason says 'all five in-repo consumers migrated', which is accurate -- ../aoc is a separate repo and was never in that count. sized-grid-bb5 migrated aoc, but for the sealed Grid constructor, not for this.

Two reasons it is worth doing beyond deleting eleven lines. It is the last evidence that the checked-movement API does not cover a real call site, and while it stands the research record is ambiguous. And it rebuilds every result through toEnum on a Clamped axis, which is the path sized-grid-tgmj reports as throwing; it only survives because the guard on the line above has already bounds-checked the value. Fixing tgmj will not break it, but it is the pattern tgmj exists to remove.

Fix: neighs = experiment neighbours fg, delete neighborsOf, delete the commented-out line, and drop whatever imports (Proxy, natVal) fall out. Verify the puzzle answer is unchanged -- neighbours on a Clamped axis gives 3 at a corner and 5 on an edge, which is what the hand-roll's bounds check also gives, so the answer must not move.

Found by the sweep in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-30-boundary-policy-audit.md.

title: scanAxisStrided Haddock: the fibre-walk comparison is cache-dependent and reads as unconditional
description:
scanAxisStrided's Haddock says the fibre-at-a-time walk 'is slower, 679 us against 575 us boxed and 254 us against 68 us unboxed on scanAxis 0 over 300x300'.

spike/utxm-paraxis could not reproduce the unboxed figure: on 300x300 unboxed, -N1, one process, the in-order pass and the fibre walk measure 75.8 us and 75.7 us -- level to 0.1%. The reason is that 300x300 Int is 720 KB and this machine's performance cluster has a 16 MB L2, so the grid never misses and the access pattern is nearly free.

The claim IS true, and larger than recorded, once the grid leaves cache. Same two arms on 2000x2000 unboxed (32 MB): 3.05 ms vs 23.14 ms, a 7.6x difference.

So the decision the Haddock records is right, but the number it quotes is not reproducible on the shape it names, and a reader sizing a grid from it would draw the wrong conclusion about small grids. Suggest restating it as: the in-order pass matters little in cache and is worth ~7.6x out of it, with both numbers and the cache size named.

Same caveat belongs anywhere else in the library that quotes a locality measurement taken on a 300x300 grid.

title: Atlas/mosaic: multi-chart grids glued by typed edge transitions
description:
A grid assumes one coordinate system covering one rectangular space. An atlas
(or mosaic) drops that: space is a collection of charts glued along their edges
by transition rules.

    coordinate  =  (ChartId, Coord cs)
    step        =  stay in chart, OR cross a seam into another chart,
                   arriving at a transformed local coordinate with a
                   transformed frame

This is what the cube map, the hexagonal mesh, the multi-room dungeon and the
hyperbolic tiling all are, and none of them is expressible as a boundary policy
on a single `Coord cs` -- see the separable/non-separable issue for why.

WHAT IT REUSES

Everything. A chart is a `Grid cs a`, indexed exactly as now, with all the
unrolling work intact. The atlas layer sits above `index` and decides WHICH
grid and WHICH coordinate before touching a vector. Nothing in
Internal/Grid.hs needs to change, and the vector invariant is untouched.

`gridTiles` (Internal/Grid.hs:543) already cuts a grid into disjoint tiles. It
is the degenerate atlas: same-shaped charts, glued in a line, identity
transitions. That is a good first target -- an atlas whose transitions are all
identity must be observationally equal to the grid it came from, which is a
free property test.

SHAPE OF THE THING

  * Charts may differ in axis type but probably not in shape, at least at
    first. Heterogeneous chart shapes are a second problem.
  * The transition is the seam rule from the sibling issue: destination chart,
    coordinate map, frame transform.
  * A cube map is 6 charts with a fixed D4 transition table. That is the
    smallest interesting non-trivial atlas and it is the one to build first,
    because the answers are all checkable by hand.

PACKAGING

Strong preference for a separate package (`grid-atlas`) depending on
`grid-sized`, not a module inside it. Reasons:

  * grid-sized has a stated thesis -- the coordinate type is the boundary
    policy -- and the atlas is explicitly the layer for the policies that
    thesis cannot express. Keeping them apart keeps both statements true.
  * It cannot destabilise the measured performance work.
  * If the atlas turns out to be the interesting library, it has a fast tested
    tile layer underneath. If it does not, nothing was lost.

NOT SCHEDULED. This is the endpoint, and the two issues it depends on are the
actual work.
notes:
WHY THIS IS THE QUIVER/fgl CONNECTION (from the decomposition-comonad transcript, 2026-08-16).

Quiver and fgl decompose a graph into a Context -- inbound edges, label, outbound edges -- and the rest of the graph. They STORE the edges, because a graph's topology is arbitrary and there is nothing else to do with it.

A grid never stores its edges. Adjacency is COMPUTED from the coordinate, by the boundary policy: neighbours c is derived, not looked up. That is the whole reason Grid cs a can be a flat vector with no per-cell overhead, and it is what makes this library fast.

An atlas is exactly the point where that stops being true. A transition table -- which chart, which coordinate map, which frame element -- is topology that CANNOT be computed from a coordinate, so it has to be stored. That is the same move fgl makes, and it is the first thing in this design that genuinely resembles a graph library rather than an array library.

So the progression is:

    Grid       adjacency computed from geometry, zero storage
    Atlas      adjacency computed WITHIN a chart, stored BETWEEN charts
    Quiver     adjacency stored everywhere

The atlas is the middle term, and it is interesting precisely because it keeps the fast computed case inside each chart and pays for storage only at the seams. That is a better argument for building it than 'Mobius strips are cool', and it should be the framing in any writeup.
close_reason: Shipped v1: new sibling package grid-atlas (grid-atlas/grid-atlas.cabal, added to cabal.project) with Data.Grid.Atlas, restoring gridTiles's own disjoint list as one addressable (ChartId, Coord cs) structure -- Atlas cs k a (sealed newtype over a Vector of Grid cs a), AtlasCoord cs k = (Ordinal k, Coord cs), atlasFromTiles (smart constructor, k fixed to CoordNat big Div CoordNat small at the type level), atlasIndex (total lookup), atlasOffsetHead (steps the tiled axis, crossing into the neighbouring chart on overflow, Nothing at the atlas's own two ends; always the head axis, matching gridTiles's own restriction). Verified: cabal build all, cabal test grid-atlas (exhaustive equivalence check against index on the untiled grid plus a 100-case QuickCheck property on atlasOffsetHead), cabal test grid-sized (473 tests, unaffected), cabal haddock grid-atlas (100% coverage). Deliberately NOT built: heterogeneous chart shapes, a general seam-transition table, any frame transform, and the cube map itself -- filed as sized-grid-68j (blocked on this issue), which is also where sized-grid-ts4 (is this a grid-independent manifold library) gets its second data point.

title: Bounded one-pass stencil table build: 1.9x and half the allocation, no threads
description:
sized-grid-kb38 measured this as a free 1.9x on one core, and it is the largest
win that spike found -- larger, per unit of risk, than the parallelism the
issue was opened to investigate.

WHAT. stencilFor asks the neighbourhood function twice per cell: once for a
length, to discover the width, once for the row. adr.15 chose that against a
one-pass build that RETAINED every row across a width pass. It did not consider
a third option: allocate at an upper BOUND on the row width, fill in one pass
recording the width actually seen, and compact if the bound turned out loose.
Nothing is retained and the neighbourhood function runs once.

The Haddock on stencilFor currently says the width is discovered rather than
derived because a derived bound would over-pad every row. That is true of a
derived FINAL width and false of a derived ALLOCATION size, which is what this
is -- the width that lands in the Stencil is still the one the fill observed.
That note needs amending along with the code.

WHERE. mooreStencil and vonNeumannStencil only: the bound is (2r+1)^d - 1 and
they are the two entry points that know r and d. The general stencilFor has no
bound available and keeps its current two-pass path. (spike/kb38-parstencil's
tableParChunked is the general one-pass answer needing no bound; it loses
everywhere -- see that README.)

MEASURED, 90,000 cells, wall clock:
  moore r=1:        57.0 ms -> 30.2 ms,  535 MB -> 260 MB allocated
  moore r=3:         385 ms ->  194 ms, 2253 MB -> 1116 MB allocated
  vonNeumann r=2:    148 ms ->  81.0 ms, 833 MB -> 426 MB allocated
Holds at 1.83-1.99x across every size from 12 cells to 90,000 and across
Clamped, Periodic and Reflective axes.

COST. Peak residency, and only when the bound is loose. Moore's bound is exact,
so residency is unchanged to three digits (6.02 MB either way at 90,000 cells).
von Neumann at r=2 has bound 24 against width 12, so it briefly holds a table
of twice the final size: 8.90 MB -> 17.5 MB. Worst case n*ub machine words,
predictable from the type and the radius, freed at the compacting copy. Decide
deliberately whether that is acceptable for vonNeumannStencil; a tighter
vonNeumann bound is available if not (the L1 ball, not the cube).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- Internal bounded builder in Data.Grid.Sized.Stencil; mooreStencil and
  vonNeumannStencil go through it, stencilFor unchanged.
- Test.Stencil states that mooreStencil/vonNeumannStencil agree exactly --
  width and positions -- with stencilFor on the same neighbourhood, over mixed
  Clamped/Periodic/Reflective/Reflect101 axis lists, including radii large
  enough that a short axis deduplicates.
- The degenerate cases: empty neighbourhood (width 0), and a grid whose every
  row is short.
- bench/Main.hs: the existing "mooreStencil r, 50x50 (building the table)"
  benchmarks should move; check they do and by how much.
- Amend the stencilFor Haddock note about derived bounds, and the module
  Haddock's build-cost numbers, which this changes.

Evidence and a working implementation (tableSeqBounded): spike/kb38-parstencil.
close_reason:
Implemented: added IsCoordList.coordListLength (axisCount wrapper), an internal
stencilBounded builder in Data.Grid.Sized.Stencil (ST-based: allocate at ub,
fill in one pass tracking width seen, compact if loose), and switched
mooreStencil/vonNeumannStencil to it via mooreUpperBound = (2r+1)^d - 1.
stencilFor is untouched.

Decision: vonNeumannStencil uses the same (loose) Moore cube bound rather than
the tighter L1-ball bound, per the issue's "decide deliberately" framing --
the looseness only costs temporary peak residency, freed at the compacting
copy, and one bound formula for both entry points is simpler.

Tests: Test.Stencil now states mooreStencil/vonNeumannStencil produce the
exact stencilFor table (width and positions) over mixed
Clamped/Periodic/Reflective/Reflect101 axis lists, dedup radii, the
empty-neighbourhood case, and a grid whose every row is short. All 821 tests
pass, plus downstream/readme suites and every other package in the workspace.

Bench: re-measured "mooreStencil r, 50x50 (building the table)" fresh, before
(two-pass) vs after (bounded): 1.46ms/16MB -> 916us/6.9MB, 1.6x faster / 2.3x
less allocated. Updated the module Haddock's build-cost numbers and derived
ratios to match, and noted the move in bench/Main.hs.

Follow-up: sized-grid-mrpb (opt-in parallel build) is now unblocked.

title: Research: additional typeclass instances for Grid (Foldable1, Ord/Read, Hashable, ComonadApply)
description: Survey of typeclasses adjacent to what Grid/FocusedGrid already implement (Functor, Foldable, Traversable, Applicative, Apply, Bind, Semialign, Zip, Distributive, Representable, FunctorWithIndex/FoldableWithIndex/TraversableWithIndex, Comonad, ComonadStore, Eq1, Show1) that are plausible next additions, found by diffing against base/semigroupoids/comonad/hashable, all already dependencies (base-4.21, semigroupoids-6.0.2, comonad-5.0, hashable confirmed via ghc-pkg list and grep of src/). Candidates, roughly in order of confidence: (1) Foldable1/Traversable1 (Grid cs) -- Data.Foldable1 is in base since 4.18 and Traversable1 is in semigroupoids' Data.Semigroup.Traversable, both already available; every element of IsCoordList is IsCoordLifted, which the library's own design doc (docs/superpowers/specs) already states guarantees 1 <= CoordNat for each axis, so MaxCoordSize cs (a product of per-axis sizes) is provably >= 1 and Grid cs a can never be empty when cs is a valid coordinate list -- but the instance head would need IsCoordList cs (or AllSizedKnown) to witness that, which is exactly the same 'a class method cannot acquire its own constraint, so it spreads to every call site' problem the Foldable haddock (sized-grid-adr.10 note in Data.Grid.Sized.Internal.Grid) already documents happening once for Foldable's length/null; a second, unconditional Foldable instance sitting next to a conditional Foldable1 is unusual and needs a design decision, not just an instance. (2) Ord (Grid cs a) and Ord1 (GridOf v cs) -- Eq1/Show1 are already newtype-derived from the underlying vector's own instances, and Vector already has Ord (lexicographic on toList order, i.e. row-major); adding Ord the same way is a export-list change, not new logic, and would let Grid values sit in Set/Map or be sorted. (3) Read (Grid cs a) -- the natural counterpart to the existing Show1, but not a safe derive: like FromJSON's checkLength, a derived Read would not validate that the parsed vector has exactly MaxCoordSize cs elements, so it needs the same hand-written validation Data.Aeson's parseJSON already has, just via readsPrec/ReadPrec. (4) Hashable (Grid cs a) given Hashable a -- every coordinate type (Ordinal, Coord, TorusCoord, Clamped, Periodic, Reflective, Reflect101) is already Hashable via newtype deriving or a hand-written instance in Data.Grid.Sized.Coord, but Grid itself is not, which blocks using a Grid as a HashMap/HashSet key (e.g. a transposition table keyed on board state, or memoising a stencil result by its window contents); a foldl'-based instance over the existing Foldable is a few lines. (5) ComonadApply (FocusedGrid cs) from the comonad package (already a dependency, already used for Comonad/ComonadStore) -- gives '(<@>)' for combining two focused grids' cell-wise values while combining their focuses, the comonadic analogue of the Apply instance Grid cs already has; needs a Semigroup (Coord cs) to combine the two focuses, which Coord already has conditionally. (6) Noted but not recommended: Grid deliberately has Apply and Bind but no Monad instance (confirmed absent by grep) -- Monad's pure needs AllSizedKnown the same way Applicative's does (see the Bind haddock), so a full Monad instance is not free the way Bind is, and MonadZip (which requires Monad) inherits that gap; this is intentional per the existing Apply/Bind design notes, not a gap to close, but is recorded here so it is not independently rediscovered as a separate issue.
acceptance_criteria: 1. For each of Foldable1/Traversable1, Ord/Ord1, Read/Read1, Hashable, ComonadApply: confirm the instance is lawful for a fixed-size, provably-nonempty Grid/FocusedGrid, and decide the constraint it needs on the instance head (IsCoordList, AllSizedKnown, or none). 2. Decide, for Foldable1/Traversable1 specifically, whether a conditional instance beside the unconditional Foldable/Traversable is acceptable given the existing adr.10 precedent against constraint-spreading, or whether it should be declined for the same reason. 3. Prototype the cheapest two (Ord/Ord1 by extending the existing deriving-newtype clause, Hashable via foldl') and measure whether they compile without widening any existing signature. 4. File follow-up implementation issues only for the instances confirmed lawful and worth their constraint cost; close this issue once the survey is recorded even if no code lands.
notes:
Foldable1 and Traversable1 landed in 858c784 (2026-08-29), with hand-rolled law bundles in Test.Utils since quickcheck-classes has none for either class. The branching-applicative law needed its own bundle and a small grid to terminate at all -- see sized-grid-e7xo, closed.

Still open on this issue: Ord/Read, Hashable, ComonadApply.
MonadFix belongs on this list, with a caveat that has to ship with it (from sized-grid-i0ob.1).

`Grid cs` is `Representable`, so it inherits the reader `MonadFix` for free:

    mfix f = tabulate (\c -> fix (\a -> index (f a) c))

Lawful and one line. The caveat is that this is a PER-CELL fixpoint -- each cell ties a knot with itself -- and it therefore cannot express the cross-cell recursion people actually reach for `mdo` to get. Cross-cell self-reference already works today with plain `fix`, because `tabulateGrid` is `VG.generate` and boxed `Data.Vector` is element-lazy:

    pascal = fix $ \g -> tabulate $ \c -> ... index g (neighbour c) ...

So the instance should land with a Haddock note saying which recursion it gives, or someone will reach for `mdo` expecting the other one and get a `<<loop>>` at runtime with no type error to explain it.

Also relevant if `Hashable`/`Ord` are being weighed: sized-grid-h6ki (HashLife demo) needs both for hash-consing and would be a real consumer to design them against rather than deciding in the abstract.

title: Research: Filterable/Witherable instances for Grid
description: The witherable package's Filterable (mapMaybe, catMaybes, filter) and Witherable (wither) classes let a functor shrink: the result can hold fewer elements than the input. Grid cs a fixes its element count to MaxCoordSize cs at the type level (GridOf's own invariant, asserted in Data.Grid.Sized.Internal.Grid and enforced by every safe constructor), and every existing instance -- Functor, Foldable, Traversable, Applicative, Monad, Apply, Bind, Distributive, Representable -- preserves that count. catMaybes :: Grid cs (Maybe a) -> Grid cs a has no total, lawful definition: when an element is Nothing there is no cs-shaped result to return, and the Filterable law catMaybes . fmap Just = id only constrains the all-Just case, so nothing rules out an instance that is total but unlawful (e.g. silently dropping to a smaller unsafe vector, or crashing). Grid is therefore not a sound Filterable/Witherable instance target, unlike lattices (sized-grid-jdzs), which fit the fixed shape pointwise. The same argument applies to FocusedGrid (Data.Grid.Sized.Focused) and Atlas cs k a (grid-atlas), both of which also fix their element count at the type level. What a fixed-size grid *can* offer, in the spirit of the library's existing $bulk non-class operations (tabulateGrid, foldlGrid', imapGrid, zipWithGrid), is shape-dropping helpers with a Vector/list result: mapMaybeGrid :: (a -> Maybe b) -> GridOf v cs a -> V.Vector b, filterGrid :: (a -> Bool) -> GridOf v cs a -> V.Vector a, catMaybesGrid :: GridOf v cs (Maybe a) -> V.Vector a, and witherGrid :: Applicative f => (a -> f (Maybe b)) -> GridOf v cs a -> f (V.Vector b). These are one-liners over Data.Vector.Generic's own mapMaybe/filter (already available, vector has no Witherable dependency) and would give callers who want to select a subset of cells (e.g. collecting all alive cells of a Game of Life board, or the walls in a maze) a documented, honest way to do it without an unlawful instance.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Confirm no lawful Filterable/Witherable instance is possible for Grid cs, FocusedGrid cs, or Atlas cs k under the fixed-size invariant, and record why. 2. Decide whether to add mapMaybeGrid/filterGrid/catMaybesGrid/witherGrid as $bulk helpers alongside foldlGrid' et al., or to close as intentionally unsupported with no new API. 3. If added, cover them with the same size-invariant-style property tests as the rest of tests/Test/Invariant.hs, checking the *output* is a subset of the input in row-major order rather than a fixed size. 4. Do not add witherable as a dependency merely to reuse its class name -- these are plain functions, not instances.
notes: Researched via search_subagent over src/Data/Grid/Sized/Internal/Grid.hs, Focused.hs, and grid-atlas/src/Data/Grid/Atlas.hs. No existing references to witherable/Filterable/Witherable anywhere in the repo. Data.Vector.Generic already exports mapMaybe and filter, so the proposed helpers need no new dependency.

title: Decision: use constraint synonyms only for stable semantic bundles
description:
Research question: is it worth exporting type synonyms for repeated constraint lists in the current grid-sized API?

RECOMMENDATION
Use ConstraintKinds synonyms selectively, but do not introduce a blanket alias for every repeated tuple. A synonym is worthwhile when the constraints form one stable, user-recognisable capability and the bundle is repeated across several public signatures. Keep the underlying constraints visible when they describe different capabilities, when callers commonly need only a subset, or when the synonym would hide an important soundness precondition.

LOCAL EVIDENCE
The tree repeats (IsCoordList cs, AllSizedKnown cs) in benchmark and example helpers, but the two constraints are not interchangeable: IsCoordList supplies coordinate structure and AllSizedKnown supplies total-size evidence. Other signatures intentionally need only one of them. AllSizedKnown, All IsCoordLifted, and AllGridSizeKnown express different obligations; the earlier consolidation work correctly converted AllGridSizeKnown to a class rather than hiding the distinction behind an alias.

A plausible future candidate, if public repetition remains high, is a narrowly named bundle for a complete sized coordinate space, for example type SizedCoord cs = (IsCoordList cs, AllSizedKnown cs). Consider it only after checking Haddock readability and downstream diagnostics. Do not alias All IsCoordLifted cs, AllSizedKnown cs, or arithmetic/equality preconditions merely because they often occur nearby. Keep inequalities and type equalities visible when they enforce Grid shape invariants.

TRADEOFFS
Pros: shorter signatures, one place to document the meaning of a capability, and less repeated API prose. Cons: ConstraintKinds is required for the declaration, error messages may report the alias instead of the failed leaf constraint, users may need to expand the alias, and changing the alias is a broad API change. A synonym does not create a class dictionary, improve type inference, discharge superclass relationships, or reduce runtime constraint dictionaries; it expands to the same tuple.

CURRENT GHC GUIDANCE
The current GHC User Guide section 6.10.3 says ConstraintKinds permits tuple constraints and type constraint synonyms, with type Stringy a = (Read a, Show a) as its example. It also notes that more exotic constraints in instance contexts require UndecidableInstances because type checking can loop. A normal tuple synonym in function signatures has no special runtime benefit.
Source: https://ghc.gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/doc/users_guide/exts/constraint_kind.html

DECISION CRITERIA
Before adding one, count public repetitions, test a representative downstream compile error with and without the alias, confirm that the name describes semantics rather than implementation, and verify that it does not over-constrain APIs that currently accept only AllSizedKnown or only IsCoordList. Prefer aliases in the owning public module, export them deliberately, and keep the expanded form in internal code where it improves local diagnosis.

This is a decision record only; no implementation is proposed by this issue.
design: No immediate code change. Revisit after the public API settles or when a concrete third-party signature demonstrates repetition. If implemented, add one alias with Haddock, migrate only a small set of public signatures, and compare `:info`/compiler diagnostics plus the downstream test suite. Reject the change if it obscures which evidence is needed or if the repetition is confined to internal code.
acceptance_criteria: A recorded decision distinguishes readability wins from evidence-solving claims, names the only plausible current candidate, preserves the separate AllSizedKnown/IsCoordList contracts, and defines a concrete threshold for revisiting implementation.
close_reason: Decision recorded: use constraint synonyms only for stable semantic capability bundles; keep distinct evidence and soundness constraints explicit.

title: Coord.Boundary enumerates the interior and not the boundary
description:
Data.Grid.Sized.Coord.Boundary gives the boundary predicates -- axisBoundary, axisBoundaries, onBoundary, isCorner -- and one enumerator, interiorCoords (Coord/Boundary.hs:47):

  interiorCoords = filter (not . onBoundary) allCoord

The other half of the same partition has no name, so the module named for boundaries hands back everything except the boundary. A caller writes filter onBoundary allCoord, which is the definition it would have had.

Proposed: boundaryCoords :: (IsCoordList cs) => [Coord cs], in allCoord order, defined as the complement of interiorCoords and exported beside it.

Worth stating in the Haddock, because it is the part that is not obvious: on a coord all of whose axes are Periodic the result is empty, not everything -- a torus has no ends, so no value reports an Extremum and interiorCoords is already the whole space. The two lists partition allCoord for every axis list, including that one.

Found by the sweep in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-30-boundary-policy-audit.md.

title: Path is not Offset: relative movement is order-dependent once a seam transforms the frame
description:
`Diff (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs)` is a displacement: one signed Int per
axis, added componentwise. That is the right representation for a flat space
and it is what the library has (Coord.hs:328).

It is NOT sufficient once a seam transforms the frame, and that is the
representation question sized-grid-448 has been blocked on.

THE PROBLEM

On a flat grid, `N` then `E` then `E` collapses to the displacement (+2, -1).
The order does not matter and neither does the route.

Cross a Mobius seam and it does. Going east twice and then north is not the
same as north then east twice, because the first east-crossing flipped what
"north" means. A displacement cannot record that; it has already summed.

So there are two distinct notions of relative movement and the library
currently has only one:

  Offset / Needle    Coord (MapDiff cs)      commutative, order-free.
                                             Correct exactly on the separable
                                             policies.

  Path               a sequence of steps      order-dependent. The steps are
                                             elementary moves, and each one is
                                             resolved -- and may transform the
                                             frame -- before the next is taken.

`coordRay` (Coord.hs:581) already walks step-by-step rather than summing, so
the library has a path-shaped operation without a path type. That is the hint
this is real: `coordRay c d` cannot be `c .+^ (n *^ d)` on anything with a
seam, and today it is only accidentally fine because nothing has a seam yet.

WHY THIS BLOCKS EVERYTHING ELSE

sized-grid-448 says a heading is "most naturally `Needle (Coord cs)` restricted
to unit steps". That is right on separable policies and wrong on the rest: on a
seam, a heading is not a needle, it is a needle PLUS the frame it is expressed
in. Which is the pair a path carries implicitly and a displacement discards.

So the order is:
    this issue (what is a relative movement?)
      -> the seam rule (what does an edge do to it?)
        -> sized-grid-448 (a walker that carries one)
          -> atlas (charts glued by seams)

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS

  * Do not throw the type-level dimensional structure away. Whatever a Path is,
    it is indexed by `cs` the way `Coord cs` is. A `[Direction]` over an
    untyped list would lose what the whole library is for.
  * A Path must collapse to an Offset where the space is flat, and that
    collapse should be the definition of "this policy is separable" -- which
    ties this back to the sibling issue and gives the separability claim an
    operational meaning rather than a descriptive one.
  * Watch the cost. The offset path is the measured hot path (see the
    unrolling notes in Coord/Class.hs); a Path representation that allocates
    per step would be a real regression for every existing caller. The likely
    answer is that Path is a separate type used only where a seam exists, and
    `Coord cs` keeps its displacement API untouched.
close_reason: Implemented Path cs (src/Data/Grid/Sized/Coord.hs): an ordered list of Diff (Coord cs) steps, with walkPath resolving them one at a time through offsetCoord and pathOffset giving the collapse to a single displacement. Documented precisely where the collapse holds (no wall interrupts) vs. where it doesn't yet (a seam transforming the frame, sized-grid-o1n, not implemented) vs. a third, orthogonal case that already existed (a wall blocking a route even when it doesn't block the net displacement -- demonstrated in tests/Test/Path.hs). Path carries an identity frame transform today since nothing produces anything else; it exists so o1n has somewhere to attach one. Unblocks o1n, sized-grid-yws (tracePath), sized-grid-448.

title: _WeakenedCoord: strengthen/weaken is a Prism at three levels, with a class-indexing wrinkle
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier B: a genuine Prism, at three
levels, and a friction point in how the classes are indexed.

The pattern is the same each time: widening is total, narrowing is checked,
and they agree on the overlap.

  Ordinal (Ordinal.hs:200, 202):
    strengthenOrdinal :: (KnownNat m, n <= m) => Ordinal n -> Ordinal m
    weakenOrdinal     :: KnownNat m => Ordinal n -> Maybe (Ordinal m)
      ==> _Strengthened :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat m, n <= m)
                        => Prism' (Ordinal m) (Ordinal n)

  Axis (Coord/Class.hs:88, 91):
    strengthenIsCoord :: (KnownNat m, n <= m) => c n -> c m
    weakenIsCoord     :: KnownNat m => c n -> Maybe (c m)
      ==> Prism' (c m) (c n) given n <= m

  Coord list (Coord.hs:811, 829):
    class WeakenCoord as bs where weakenCoord :: Coord as -> Maybe (Coord bs)
    class StrengthenCoord as bs where strengthenCoord :: Coord as -> Coord bs
      ==> _WeakenedCoord :: (StrengthenCoord as bs, WeakenCoord bs as)
                         => Prism' (Coord bs) (Coord as)

Laws: `weaken (strengthen c) = Just c` because strengthening does not change
the index, only the type's claim about its bound; and `weaken c = Just c'
==> strengthen c' = c` for the same reason. `strengthenOrdinal`'s own
Haddock states the argument: "i < n and n <= m give i < m".

== The friction, which should be recorded whether or not it is fixed here

The two classes are both indexed `as bs` meaning "from as to bs", so the
Prism needs `StrengthenCoord as bs` AND `WeakenCoord bs as` -- the same two
type lists in opposite orders in the two constraints. That reads badly and
will read worse at a call site with a type error in it.

Options, in order of preference:
  1. Leave the classes alone and eat the two-constraint signature. Cheapest,
     and the awkwardness is confined to one type signature in the library.
  2. Add a single `CoordEmbeds small big` class with both methods and a
     default implementation of each in terms of the existing classes. Better
     call sites, one more class in an API that already has a lot of them.
  3. Re-index one of the two classes. Breaking, and the current naming
     ("weaken as into bs") is defensible on its own terms.

Take (1) unless writing it makes a case for (2).

What it buys: `bigCoord ^? _WeakenedCoord` is "is this coordinate of the big
grid also a coordinate of the small one", which is the interesting half of
sub-grid work, and `review` is the embedding. Composes with `_Position`
(companion issue) to go straight from a raw index in one space to a coord in
another.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Implemented the requested lawful optics, renamed _WrappedCoord to _CoordAxes, and validated tests.

title: Named type aliases for common separable coord products (Torus, Cylinder, ...)
description: sized-grid-3u1's doc note on IsCoordList calls out that every product of separable axes is free: `'[Periodic 10, Clamped 5]` is a cylinder, `'[Periodic w, Periodic h]` a torus. Consider adding named type aliases in Coord.hs for the common cases (e.g. `type Torus w h = Coord '[Periodic w, Periodic h]`, `type Cylinder w h = Coord '[Periodic w, Clamped h]`) so callers can name the topology instead of spelling out the axis list. Pure sugar -- no new capability -- so scope and naming need a pass before committing to public API surface.
design:
Design discussion (2026-08-18), before implementing:

1. Alias the axis list (`cs :: [Type]`), not `Coord` directly.
   `Grid`, `FocusedGrid`, and `Coord` are all parametric over the same
   `cs :: [Type]` (see `GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a`, Internal/Grid.hs:162).
   aoc call sites spell out the axis list at `Grid`/`FocusedGrid`/`Coord`
   alike, so `type Torus w h = Coord '[...]` only sugars the minority of
   `Coord`-typed signatures. Prefer:

     type TorusAxes w h    = '[Periodic w, Periodic h]
     type CylinderAxes w h = '[Periodic w, Clamped h]

   so it drops into `Grid (TorusAxes w h) Cell`, `Coord (TorusAxes w h)`,
   `FocusedGrid (TorusAxes w h) Cell` uniformly.

2. Cylinder-style (mixed) names are inherently 2D-only and don't generalize.
   Past two axes, "which axes wrap" has to be stated per-axis anyway, which
   is exactly the axis list the alias was meant to save writing out. Don't
   imply a general pattern -- scope the mixed-product aliases explicitly to
   the 2-axis case in the haddock.

3. Torus *does* generalize to n dimensions (every axis periodic is a
   coherent n-torus, e.g. periodic boundary conditions in a 3D sim). If
   that's wanted, it needs a type family over a `[Nat]` list rather than a
   fixed 2-arg synonym:

     type family MapPeriodic (ns :: [Nat]) :: [Type] where ...
     type TorusAxesN ns = MapPeriodic ns

   This is more machinery than a plain `type` synonym -- treat it as a
   separate decision from the 2D aliases, not a default inclusion.

4. Naming convention still needs pinning down before committing to public
   API surface: for `CylinderAxes w h`, which parameter is the wrapping
   (circumference) axis and which is the clamped one? Document the
   convention explicitly wherever the alias is defined.

Net: scope this issue to the 2D axis-list aliases (TorusAxes/CylinderAxes)
as the concrete deliverable; the n-D torus type family is an optional
follow-on, not bundled in.
notes:
CHALLENGE TO THE 'PURE SUGAR -- NO NEW CAPABILITY' FRAMING, from sized-grid-lopy.3.

sokoban needed to ask whether a level solvable on a Mobius strip is still solvable on a cylinder of the same shape -- which is the test that separates a real topology puzzle from a level drawn on one. There was no way to say it. sokoban/src/Sokoban/Flat.hs is forty lines of Int arithmetic re-implementing move-and-push on a cylinder and on a rectangle, written because naming the topology is not the same as being able to run something on it.

The alias would not have helped. What the caller wanted was a cylinder it could STEP on, with the same algorithm it already had. So the aliases are worth having, and they are worth landing next to whatever sized-grid-xbms concludes about a surface abstraction, rather than on their own -- otherwise a caller who writes CylinderAxes w h has named the thing and still cannot use it.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
A reason these aliases could carry a property rather than only a name, if
wanted later. Recording it here rather than filing an issue, because it is
speculative and should not be built before a caller wants it.

Only Periodic's (.+^) is a total group action. Clamped/Reflective/Reflect101
are retractions: measured at n=7 over 567 (p,u,v), (p .+^ u) .+^ v ==
p .+^ (u+v) holds 567/567 for Periodic but 487/567, 407/567, 407/567 for the
others -- and 269/269 for all four when restricted to routes no wall
interrupts. See sized-grid-8nz for why this is forced by the Z^n/G structure
(translations descend to the quotient only when G commutes with them) and so
cannot be fixed.

That means TorusAxes is exactly the case where pathOffset fuses
unconditionally and step order does not matter, which is precisely what
tests/Test/Path.hs 'collapseTests' already checks on '[Periodic 5, Periodic 5]
and 'wallTests' shows failing on '[Clamped 5, Clamped 5].

If that distinction is ever wanted in a type rather than in a test, the shape
is an empty marker class, not a newtype and not a type synonym:

    class IsCoord c => Boundaryless c
    instance Boundaryless Periodic

It is the type-level form of Periodic's existing axisBoundaryIsCoord _ =
Nothing, costs nothing at run time, and is open to any future
translation-quotient axis. Then All Boundaryless cs on a fusion-dependent
signature means "summing the path first is safe", and TorusAxes satisfies it
by construction.

Two non-options, for the record:
  - A type synonym CANNOT carry a distinct instance. Verified on GHC 9.12.3:
    'type Torus n = Periodic n' plus separate instances for Torus and Periodic
    is rejected as "Duplicate instance declarations". Synonyms are transparent,
    so TypeSynonymInstances only lets you WRITE a synonym in an instance head;
    it resolves to the same instance and gives no discriminating power. This
    does not affect the aliases proposed in this issue, which are pure naming
    -- it only rules out hanging behaviour off them.
  - A newtype would work, but wraps the type that is already correct and adds
    coercion noise at every call site to express what the empty class
    expresses for free. Newtypes earn their keep when one representation needs
    two behaviours (Sum/Product); Periodic has one behaviour and it is the
    right one.

Not proposed now: ../aoc uses neither pathOffset nor walkPath, so nothing is
currently asking for the guarantee to be type-level.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Correction to the Boundaryless sketch in the comment above, and where it went.

The sketch's `All Boundaryless cs` does not typecheck with the class declared
at the container kind. IsCoord is indexed by Nat -> Type, but cs :: [Type]
holds Periodic 10, not Periodic. GHC 9.12.3:

    Couldn't match kind 'Nat -> *' with '*'
    Expected kind '[*]', but 'cs' has kind '[Nat -> *]'

The class has to sit at kind Type, mirroring the IsCoord / IsCoordLifted
split. A marker class has no methods with n quantified, so one lifted class
suffices -- no container-level twin is needed.

Also, the closing "nothing is currently asking for it" is not by itself a
reason to defer: the library is meant to serve consumers not yet thought of.
The property does earn its keep independent of ../aoc, because it changes a
type rather than only documenting one -- walkPath goes from Maybe (Coord cs)
to Coord cs on a boundaryless axis list.

Split out to sized-grid-2r3 with the corrected shape, its laws, and measured
evidence (3360/3360 fusion agreement at '[Periodic 5, Periodic 7]). This
issue stays scoped to the naming aliases; TorusAxes satisfies All Boundaryless
by construction and CylinderAxes does not, which is the sharpest thing those
aliases could come to mean.

title: Adopt ghc-typelits-natnormalise and ghc-typelits-knownnat to remove manual Nat proof plumbing
description:
The library currently discharges type-level arithmetic by hand with Data.Constraint.Nat
and, in places, unsafeCoerce.

Manual plumbing in the library:
  - src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:61  '\\ plusNat @n @1'
  - src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:68  '\\ leTrans @(x + 1) @n @m'
  - src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:79  '\\ plusMinusInverse3 @1 @m \\ minusNat @m @1'
  - src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:294-305  the whole AllSizedKnown class exists only to
    thread 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)' through timesNat

And it leaks all the way into user code. ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs:78-80 has to write:

    \\ plusNat @n @1
    \\ leTrans @1 @n @(n + 1)
    \\ plusMonotone2 @n @0 @1

and ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs:96-97 the same again via withDict. That is the library's
proof obligations showing up in a puzzle solution.

../aoc already depends on ghc-typelits-natnormalise and ghc-typelits-knownnat.
sized-grid does not. Adding

    ghc-options: -fplugin=GHC.TypeLits.Normalise -fplugin=GHC.TypeLits.KnownNat.Solver

discharges most 'KnownNat (n * m)', 'n <= n + 1' and 'n + 1 <= m' goals automatically.

Expected wins:
  - AllSizedKnown (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:294-305) likely disappears entirely, which
    simplifies the constraint on nearly every Grid function.
  - Callers stop needing KnownNat (n * n) in signatures -- cf. ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:33
    'parse :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => ...'
  - The unsound axioms in SizedGrid/Internal/Type.hs become unnecessary.

Caveat: plugins are a build-time dependency for *users* too if the constraints appear
in exported signatures. Measure how much of the public API simplifies before
committing. Do this before the Ordinal representation change -- it will make that
refactor much less painful.
close_reason: Merged to master (387cde5..ecd572f). Plugins adopted; the two hand-written Nat axioms (timesNat in the AllSizedKnown instance, plusNat @k @1 in reifyOrdinal) and the Data.Constraint.Nat imports are gone. Verified: nix flake check passes on GHC 9.12.3 and 9.14.1, 283 tests pass, the plugin-free example packages still build, and sized-grid builds under ../aoc's bare-ghc912 toolchain where cabal resolves natnormalise 0.9.6 / knownnat 0.8.4 / tcplugin-api 0.19.0.0 straight from Hackage. Public API unchanged: windowFits stays an asserted axiom (needs presburger) and AllSizedKnown stays (it is plugin-free induction, not plumbing). The predicted caller-side win is NOT achievable via plugins -- they are not transitive -- and is tracked as sized-grid-k6n.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
EVIDENCE AGAINST, from trying it during the wave-02 fixes (sized-grid-2h0 / sized-grid-px9).

Both plugins were added and then REMOVED again:

1. They did not solve the problem. The wanted was 'z <= y - n' from a given 'n + 1 <= x' plus 'x + z <= y + 1'. ghc-typelits-natnormalise does not use given <= premises to discharge wanted <= goals, so the error was unchanged ('Cannot satisfy: z <= y - m'). ghc-typelits-presburger is the plugin that does this, and it is marked BROKEN in nixpkgs.

2. They break GHC 9.14. ghc-typelits-natnormalise depends on ghc-tcplugins-extra, whose bound is 'ghc >=7.10 && <9.13'; with GHC 9.14.1 the nix build fails at configure with [Cabal-8010]. Since the flake checks both 9.12.3 and 9.14.1, adopting them would have cost 9.14 support outright.

What worked instead: restate constraints as additions rather than truncating Nat subtractions where possible ('x + z <= y + 1' not 'z <= y - x + 1'), and assert the residual existential facts in SizedGrid.Internal.Type.windowFits, in the same style as the pre-existing takeAddIsId.

Recommend this issue be reconsidered or closed unless presburger becomes usable AND ghc-tcplugins-extra gains a 9.14 bound. Retest before adopting.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
RETESTED 2026-08-09 as the previous comment asked. Both blockers still stand, and one
of them is worse than 'nixpkgs has not caught up'.

1. ghc-tcplugins-extra has NO GHC 9.14 release at all -- this is upstream, not a pin
   problem. Hackage's version list tops out at 0.5, whose bound is literally
   'ghc >=7.10 && <9.13', and whose tested-with stops at GHC 9.12.1. Reproduced the
   failure end to end by building the plugin against the 9.14 package set:

       Configuring ghc-tcplugins-extra-0.5...
       Error: [Cabal-8010]
       Encountered missing or private dependencies:
           ghc >=7.10 && <9.13 (installed: 9.14.1)

   ghc-typelits-natnormalise 0.7.12 and ghc-typelits-knownnat 0.7.13 both sit on top of
   it, so all three are unavailable on 9.14 together.

2. ghc-typelits-presburger 0.7.4.2 is still meta.broken = true in nixpkgs for both
   ghc912 and ghc914. It remains the only plugin that would discharge the actual wanted
   from the wave-02 work (a '<=' goal from '<=' givens); natnormalise does not do that.

Not a stale-pin excuse: flake.lock's nixpkgs is 2026-08-06, three days old.

Also ruling out the obvious workaround, so nobody spends time on it: adopting the
plugins only for GHC < 9.13 via 'if impl(ghc < 9.13)' in the cabal file does not work
for this library. The plugins do not simplify signatures by themselves -- they let us
WRITE simpler ones. Any signature written to depend on them would then fail to compile
on 9.14, so the public API would differ by compiler. That is not acceptable for a
library, and API simplification is the entire point of this issue.

Deferring rather than closing: the plan is sound the moment upstream moves. RETEST
CONDITION, both must hold:
  - a ghc-tcplugins-extra release accepting ghc >= 9.14 (check Hackage, not just
    nixpkgs), and
  - ghc-typelits-presburger no longer marked broken in nixpkgs.
Until then sized-grid-qh9 should proceed on its own option 2.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
RETESTED 2026-08-12. The deferral's blocker is gone -- it dissolved rather than being
fixed, so the stated retest condition never triggers as written.

The condition asked for "a ghc-tcplugins-extra release accepting ghc >= 9.14". That
will not happen and no longer matters: natnormalise 0.9 and knownnat 0.8 DROPPED
ghc-tcplugins-extra and moved to ghc-tcplugin-api. Current Hackage:

  ghc-typelits-natnormalise 0.9.6   ghc >=8.8.1 && <9.15   (was 0.7.12)
  ghc-typelits-knownnat     0.8.4   ghc >=8.0.1 && <9.17   (was 0.7.13)
  ghc-tcplugin-api          0.19.0.0

ghc-tcplugins-extra is still stuck at 0.5 / 'ghc <9.13', and presburger 0.7.4.2 is
still 'ghc <9.13' and still meta.broken in nixpkgs. Neither is on the path any more.

VERIFIED, not just read off Hackage: all three build against GHC 9.14.1, and the
library + tasty suite build and pass on 9.12.3 (283 tests) and 9.14.1. 'nix flake
check' covers both.

nixpkgs' hackage snapshot still ships the 0.7.x line for both compilers, so flake.nix
pins all three with callHackageDirect. Drop those overrides once nixpkgs ships
natnormalise >= 0.9.

DONE on branch worktree-natnormalise-h56 (commit 98b9a2c): plugins enabled in
'common lang', and the two hand-written axioms removed --
'timesNat' in the AllSizedKnown instance, 'plusNat @k @1' in 'reifyOrdinal' --
along with the Data.Constraint.Nat import in both modules. Library is warning-clean.

MEASURED, since this issue said to measure before committing: the public API
simplifies by nothing. One of the three predicted wins materialised, the smallest.

  1. AllSizedKnown does NOT disappear, and should not. Its instances are what derive
     'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)' inductively from per-axis KnownNats WITHOUT a
     plugin. Replacing it with a bare 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)' would push the
     plugin requirement onto every downstream package writing polymorphic grid code.
     The class is load-bearing, not plumbing.

  2. "Callers stop needing KnownNat (n * n)" is NOT achievable this way, at all.
     Type-checker plugins are not transitive: sized-grid enabling them affects only
     sized-grid's modules. ../aoc solves its own constraints and does NOT enable them
     (no 'typelits' in aoc.cabal, cabal.project or flake.nix -- the premise in this
     issue's description that it already depends on them is false). Filed
     sized-grid-k6n for the actual cause: AllGridSizeKnown is a type *family*, so it
     emits 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize ...)' at the call site instead of solving it.
     That fix needs no plugin.

  3. windowFits stays. Retested by deleting it: 'Cannot satisfy: z <= y - m' and
     'Cannot satisfy: m <= y', unchanged. Still presburger's job.

Also stale in the description: the '\\ plusNat @n @1 \\ leTrans ...' plumbing cited at
../aoc/src/2024/04.hs:78-80 is already gone -- the wave-02 work removed it.

RECOMMENDATION: merge is a judgment call, and a close one. For it: two hand-written
Nat axioms and a proof-axiom dependency surface go away, and future Nat work gets
easier. Against it: three hand-pinned Hackage overrides to carry until nixpkgs
catches up, in exchange for zero public-API simplification. The concrete pain this
issue was filed about is sized-grid-k6n, which is independent of the plugins.

title: Demo: HashLife, with a quadtree node that is a Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2]
description:
A HashLife demo executable alongside `maze/`, `automata/`, `gameOfLife/` and `ising-example/`, asking the question those demos ask: does `Grid` work as a *recursive node payload*?

Gosper's HashLife represents the universe as a hash-consed quadtree, each node memoising "2^k generations forward for a 2^(k+1) square" from its four half-size children, so repeated substructure costs nothing after the first computation and a repetitive pattern can be skipped forward exponentially.

The library-facing observation that motivates the demo: a quadtree node **is** a `Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2] (Node (k-1))`. The recursive type is a level-indexed newtype whose payload is an ordinary library value, so this exercises `Grid` at 2x2 shapes, nested, in a way nothing else in the repo does.

Sketch:

    data Node (k :: Nat) where
      Leaf  :: !Bool -> Node 0
      Quad  :: !(Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2] (Node k)) -> Node (k + 1)

plus a hash-cons table keyed on node identity, and `step :: Node (k+1) -> Node k` memoised per node.

Scope boundaries, decided in sized-grid-i0ob.1:

- This is a demo executable, NOT a library module and not a separate package. HashLife uses nothing else of the library: its universe is unbounded so there is no boundary policy, there is no `Coord` arithmetic, and `Stencil` appears only at the leaf. It is not a feature of `grid-sized` under any framing.
- The `unsafePerformIO`-backed memo table stays quarantined inside the executable. The library stays pure and total; that was the real objection to putting HashLife anywhere near `Grid`/`Atlas`.
- Not a child of sized-grid-i0ob: that epic tracks concept gaps in the grid abstraction, and the conclusion of i0ob.1 is that HashLife is not one.

Cost, stated honestly: hash-consing, node canonicalisation and the level-indexed `Node k` GADT are a few days of work, not an afternoon. File is P3 because the value is exploratory, not because the work is small.

Two things it would force out of the abstract, which is most of why it is worth building:

- `Hashable`/`Ord` for `Grid` (sized-grid-g4xz) would get answered by a real consumer instead of in principle -- hash-consing needs both.
- sized-grid-i0ob.2 bites this directly: `offsetCoord` does not typecheck on an `Ordinal` axis, so a `Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2]` node cannot be stepped in today.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A runnable executable in the repo's demo style, with a ChangeLog.md, showing at least one pattern advanced by a large generation count that a naive stepper could not reach in comparable time. 2. The memo table and any unsafePerformIO are confined to the demo; grid-sized itself gains no impure dependency. 3. The quadtree node is a Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2] (Node k), or the writeup says concretely why that shape did not work -- a negative answer here is a real finding about the library. 4. Whatever instances hash-consing needed from Grid are reported back to sized-grid-g4xz, with the shape actually used.

title: Six benchmarks diverge from the checked-in laptop baseline on unmodified source; the baseline's numbers for them were never real work
description:
Found while measuring sized-grid-adr.14 on 2026-08-19. Not caused by that change: the divergence reproduces with adr.14's diff stashed out, and again on a full 'cabal clean' rebuild.

Running the suite at 689e9e8 -- the commit that recorded bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv, and the same source that recorded it -- six lines do not match the CSV. Allocation, which bench/README.md says does not drift:

                                                    baseline        today
  (.-.) x10000, Clamped 100x100 (coord list shared)       17 B     1.04 MB
  toEnum/fromEnum x300, Clamped 300                    31.2 KB     57.6 KB
  fmap 300x300 [no coord at all]                          32 B     4.32 MB
  index x90000, 300x300 (coord list shared)               48 B     7.92 MB
  mapGrid then sum 300x300   boxed                        32 B     4.32 MB
  mapGrid then sum 300x300 unboxed                        20 B    720.1 KB

Time moved with allocation on three of them and not on the others:

  fmap 300x300                     0.316 ms  ->  1.500 ms
  mapGrid then sum boxed           0.316 ms  ->  1.484 ms
  index x90000                     0.743 ms  ->  1.493 ms
  (.-.) x10000                     0.066 ms  ->  0.136 ms
  mapGrid then sum unboxed         0.092 ms  ->  0.088 ms   (same time, 20 B -> 720 KB)
  toEnum/fromEnum x300             0.006 ms  ->  0.007 ms

Which way is wrong is not in doubt. 'nf (fmap (+1)) bigGrid' over 90,000 boxed Ints cannot allocate 32 bytes. 4.32 MB is about 48 B a cell, which is what the work costs; 32 B is the signature of GHC floating the whole expression out of the benchmarked function and the harness timing a shared result. The baseline is the side that is not measuring anything, and today's numbers are the honest ones. bench/Main.hs already documents this exact hazard for the stencil radius benchmarks ('as a literal GHC floats mooreStencil 1 out ... and what gets measured is the step alone under a label claiming otherwise'), so it has bitten this suite before.

Two things to find out, in order:

1. What stopped the floating. The source is identical, so it is the environment: a GHC or dependency version different from the one that recorded the CSV, or the CSV having been recorded from a build with non-default flags. 'mapGrid then sum unboxed' is the clue -- its time did not change at all while its allocation went from 20 B to 720 KB, which reads like a measurement/accounting difference rather than a code one, while fmap's 4.7x says the opposite. Both patterns in one run need explaining.

2. Whether the five affected benchmarks should be rewritten so they cannot float in the first place, the way the stencil radius ones were (take the input as an argument the harness varies rather than a CAF). A benchmark whose recorded number is 32 B is not guarding anything.

Until this is settled, treat those six lines of the baseline as unusable. The rest of the CSV was reproduced exactly.
notes:
INVESTIGATED 2026-08-19.

Part 1, what stopped the floating: bisected via git log on the CSV file.
689e9e8's checked-in baseline has the six small/fake numbers this issue
opened with (17 B, 32 B, 48 B, 20 B ...). The very next baseline
re-record, at 537bca4 (closes adr.14, "Make unsafeOrdinal's range check
free"), already has today's honest numbers. A fresh build of current
HEAD reproduces the checked-in CSV for all six lines to within 3%
(verified: cabal build + a --csv run against
bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv, all 57 benchmarks pass
--fail-if-slower 25). So the checked-in baseline is NOT stale -- the
divergence this issue found was specific to reproducing the OLD commit
689e9e8 against its OWN period CSV; current HEAD's CSV is trustworthy.

I could not pin the exact GHC mechanism further. Tried reintroducing
just unsafeOrdinal's old `assert`-based check (adr.14's own diagnosis:
assert desugars to opaque assertError, forcing boxing and blocking
inlining) in isolation, on top of today's tree, and rebuilt -- that did
NOT reproduce the float, so "assert vs guard" alone isn't the trigger;
whatever tipped GHC's decision at 537bca4 is more diffuse than that one
function. Not pursued further -- the cost of a real bisection (several
full -O2 library rebuilds per candidate commit) wasn't worth it once
part 1's actual question (is the current baseline usable) was answered
yes.

What IS certain, and is the actionable finding: tasty-bench's own
source documents this exact hazard class. From Test/Tasty/Bench.hs
(funcToBench, ~line 1359): "GHC ... does not notice that `f` and `x`
arguments are loop invariant and could be floated, and the whole `f x`
expression shared" -- UNLESS it does, which is exactly what happened
to these six. All six share one shape: `nf f x` (or `whnf f x`) where
both f and x are fully static (a top-level CAF grid, or a bare
integer/coord literal) -- structurally identical to the mooseStencil
radius hazard already documented and fixed elsewhere in bench/Main.hs,
just tripped by an unrelated inlining-threshold change instead of a
literal-vs-argument mistake.

Part 2, fix: wrapped all six in `env (pure <shared value>) $ \x -> ...`,
pushing the value through tasty-bench's withResource/unsafePerformIO
boundary, which GHC's simplifier does not see through -- this is
tasty-bench's own documented idiom for exactly this ("consider forcing
its evaluation separately, e.g. via env or withResource"). env doesn't
add a name segment, so --baseline matching by name is unaffected.
Verified: full `cabal test all` (589+ tests, all suites) passes, full
benchmark suite (57/57) passes --fail-if-slower 25 against the existing
checked-in CSV with no baseline re-record needed -- the six wrapped
lines report the same honest numbers as before wrapping, within noise.

This is a structural mitigation, not a proof: it removes the top-level-
CAF/literal shape that this hazard needs, using the mechanism
tasty-bench itself relies on to prevent it, but I can't produce a
GHC-internals guarantee that no future change could still tip some
other benchmark in this file the same way. Worth remembering as a
pattern for adr.5/adr.8 or any new benchmark that applies a function to
nothing but a shared grid and a literal.

title: State the odd-extent precondition for windows, with the centre coordinate
description:
Window-shaped operations only make sense when every extent is odd: a window
with an even side has no centre cell, so there is no coordinate for the focus
to sit at. Today nothing states that. gridTiles and the neighbourhood
functions either work it out at the call site or quietly produce something
off-centre.

Prior art: Chris Penner's 'grids' states it as a class with the precondition
attached, in Data.Grid.Internal.Shapes:

  type Even n = Mod n 2 == 0
  type Odd  n = Not (Even n)
  type OddC n = Odd n ?! 'Text "Dimension '" ':<>: 'ShowType n
                      ':<>: 'Text " must be odd to use 'neighbouring' functions"

  class Centered (dims :: [Nat]) where
    centerCoord :: Coord dims

So the class both supplies the centre coordinate and refuses, with a sentence
rather than an unsolved Nat goal, to instantiate at an even extent.

Two things to keep and one to drop:
  KEEP the pairing of the precondition with the thing it guards. A standalone
       'isOdd' constraint that callers must remember is worth much less than
       a class you cannot obtain without it.
  KEEP the error text naming the offending dimension via ShowType.
  DROP the OVERLAPPING/OVERLAPPABLE instance pair. We have SList and the
       IsCoordList machinery and should fold over the axes the way the rest
       of the library does, which also keeps it consistent with the unrolling
       work in sized-grid-5uq.

Depends on sized-grid-0kq for the '?!' operator; the natural consumer is the
neighbourhood decomposition issue and sized-grid-7gs.
notes: Correction to the description's last line: sized-grid-7gs is CLOSED, not pending -- it delivered neighbours/mooreNeighbours/vonNeumannNeighbours already. So the odd-extent precondition is not blocking new work there; it is a precision upgrade to an API that already ships, and its live consumer is sized-grid-meg. Also relevant: sized-grid-3t6 (sliding windows, stride 1), which wants the same precondition.
close_reason: Landed: Odd/Even/OddC in Data.Grid.Sized.Coord.Class (via ?!), and centreCoord/CentredAxis in Data.Grid.Sized.Coord, folding over the axis list with the same hcpure/IsCoordLifted shape zeroCoord uses -- no OVERLAPPING/OVERLAPPABLE instances. Tests in tests/Test/Neighbours.hs (centredTests). Manually verified the readable compile error: centreCoord :: Coord '[Clamped 4] -> "Dimension '4' must be odd to have a centre coordinate". Unblocks sized-grid-meg.

description: gh run 32794285516: all cabal jobs (9.10.1/9.12.3/9.14.1) and the bench job fail at src/Data/Grid/Sized/Internal/Grid.hs:303 with 'Could not deduce semialign-1.4:Data.Semialign.Internal.Unzip (Grid cs)'. semialign 1.4 reordered the class hierarchy so Unzip sits directly above Functor and is now a superclass of Semialign. grid-sized.cabal allows semialign >=1.3 && <1.5, so CI picks up 1.4.
