title: Concept gaps in the grid abstraction
description: This epic tracks the library’s major conceptual gaps: boundary-aware checked movement, general grid-view wrappers, and walker/path semantics around FocusedGrid. These are not isolated helper requests; they are different faces of the same design question: what is the conceptual vocabulary of a grid library once the coordinate type encodes the boundary policy? The concrete issues under this epic should determine whether the library needs explicit checked movement, first-class view/wrapper abstractions, and a coherent path or context model for focused traversal.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Review the design thesis and the library API for conceptual mismatches. 2. Confirm which concept gaps are true missing abstractions versus intentional omissions. 3. Determine whether a common design vocabulary should be introduced. 4. Close the epic only after the sub-issues converge on an explicit library direction.
close_reason:
Converged. Both children closed and the direction is explicit, recorded in the library's own documentation rather than only in an issue.

The answer to the epic's question -- what is the conceptual vocabulary of a grid library once the coordinate type encodes the boundary policy -- is that the vocabulary already existed at the Coord layer and was complete; what was wrong was how three things were typed on top of it. None of the three suspected gaps turned out to need a new abstraction.

1. Boundary-aware checked movement (sized-grid-i0ob.2, P1). Not missing: mis-indexed. offsetCoord and everything on it took Diff, an affine notion, when a checked step needs only a per-axis bounds check. That excluded Ordinal, the one axis every restriction produces, so a window was a grid nothing could move in -- while the plural neighbours/stepsWithin worked on it all along. Fixed by MapStep. One type family, no new class, no new type, and no call site changed here or in ../aoc.

2. General grid-view wrappers (sized-grid-d9o9, closed). Two families, not one: a restriction destroys the boundary policy, a pointing preserves it. That is a rule about existing return types, stated in the README thesis and enforced by sized-grid-mbh0, not a wrapper type.

3. Walker/path semantics (sized-grid-ylhl, closed). The model is a 2x2 -- checked/total x step/route -- and Coord fills every cell. The pointing layer adds no semantics; it lifts three operations and two of them discard the position. Countable gap, mechanical fix: sized-grid-qbal, now unblocked.

So: no common design vocabulary needed introducing. The one that decides everything -- an operation that can leave the space is either total because the type licenses it, or it returns Maybe -- was already the README's first rule, and every finding here was that rule applied at a place it had not been. i0ob.2's negative half is the same rule read the other way and is now a compile-fail test: (.+^) and stepWalker still refuse Ordinal, deliberately.

Also settled: HashLife is not a concept gap (sized-grid-i0ob.1) -- it is a demo, sized-grid-h6ki, using nothing of the library but Grid as a quadtree node's payload.

Open work that inherits the direction rather than blocking it: sized-grid-qbal (lift the checked vocabulary through FocusedGrid and Walker), sized-grid-xmxm, sized-grid-6glh, sized-grid-3ybi, sized-grid-43zv.

title: Research: recursive/HashLife-style Game of Life — feasibility with current abstractions
description: Prompted by: 'would a recursive Game of Life be cool/easy with what we have — MonadFix or not?' Surveyed the current abstractions (Grid, FocusedGrid, Stencil, Atlas) against three readings of 'recursive Game of Life' and recorded feasibility for each. See design notes for the full writeup.
design:
Current state:
- Grid cs a: Representable/Distributive/Applicative/Monad over a fixed, type-level-sized (Nat) shape; tabulate/index are total.
- FocusedGrid cs a: Comonad + ComonadStore. duplicate builds a Grid cs (FocusedGrid cs a) — already a 'grid of grids', and extend is exactly the comonadic n-generations-at-once Life step (see bench/Main.hs iterateExtend). This already IS a recursive/self-similar structure in the comonad sense.
- Stencil: precomputed neighbour-offset table, the fast bulk-step path the real gameOfLife/Main.hs demo uses instead of extend.
- Atlas cs k a: a flat vector of k same-shape charts glued by a seam table (topology, not hierarchy) — no atlas-of-atlases, no multi-resolution nesting.
- No MonadFix, mfix, unsafeInterleaveIO, or knot-tying pattern anywhere in the repo today.

Three readings of 'recursive Game of Life', and feasibility:

1. HashLife (Gosper's algorithm): universe as a hash-consed quadtree of quadtrees, each node memoizing '2^k generations forward for a 2^(k+1) square' from its four half-size children, so repeated substructure is O(1) after first computation. This is the canonical meaning of 'recursive Game of Life'.
   - Fit: medium-hard. Grid/Coord are monomorphic-shaped per type (Nat-indexed), not a genuinely recursive sum type. HashLife needs (a) a recursive node type indexed by level, e.g. data QuadNode n = Leaf a | Node (QuadNode (n-1)) (QuadNode (n-1)) (QuadNode (n-1)) (QuadNode (n-1)), and (b) a hash-consing/memo table (StableName- or content-hash-keyed, backed by an IORef/HashMap) so identical subtrees are shared and 'step' is memoized per node. That memo table is inherently effectful under the hood (unsafePerformIO-backed memoization is how every real Haskell HashLife implementation does it), which is a different engineering posture from the rest of this library, which is scrupulously pure and total. Atlas's seam machinery solves a different problem (surface topology) and doesn't give hierarchy for free. Conclusion: not a small addition — a legitimate new module/package (grid-hashlife?) reusing Coord/Stencil only at the leaf/base case, not a Grid-shaped feature.

2. Self-referential single-pass step ('does MonadFix help?'): a boxed Grid can already be tied in a knot with ordinary laziness — tabulate on a boxed vector produces lazy thunks per cell even though the vector spine is strict, so `fix (\g -> tabulate (rule g))`-shaped definitions work today with plain fix/let, no MonadFix required. MonadFix only earns its keep when the recursive value must be produced *inside* a monadic action (e.g. mfix over ST/IO to build a mutable circular structure while it's still being filled). The actual demo (gameOfLife/Main.hs) runs on UGrid (Data.Vector.Unboxed), which cannot hold thunks at all — Stencil/applyRule exists precisely because the fast path gives up self-reference for cache-friendliness. So: MonadFix is not the missing abstraction; the real fork is boxed-and-lazy (self-reference already works, no new machinery) vs unboxed-and-strict (self-reference is impossible by construction, independent of MonadFix). A genuine MonadFix use case — mutably knot-tying an STUArray/MVector while filling it — would live under sized-grid-0h4u (open: 'Investigate mutable or in-place execution for UGrid'), not here.

3. Meta-Life / Life-in-Life (a cell's state IS another Life pattern, OTCA-metapixel style): needs no new abstraction — a cell type of Grid cs' Bool and two independent applyRule calls at different cadences already does this today. Not a hard research question, more a worked example/demo.

Recommendation: the interesting, non-trivial one is (1) HashLife; (2)'s real answer is 'already possible on boxed Grid, blocked by design on UGrid, and not a MonadFix question'; (3) needs no new work. If HashLife is wanted, treat it as a new, separate module rather than an extension of Grid/Atlas, since its core trick (hash-consing + memoization) is a different engineering discipline from the rest of the library.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Decision recorded on whether to pursue HashLife as a new module/package vs. leave as a documented non-goal. 2. MonadFix conclusion (not the blocker; boxed-vs-unboxed representation is) is captured for future readers hitting the same question. 3. If pursued, a follow-up spike/prototype issue is filed for a minimal QuadNode + memoized step, scoped separately from Grid/Atlas.
notes:
Decided. Both halves of this issue are answered, one by argument and one by experiment.

AC1 -- HashLife: pursue as a DEMO EXECUTABLE, not a library module and not a separate package.

The framing in the design notes above ("a legitimate new module/package, grid-hashlife?") is wrong in one detail that changes the answer: a quadtree node IS a `Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2] (Node (k-1))`. The recursive node type is a level-indexed newtype whose payload is already a library value, so the "Grid is not a genuinely recursive sum type" objection is about the wrong layer -- nobody needs `Grid` to be recursive, they need it to be a node's payload.

What that reframing does NOT change: HashLife uses nothing else of the library. Its universe is unbounded, so there is no boundary policy; there is no `Coord` arithmetic; `Stencil` appears only at the leaf. So it is not a feature of this library under any framing.

What it IS good for is a probe: does `Grid` work as a recursive node payload at all? That is the same kind of question `maze/` asks about focus-as-carving-head and `automata/` asks about total-vs-checked rules, and it is answered the same way -- by building the thing. A demo also quarantines the `unsafePerformIO` memo table inside an executable, so the library stays pure and total, which was the real objection.

Cost, stated honestly rather than as "medium-hard": hash-consing, node canonicalisation and the level-indexed `Node n` GADT are a few days, not an afternoon.

Follow-up filed per AC3 (see below). It is deliberately not a child of sized-grid-i0ob: the epic tracks concept gaps in the grid abstraction, and the conclusion here is that HashLife is not one.

AC2 -- MonadFix: not the missing abstraction, on either side of the boxed/unboxed line. Three findings, each checked rather than argued.

1. Knot-tying already works on a boxed `Grid` with plain `fix`. `tabulateGrid` is `VG.generate` and boxed `Data.Vector` is spine-strict but element-lazy, so every cell is a thunk that may read any other cell. Pascal's triangle, cross-cell recursion, no `mfix` and no `RecursiveDo`:

    pascal = fix $ \g -> tabulate $ \c ->
        let up   = index g <$> offsetCoord c (deltaFromTuple (-1,0))
            left = index g <$> offsetCoord c (deltaFromTuple (0,-1))
        in case (up, left) of
             (Nothing, Nothing) -> 1
             _                  -> fromMaybe 0 up + fromMaybe 0 left
    -- Grid '[Clamped 6, Clamped 6] Integer
    -- [1,1,1,1,1,1, 1,2,3,4,5,6, 1,3,6,10,15,21, 1,4,10,20,35,56, ...]

2. A `MonadFix (Grid cs)` instance is free -- `Grid cs` is `Representable`, so it inherits the reader instance, `mfix f = tabulate (\c -> fix (\a -> index (f a) c))`. But that is a PER-CELL fixpoint: each cell ties a knot with itself, and it cannot express Pascal, whose recursion is cross-cell. So the recursion `MonadFix` licenses is the one nobody wants and the one people want is already served by plain `fix`. The instance is still worth having as a law-completing one-liner, with a Haddock note saying exactly this, or someone will reach for `mdo` expecting cross-cell recursion. Recorded on sized-grid-g4xz, not here.

3. `mfix` over `ST` does not rescue the unboxed case. `fixST` ties the knot on the RETURNED VALUE, not on the mutable buffer -- reading a cell already written is an ordinary `MV.read` needing no `mfix`. The one thing `mfix` buys is the ability to store a reference to the not-yet-existing result, and storing a reference is exactly what an unboxed vector cannot do: `UM.write` forces its argument to a machine word, which forces the knot before it is tied.

Measured, same program twice, filling front-to-back where each cell depends on a LATER cell so the knot is load-bearing:

    boxed   mfix/ST: [6,5,4,3,2,1]
    unboxed mfix/ST: <<loop>>

(`Data.Vector.Mutable` vs `Data.Vector.Unboxed.Mutable`, GHC 9.12.3, -O0, `NonTermination` caught. Note the failure is blackhole detection, not a guarantee -- other shapes hang instead of reporting `<<loop>>`.)

So: for unboxed grids -- the entire point of sized-grid-0h4u -- `mfix` is unavailable in principle, and self-reference is not a thing 0h4u can deliver by trying harder. For boxed grids `mfix`/`ST` works but buys nothing over finding 1, while adding a real hazard: one stray `seq`, bang or strict fold anywhere in the fill turns a working program into a runtime `<<loop>>` with no type error.

The strict counterpart of the pattern is already in the library. `scanAxis`/`scanl1Grid` are staging rather than knot-tying -- write in an order where dependencies are already resolved and read them back -- which is total, unboxed-safe, and per Internal/Grid/Axis.hs:322 "a single in-order pass over the grid and one allocation", 1.6x boxed / 2.2x unboxed over the hand-fused transpose pipeline. Anything expressible as a staged pass belongs there. Anything not so expressible is a true cyclic dependency, which is not a fill but an iteration to a fixed point: `iterate`/`extend`, not `mfix`.

The only knot that would genuinely earn its keep is a linked-neighbour cell type (each cell holding direct references to its four neighbours). That trades away the flat row-major representation every fast path depends on -- `index` becomes pointer-chasing instead of arithmetic -- and it does not need `ST` either, since plain `fix` over a boxed `tabulate` builds it.

AC3 -- follow-up filed: see the discovered-from link.

Also discovered while checking finding 1: `offsetCoord` and everything built on it does not typecheck on an `Ordinal` axis at all, which is a thesis-vs-API mismatch in its own right and the strongest concept gap this epic was looking for. Filed as sized-grid-i0ob.2 (P1). It bites HashLife too -- a `Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2]` node inherits the same hole.
close_reason: Decided. HashLife: a demo executable (sized-grid-h6ki), not a library module or package -- a quadtree node is a Grid '[Ordinal 2, Ordinal 2] (Node k), but HashLife uses nothing else of the library and its memo table stays quarantined in an executable. MonadFix: not the missing abstraction on either side of the boxed/unboxed line -- cross-cell knot-tying already works with plain fix on a boxed Grid (Pascal, verified); the free Representable MonadFix instance is a per-cell fixpoint that cannot express it (noted on g4xz); and mfix over ST does not rescue the unboxed case, verified by experiment (boxed [6,5,4,3,2,1], unboxed <<loop>>), because fixST ties the returned value while UM.write forces it. scanAxis/scanl1Grid are already the strict, unboxed-safe staging counterpart. Discovered en route: sized-grid-i0ob.2 (P1).

title: Ordinal has no checked step, so nothing can move inside a window
description:
The README's design thesis says a restriction narrows its axis to `Ordinal` because that is "the policy-free axis, with no walls and no wrap, whose off-grid step is `Nothing` rather than an invented answer" (README.md, "A restriction destroys the boundary policy"; the same sentence is in the `$windows` Haddock in src/Data/Grid/Sized.hs).

That step does not exist. No checked movement operation typechecks on a coord containing an `Ordinal` axis, so the capability the window's own type is chosen to promise is unreachable.

Reproduced in `cabal repl lib:grid-sized`:

    ghci> :t offsetCoord (zeroCoord :: Coord '[Ordinal 5, Ordinal 5])
    error: [GHC-18872]
      Couldn't match type 'Data.AffineSpace.Diff (Ordinal 5)' with 'Int'
        arising from a use of 'offsetCoord'

    ghci> :t coordRay (zeroCoord :: Coord '[Ordinal 5, Ordinal 5])
    error: [GHC-18872]
      Couldn't match type 'Data.AffineSpace.Diff (Ordinal 5)' with 'Int'
        arising from a use of 'coordRay'

Cause: every checked operation carries `AllDiffSame Int cs` (src/Data/Grid/Sized/Coord/Class/List.hs:44), and `MapDiff` is defined as `Diff x ': MapDiff xs` (List.hs:37-39). `Diff` is the associated type of `AffineSpace`, and `Ordinal` deliberately has no `AffineSpace` instance -- Class/Axis.hs:58 states the reason: "`Ordinal` has no affine action because it cannot leave its interval." So `Diff (Ordinal n)` is stuck and the constraint can never discharge.

Affected (everything that routes through `offsetCoord`): `offsetCoord`, `coordRay`, `offsetCoordUpTo`, `walkPath`, `walkPathTotal`, `traceOffset`, `tracePath`, `walkEverywhere`.

The inconsistency is visible from inside the library. `neighbours`/`mooreNeighbours`/`vonNeumannNeighbours`/`stepsWithin` need only `IsCoordList` and work correctly on `Ordinal` today:

    ghci> neighbours (zeroCoord :: Coord '[Ordinal 5, Ordinal 5])
    [Coord [Ordinal (0/5), Ordinal (1/5)],Coord [Ordinal (1/5), Ordinal (0/5)],Coord [Ordinal (1/5), Ordinal (1/5)]]

Three neighbours at the corner, correctly bounded. The plural works; the singular does not compile.

User impact: `gridWindows :: GridOf v (big : rest) a -> [GridOf v (Ordinal n : rest) a]`. Window a `Periodic 9` grid and you cannot take one checked step inside the result -- not even the step that stays in bounds. Same for `shrinkGrid`, `gridTiles`, `takeGrid`, `dropGrid`, `sliceGrid`, `splitHigherDim` and the `slice`/`prefix`/`suffix` lenses, all of which narrow to `Ordinal` by the same rule.

This is a thesis-vs-API mismatch rather than a missing feature: the per-axis capability is already implemented and already correct. `IsCoord`'s `offsetIsCoord :: (KnownNat n, 1 <= n) => c n -> Int -> Maybe (c n)` (Class/Axis.hs:84) takes a plain `Int`, and its default `offsetByPosition` (Class/Axis.hs:117) is a pure bounds check that works on `Ordinal` unchanged. Only the `Coord`-level constraint is wrong.
design:
Diagnosis: checked movement is typed in terms of `Diff`, which is an *affine* (total-movement) notion, when what it actually needs is "one signed step count per axis". `offsetIsCoord` already says so -- its displacement is `Int`, not `Diff (c n)`. `MapDiff` is the right index for `(.+^)`, which genuinely requires the affine action; it is the wrong index for `offsetCoord`, which requires only a bounds check the axis already knows how to do.

Proposed fix, to be confirmed by the spike in AC2: give the checked operations their own displacement family, mapping every axis to `Int`:

    type family MapStep cs where
      MapStep '[]       = '[]
      MapStep (x ': xs) = Int ': MapStep xs

and index checked displacements by `Delta (MapStep cs)` instead of `Delta (MapDiff cs)`, dropping `AllDiffSame Int cs` from those signatures.

Why this is expected to be close to source-compatible: `Delta` is indexed by the displacement list directly, not derived from `cs`. Every call site that compiles today does so under `AllDiffSame Int cs`, i.e. with `MapDiff cs` already reduced to a list of `Int` -- so `Delta (MapStep cs)` and `Delta (MapDiff cs)` are the *same type* at every currently-valid instantiation. `Automata.Ant`'s heading is already written as `Delta '[Int, Int]` with a `MapDiff cs ~ '[Int, Int]` constraint, which is the shape this change makes unnecessary rather than breaking. Verify against ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs, which uses `coordRay` and `offsetCoord` directly.

Deliberately out of scope, and why:

- `(.+^)`, `walkPathTotal`, `transportCoord` and `stepWalker` keep `AffineSpace`/`MapDiff`. Those are *total* movement, which is licensed by the axis type having an affine action; excluding `Ordinal` from them is the thesis working correctly, not a bug.
- That leaves `Walker` with no checked step, so a walker cannot exist on a grid with an `Ordinal` axis at all ("the ant that walks off the board" is inexpressible). That is a separate gap in the movement vocabulary; it belongs to sized-grid-ylhl, not here.
- Giving `Ordinal` an `AffineSpace` instance is rejected: `(.+^)` would have to clamp or throw, and clamping on the one axis whose whole purpose is to have no policy is exactly the silent-clamp the thesis forbids.
acceptance_criteria: 1. offsetCoord, coordRay, offsetCoordUpTo, walkPath, traceOffset, tracePath and walkEverywhere all typecheck and behave correctly on a coord with one or more Ordinal axes. 2. A spike confirms whether the MapStep change is source-compatible for every in-repo call site and for ../aoc; if it is not, the breakage is enumerated before the change lands. 3. A test walks inside a gridWindows result: a window of a Periodic source steps in bounds and returns Nothing at the window's own edge, never wrapping to the source's policy. 4. A test asserts the negative half: (.+^) and stepWalker still do not typecheck on an Ordinal axis. 5. README and the $windows Haddock claim about Ordinal's off-grid step is true as written once this lands.
close_reason:
Landed. Checked movement is indexed by MapStep (one signed Int per axis) instead of MapDiff (the affine Diff per axis), so it asks each axis only for the bounds check offsetIsCoord already provides -- and Ordinal, which has no affine action, can now be stepped.

Changed: MapStep added in Coord/Class/List.hs and exported through Coord.Class and Data.Grid.Sized.Coord; IsCoordList's posOffset re-indexed and its AllDiffSame Int cs obligation dropped; offsetCoord, offsetCoordUpTo, coordRay, Path, walkPath, pathOffset, traceOffset, tracePath and walkEverywhere all follow. walkPathTotal keeps (.+^) and so gains one explicit MapDiff cs ~ MapStep cs -- the seam between the checked and total halves, free at any concrete axis list, unstatable at an abstract one because neither family reduces there.

AC1: verified in the repl on Coord '[Ordinal 5, Ordinal 5]'. offsetCoord's displacement reports as Delta [Int, Int], exactly as the design predicted; all seven functions typecheck and answer correctly.

AC2: source-compatible, as predicted. title: Replace CoordDiff's per-arity tuple family with a manifolds-style Needle
description:
Inspiration: the `manifolds` package (Justus Sagemuller), `Semimanifold`'s associated
`Needle` type.

    class AdditiveGroup (Needle x) => Semimanifold x where
      type Needle x :: Type
      (.+~^) :: x -> Needle x -> x

`Needle` is an associated type, and products get theirs structurally:
`Needle (a,b) = (Needle a, Needle b)`, from the pair instance. There is no arity
ceiling and no per-arity boilerplate.

sized-grid does the opposite. src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:204-215 declares CoordDiff by hand,
one `type instance` per arity:

    type instance CoordDiff '[]              = ()
    type instance CoordDiff '[a]             = Identity (Diff a)
    type instance CoordDiff '[a, b]          = (Diff a, Diff b)
    ... up to ...
    type instance CoordDiff '[a, b, c, d, e, f] = (Diff a, ..., Diff f)

Seven instances, so six dimensions. THE CEILING IS REAL: a `Coord` of seven or more axes
has no `CoordDiff` instance, therefore `Diff (Coord cs)` is stuck, therefore no
`AffineSpace (Coord cs)` instance and no `offsetCoord`. The user can in principle add
their own `type instance` (these are open families) plus a 7-tuple, but that is an orphan
instance for something the library should supply.

The tuple encoding also forces `IsProductType (CoordDiff cs) (MapDiff cs)` into the
context of everything that offsets --- see `offsetCoord` (Coord.hs:361-368) and the
`AffineSpace (Coord cs)` instance (Coord.hs:222-226) --- which is why generics-sop
appears in consumer signatures that have no other reason to mention it.

PROPOSAL

Make the displacement coord-shaped instead of tuple-shaped:

    type Needle (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs)

`MapDiff` (Coord.hs:218-220) is already a closed, recursive family, so it needs no new
per-arity code. The payoff:

  - no arity ceiling
  - `IsProductType (CoordDiff cs) (MapDiff cs)` disappears from every signature
  - the needle inherits `:|`, `EmptyCoord`, `Show`, `Eq`, `AdditiveGroup`, `Random`
    from the existing `Coord` instances for free
  - `CoordDiff` and its seven instances are deleted outright

The `AffineSpace` helper functions at Coord.hs:234-244 and the `offsetCoord` helper at
Coord.hs:375-382 already recurse structurally over `NP I (MapDiff xs)`; they get simpler,
because `productTypeTo` / `productTypeFrom` are no longer needed at either end.

COST

Tuple literals at call sites stop working. Today ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs:98 writes
`c .+^ (-1, -1)` and ../aoc/src/2016/02.hs:45 writes `mempty .+^ (0, toInteger col)`;
both would become `(-1) :| (-1) :| EmptyCoord`. That is more uniform but more verbose in
two dimensions, which is the overwhelmingly common case.

Mitigation worth evaluating as part of this issue: keep a small `IsProductType`-based
conversion available as an explicit function (say `needleFromTuple`), or supply a pattern
synonym for the 2D needle, so the ergonomic case is one short call rather than a
structural literal. Do NOT keep it as an implicit coercion in the class --- that
reintroduces the constraint this issue exists to remove.
design: Follow manifolds: the displacement type is associated and products get theirs structurally. Reuse Coord itself as the needle (Needle (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs)) rather than introducing a new product type, so all existing Coord instances and patterns apply unchanged. Keep any tuple conversion as an explicit opt-in function, never as a class constraint.
acceptance_criteria: A Coord of seven or more axes has a working AffineSpace/offset API; IsProductType (CoordDiff cs) (MapDiff cs) appears in no exported signature; the seven CoordDiff type instances are deleted; ../aoc builds against the new needle.
close_reason: Closed

title: Benchmark "mapGrid then sum 300x300" does not sum
description:
The two benchmarks named `mapGrid then sum 300x300 {boxed,unboxed}` (bench/Main.hs:598 and :601) have the body `nf (mapGrid (+ 1)) g`. There is no sum: `nf` deep-forces the whole new 90,000-cell grid, so what is measured is a map plus a full NFData walk over the result.

The name misleads. sized-grid-adr.10 was filed partly on the strength of these numbers reading slower than `foldlGrid' 300x300`, and concluded from that that Foldable's `sum` built a thunk chain. It does not -- `sum` over that grid allocates 1,128 bytes, identical to `foldlGrid'`. The gap was map-and-force versus fold, which is not a comparison of anything.

Fixing it is not a free rename. The full benchmark name is the key both for the checked-in laptop baseline (bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv lines 46-47) and for the CI baseline in the Actions cache, and `--baseline` matches by full name. Renaming orphans both rows: the laptop CSV can be edited in the same commit, but the CI cache cannot, so the first PR after the rename compares against nothing for these two and the gate silently passes them.

Options, in preference order:
  1. Rename to what it measures (`mapGrid 300x300`) and edit the two baseline CSV rows in the same commit, accepting one CI run with no comparison for this pair.
  2. Keep the name and add the sum: `whnf (total . mapGrid (+ 1))`. Preserves both baselines' continuity but changes what the number means, which is worse -- a silently redefined baseline row is the thing the bench README exists to prevent.

Recommend (1).
close_reason: Closed

title: Test suite and README have warnings that only appear on a cold build
description:
'cabal build all --enable-tests --ghc-options=-fforce-recomp' on master (c697f1b) reports 8 warnings that a normal incremental build never shows, because GHC only emits warnings when it actually recompiles:

  README.lhs:104:8   -Wredundant-constraints
  README.lhs:129:16  -Wredundant-constraints
  tests/Main.hs:85:8    -Wredundant-constraints
  tests/Main.hs:101:11  -Wunused-matches
  tests/Main.hs:101:16  -Wunused-matches
  tests/Main.hs:145:8   -Wredundant-constraints
  tests/Main.hs:213:20  -Wunused-matches
  tests/Main.hs:213:25  -Wunused-matches

src/ is clean; this is test and README code only.

Found while working sized-grid-wrc, where a cached 'Up to date' build made a
before/after warning comparison look clean when it had simply not recompiled
anything. That is the more general trap: any check of the form 'did my change
add a warning' is worthless unless the build actually ran, so use
-fforce-recomp or compare against a forced baseline.

Two things worth doing:
 - fix the eight warnings
 - decide whether CI should build with -Werror on a cold cache, which is what
   would have caught these when they were introduced (relates to sized-grid-rt9,
   the GitHub Actions issue)
close_reason: Both parts resolved. (1) The 8 warnings (README.lhs, tests/Main.hs) are already gone -- verified via a clean 'rm -rf dist-newstyle && cabal build all --enable-tests --ghc-options=-fforce-recomp': zero warnings on a genuinely cold build, all 485+4 tests pass. Fixed incidentally by later refactors (likely sized-grid-4xh's AllSizedKnown/AllGridSizeKnown merge touching the same signatures). No code change needed. (2) The -Werror-on-CI decision is: yes, do it -- filed as sized-grid-dvm with the two pre-existing example-package warnings (sudoko missing-export-lists, ising-example unused-top-binds) that currently block turning it on repo-wide.

title: fromJust in Ordinal construction: seven call sites total only by an unchecked invariant
description:
Split out of sized-grid-0vq part (b); part (a), the four unreachable 'error' calls, is done.

'fromJust . numToOrdinal' appears in arithmetic that is total only because a mod or a
clamp happened just beforehand, which nothing checks:

  - src/SizedGrid/Coord/Periodic.hs:42, 54, 65, 74
  - src/SizedGrid/Coord/HardWrap.hs:44, 61
  - src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:82        toEnum = fromJust . numToOrdinal
  - src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:83    maxCoord

Each is correct today, but the invariant lives in the reader's head, and every one of
them turns a future off-by-one into 'Maybe.fromJust: Nothing' with no indication of
which coordinate or which operation produced it.

This is deliberately NOT fixed by sprinkling error messages on the existing code. The
right fix arrives with sized-grid-upo: once Ordinal is a newtype over Int, all of these
collapse into a single 'unsafeOrdinalFromInt' whose precondition is stated once, checked
with an assert in a debug build, and free in a release build. Doing it before upo means
writing the same defensive code twice.
acceptance_criteria: No fromJust remains in src/; the single unchecked construction point documents its precondition and is assert-checked when compiled with -fno-ignore-asserts.
close_reason: Fixed in commit 'Make Ordinal a newtype over Int' on branch worktree-ordinal-int; 100 tests pass, zero warnings

title: Research pointwise lattices interoperability for Grid
description: The BSD-3 lattices package (locally inspected at 2.2.1.1) provides constructive Algebra.Lattice.Lattice join/meet, BoundedJoinSemiLattice bottom, BoundedMeetSemiLattice top, and Algebra.PartialOrd.PartialOrd. Grid has zipWithGrid, Functor, Apply, and Applicative instances, so a fixed-shape Grid can support these operations pointwise without defining an Ord instance for grids or coordinates. Candidate instances are Lattice a => Lattice (Grid cs a), PartialOrd a => PartialOrd (Grid cs a), and bounded instances requiring AllSizedKnown cs to tabulate bottom/top. The package is BSD-3 and its base range includes this projects supported compiler family, but it is not currently a dependency. Keep the adapter separate until a consumer demonstrates use of lattice fixed-point or data-flow operations; do not add an order over coordinate shapes.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Build a minimal adapter proof of concept against grid-sized and lattices 2.2.1.1. 2. Verify join, meet, PartialOrd, bottom, and top pointwise laws on at least two grid shapes. 3. Measure whether instances belong in an optional component or a separate package, including dependency impact. 4. Identify one concrete consumer use case; otherwise close as intentionally unsupported.

title: Hashable for Ordinal, the four axis types and Coord
description:
From the sized-grid-90f survey. Promoted out of "Tier 2: one small
dependency" -- hashable is not a new dependency, see Cost.

== Why

HashMap (Coord cs) v is an obvious thing for a consumer to want -- a sparse
overlay on a dense grid, a memo table keyed by coordinate, a visited set --
and it is currently unreachable without an orphan instance. Ord (Coord cs)
exists (Coord.hs:129) so Data.Map works today; that is the reason this is a
gap worth closing rather than a hole in the type's usability.

== The design question, which is not just "derive it"

Two honest implementations:

  a) hashWithSalt s = hashWithSalt s . coordPosition
     Needs only IsCoordList. One Int hashed, whatever the dimension.
     coordPosition is injective on Coord cs, so this is collision-free within
     a shape, and it is the cheapest possible.

  b) fold hashWithSalt over the NP, componentwise.
     Needs All Hashable cs. Matches what a tuple instance does.

Prefer (a), and say why in the Haddock: the coordinate space is a dense
prefix of the naturals by construction, so the position IS the perfect hash,
and (b) would pay per-axis for a worse distribution. The one thing (a) gives
up is that two Coords of DIFFERENT shapes with the same position hash the
same -- which is not observable, because they are different types.

Ordinal and the four axis types get the same treatment through
ordinalToInt.

== Cost

None. hashable is already in the build plan, pulled in by aeson and lens,
both already direct dependencies.
close_reason: Added Hashable instances for Ordinal, all four axis types, and Coord using their dense positions; added hashable to direct library dependencies. cabal build succeeds.

title: Keep chart/seam machinery in grid-atlas; do not extract a grid-independent manifold library yet
description:
## Decision

Do not extract Data.Grid.Atlas / Data.Grid.Atlas.CubeMap's chart/seam machinery into a separate grid-independent package (e.g. 'manifold' or 'atlas-topology') at this time, despite sized-grid-ts4's evidence bar (two concrete atlases) now being met.

## Rationale

sized-grid-ts4 asked for two concrete atlases before revisiting extraction. Both now exist: the tiled atlas (fh2, identity seams) and the cube map (68j, a hand-derived D4 transition table). Comparing them does show a real seam: Face/Axis/Extremum/Heading and cubeSeam's shape -- (Face, Axis, Extremum) -> (Face, Axis, Extremum, Bool) -- never mention Grid or cell contents anywhere load-bearing. AtlasCoord's only grid-specific half is the `Coord cs` component; the chart-index half is bare Ordinal k.

But both data points come from inside the same package, with the same author guessing at what a non-grid consumer would want. There is still zero actual non-grid (or even second-grid-package) consumer: `../aoc`, the fork's real external consumer (see memory sized-grid-aoc-relationship), has no call site touching grid-atlas at all. Extracting now would mean fixing an API boundary -- what a chart interface looks like, whether a bare-coordinate/no-payload atlas is representable, what a portable 'Seam' type looks like -- against zero outside pressure. That is exactly the speculation Data.Grid.Atlas's own haddock warns against when justifying why it deferred a general seam-transition table until the cube map existed, applied one level up: a second internal example is not the same evidence as one real external pull.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Extract now into a new package with no grid-sized dependency**: rejected -- no real non-grid consumer exists to drive the cut; the resulting API would be shaped by guesswork, not by a call site.
- **Extract only the clearly grid-independent leaf types (Face, Axis, Extremum, Heading) while leaving Atlas/AtlasCoord/cubeSeam in grid-atlas**: rejected for now -- splitting small helper types into their own package with zero consumers is pure churn; revisit alongside the fuller cut if/when the trigger below fires.
- **Close the question permanently / never revisit**: rejected -- the tension is real and documented (cubeSeam's shape is already payload-agnostic), so it should stay visible as a decision rather than be dropped silently.

## Trigger to revisit

When a concrete non-grid consumer actually wants Face/Axis/Extremum/Heading/cubeSeam-shaped chart/seam machinery without depending on Grid -- e.g. a pathfinding/graph problem in ../aoc, or a bare-coordinate topology (Mobius strip, arbitrary graph) elsewhere in this repo -- extract then, with that consumer's real call sites driving the API, not before.

## Affects

- sized-grid-ts4 (the issue this decision resolves)
- sized-grid-fh2 (tiled atlas)
- sized-grid-68j (cube map)
close_reason: Superseded by sized-grid-1av

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text: Superseded by sized-grid-1av: the 'wait for a non-grid consumer' gate was the wrong criterion. The seam-table half of cubeSeam (chart id + boundary label + involution) is already payload-agnostic and evidenced by existing tests, not a guess -- that part gets designed now (target: atlas-topology package) even with zero outside consumers. Only the coordinate-stepping half (cubeStep) stays gated on more evidence.

title: Each for Grid: each = traverse, so generic 'over each' code works on grids
description:
From the sized-grid-90f survey.

  instance IsCoordList cs => Each (Grid cs a) (Grid cs b) a b where
    each = traverse

Two lines. Grid is Traversable already (Internal/Grid.hs:92 gives
Traversable (GridOf v cs) for Traversable v), so this is the class default
under another name; lens ships no blanket Traversable-implies-Each instance,
so it has to be written.

Value is modest and deliberately recorded as such: it buys nothing traverse
does not already buy, except that code written against 'each' -- which is a
fair amount of lens-idiomatic code -- starts working on grids.

Boxed Grid only. The unboxed GridOf cannot be Traversable, so 'each' there
would need a hand-written round trip; that is not worth it, and Ixed
(see the companion issue) already covers unboxed element access.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Added the boxed Grid Each instance as each = traverse in Internal/Grid.hs. Validated with nix develop --command cabal test grid-sized:test:tests; compilation and Grid traversal tests passed. The suite still has two unrelated existing Periodic Enum law failures.

title: Replace the AllGridSizeKnown type family with a class, so callers stop writing KnownNat (n * n)
description:
AllGridSizeKnown is a type family, so it emits 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize ...)' goals
at the call site instead of solving them. That is what makes puzzle code in ../aoc
write type-level arithmetic by hand:

    ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:33
    parse :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => String -> Maybe (Grid '[Clamped n, Clamped n] Cell)

'gridFromList' asks for 'AllGridSizeKnown cs' (src/SizedGrid/Internal/Grid.hs:253).
Being a *family* (Internal/Grid.hs:213-219) it expands to a conjunction --

    AllGridSizeKnown cs = ( KnownNat (CoordNat (Head cs))
                          , KnownNat (MaxCoordSize (Tail cs))
                          , KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)
                          , AllGridSizeKnown (Tail cs) )

-- and then does no solving at all: the raw 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)' goal lands
on the caller. For cs ~ '[Clamped n, Clamped n] that is 'KnownNat (n * (n * 1))',
which GHC cannot get from 'KnownNat n', so the caller states it by hand.

Contrast the AllSizedKnown *class* (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:783-791): its instances
derive 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)' inductively from the per-axis KnownNats, so a
caller with 'KnownNat n' needs nothing else. Same obligation, discharged by
instance resolution rather than dumped on the caller.

Proposed: give the structural-recursion classes the same treatment -- replace the
AllGridSizeKnown family with a class carrying the evidence it currently demands
(gridFromList, collapseGrid, and the ToJSON/FromJSON instances at
Internal/Grid.hs:265,283 are the users), so the induction happens during instance
resolution.

Expected: '../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:33' loses 'KnownNat (n GHC.* n)' and reads
'parse :: KnownNat n => ...'.

WHY THIS AND NOT sized-grid-h56: h56 predicted the plugins would fix this. They
cannot -- type-checker plugins are not transitive. sized-grid enabling them affects
only sized-grid's own modules; ../aoc solves its own constraints and does not enable
them (verified: no 'typelits' in aoc.cabal, cabal.project or flake.nix). So this
leak is fixable only by an API change, and needs no plugin.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Done. AllGridSizeKnown is now a class with a GridSizeProof GADT method carrying the tail's dictionary; gridFromList, collapseGrid and the ToJSON/FromJSON instances case on it and no longer ask for SListI cs either.

VERIFIED, and verified the way this issue actually needed: a new plugin-free test suite. sized-grid.cabal's 'common lang' is split into 'lang-base' (language + warnings) and 'lang' (that plus the two solvers); the new 'downstream' test-suite imports lang-base only, because -fplugin is not transitive and a consumer therefore compiles without them. tests-downstream/Main.hs is ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs's signature with the leak deleted:

    parseSquare :: KnownNat n => String -> Maybe (Grid '[Clamped n, Clamped n] Char)
    renderSquare :: KnownNat n => Grid '[Clamped n, Clamped n] Char -> [String]
    roundTripJSON :: KnownNat n => Grid '[Clamped n, Clamped n] Char -> Maybe (...)

Negative control: reverting only the three source files and rebuilding that suite fails at exactly three sites --

    tests-downstream/Main.hs:41 Could not deduce KnownNat ... from the context: KnownNat n  (gridFromList)
    tests-downstream/Main.hs:48 ... (collapseGrid)
    tests-downstream/Main.hs:56 ... (decode)

so the suite is a real regression test and not a tautology.

Green: library builds with no warnings, 283 tests pass, downstream 3/3, readme test-suite and all three example executables build. Test warning count in tests/Main.hs is 6 before and after (pre-existing -Wunused-matches / -Wredundant-constraints, unrelated).

Head and Tail are now unused by the library but still exported -- see the follow-up.

title: Perf research: parallel stencil table construction
description: Investigate multicore parallelization of stencil table build path (`stencilFor`, including width discovery and row materialization) in `src/Data/Grid/Sized/Stencil.hs`. Current build does two full passes over all coordinates and is CPU-heavy but embarrassingly parallel per-coordinate.
design:
RESULT: parallelising the build works (up to 4.9x at -N4), but the larger and
safer finding is that a one-pass BOUNDED build is a free 1.9x on one core.
Spike: spike/kb38-parstencil, with four checked-in result CSVs (-N1/2/4/8) and
a README carrying the full argument.

METHOD NOTE, and it cost a full round of measurement: tasty-bench measures CPU
TIME by default -- its own Haddock says that for a multithreaded algorithm it
"reports total elapsed CPU time across all cores". So every parallel variant
first came back within noise of its sequential twin at -N4 and worse at -N8,
which reads exactly like "parallelism does nothing". +RTS -s gave it away: 3.0s
mutator against 1.25s elapsed on a run tasty-bench had called flat. Anything
parallel MUST be measured with --time-mode wall. This applies to the sibling
issues sized-grid-49hi, sized-grid-0bej and sized-grid-utxm; a note is now in
bench/README.md so the trap is not re-entered.

THE TWO AXES, which turned out to be separable:

(a) Passes. stencilFor asks the neighbourhood function twice per cell -- once
    for a length to discover the width, once for the row. That was chosen in
    adr.15 against a one-pass build that RETAINED every row across a width
    pass. It did not consider one that allocates at an upper BOUND on the row
    width, fills in one pass recording the width it actually saw, and compacts
    if the bound was loose. Nothing is retained, the neighbourhood function
    runs once. mooreStencil and vonNeumannStencil can supply such a bound,
    (2r+1)^d - 1; the general stencilFor cannot.

(b) Cores. Both the width pass and the fill split by index range with no
    communication: disjoint slices of one mutable vector, joined before freeze.

MEASURED (wall clock, best over -N1/2/4/8, against the library at -N1; the full
matrix is 13 shape/neighbourhood groups x 8 variants x 4 -N settings):

  variant       400    2,500   90,000   90,000 moore 3
  seqBounded    1.93x   1.90x   1.89x   1.94x
  parWidth      1.32x   1.41x   1.45x   1.53x
  parFill       1.48x   1.63x   1.58x   1.75x
  parBoth       2.37x   2.84x   2.88x   3.11x
  parBounded    4.14x   4.96x   4.89x   5.42x
  parChunked    1.53x   1.24x   0.97x   1.06x

  - seqBounded is the free 1.9x: no threads, no unsafePerformIO threading, no
    threshold, and half the allocation (535 MB -> 260 MB per 90,000-cell build).
  - Half a two-pass build is still a full serial pass: parWidth and parFill cap
    at 1.4x/1.6x alone and only reach 2.9x together. Both or neither.
  - Past four cores the returns stop. parBounded on 90,000 cells: 29.9 / 16.2 /
    11.7 / 14.6 ms at -N1/2/4/8. SLOWER at eight. The build is allocation-bound
    (still one list per cell out of the neighbourhood function), so past a few
    cores it competes for memory bandwidth and GC, not arithmetic.
  - Turning -N on costs the SEQUENTIAL path: unchanged stencilFor measures
    57.0 ms at -N1, 61.2 at -N4, 78.9 at -N8. Parallel GC on a single-threaded
    mutator. A threshold that falls back to sequential on a consumer who asked
    for -N falls back to a path -N has already made slower.
  - parChunked -- the one-pass variant needing NO bound, each chunk at its own
    width then copied into the widest -- loses everywhere, and copies 122 MB
    per build against 600 KB for everything else. Do not reach for it again.

MEMORY TRADEOFF (90,000 cells, isolated +RTS -s runs):
                              allocated/build   peak residency
  library, moore r=1              535 MB           6.02 MB
  bounded, moore r=1              260 MB           6.02 MB
  library, vonNeumann r=2         833 MB           8.90 MB
  bounded, vonNeumann r=2         426 MB           17.5 MB
  The bound halves allocation always. It costs residency only when it is
  LOOSE: Moore's bound is exact so residency is unchanged to three digits;
  von Neumann r=2 has bound 24 against width 12 and so briefly holds a table of
  twice the final size. Worst case n*ub words, predictable from the type and
  the radius, freed at the compacting copy. Parallelism on its own changes
  neither column -- it is the bound that does both.

THRESHOLD POLICY: large grids only, threshold 1024 cells.
  The parallel dispatch costs ~20-30 us of fork/join and does NOT vary with
  chunk count (one chunk per capability and eight measure within 2% on the
  90,000-cell build -- no load-balancing win to chase, keep the static split).
  Crossover, seqBounded at -N1 against parBounded at -N4:
     12 cells    3.7 us   vs   11.8 us   (parallel loses 3x)
    100 cells   29.7 us   vs   21.3 us   (break-even)
    400 cells  123.0 us   vs   57.5 us   (2.1x)
  1,024 cells  319.9 us   vs  131.5 us   (2.4x)
  Break-even is ~100 cells; 1024 has an order of magnitude of margin on both
  sides and is a >= test on coordSpaceSize, which the type already knows.
  Also gate on getNumCapabilities > 1, so a consumer not linked -threaded pays
  nothing.

CORRECTNESS: the spike's benchmark checks all seven variants against the
library's stencilFor before measuring anything -- eleven shape/neighbourhood
combinations over Clamped, Periodic and Reflective axes, including an
asymmetric kernel and the empty neighbourhood -- and exits non-zero on the
first disagreement. All seven agree exactly, at every -N.

RECOMMENDATION, split into two follow-ups because they are independent:
  1. Land the bounded one-pass build sequentially, in mooreStencil and
     vonNeumannStencil only (they are what can supply the bound). 1.9x, half
     the allocation, no threads, no threshold, no API change. stencilFor keeps
     its two-pass path since it has no bound to use.
  2. Parallelism as an OPT-IN entry point rather than silently inside
     stencilFor. It is worth 2.6x on top of (1), but unsafePerformIO + forkOn
     inside a pure library function, and taking a consumer's cores without
     being asked, are policy decisions rather than optimisations -- and the
     win only exists for a consumer linked -threaded with -N.
acceptance_criteria:
- Prototype parallel width pass (max row length) and parallel row fill into final `VU.Vector Int` (or equivalent), preserving row-major layout and sentinel contract.
- Avoid retaining all rows in memory; keep current GC-friendly properties or improve them.
- Benchmark build-only cases (`mooreStencil` in bench/Main.hs) with +RTS -N1/-N4/-N8.
- Add a regression check that table semantics match current implementation exactly for mixed boundary policies.
- Report memory tradeoffs and choose threshold policy (always parallel vs large grids only).
close_reason: Research complete. Spike at spike/kb38-parstencil with four checked-in result CSVs; findings, memory tradeoffs and the chosen threshold policy are on the issue's design field. Follow-ups filed: sized-grid-fup0 (bounded one-pass build, the 1.9x, sequential) blocking sized-grid-mrpb (opt-in parallel build, threshold 1024 cells).

title: Grid.Sized.Grid.* repeats 'Grid' twice in the module path
description:
The rename in sized-grid-85n mapped SizedGrid.* to Grid.Sized.* mechanically, preserving the existing tree. That is correct for a rename but leaves four modules whose paths stutter:

  Grid.Sized.Grid.Class
  Grid.Sized.Grid.Focused
  Grid.Sized.Grid.Grid     <- worst offender
  Grid.Sized.Grid.Unsafe
  Grid.Sized.Internal.Grid

Under the old prefix 'SizedGrid.Grid.Grid' read as one stutter; now it is two.

Options: flatten the Grid.* layer (Grid.Sized.Class, Grid.Sized.Focused,
Grid.Sized.Unsafe) since Grid.Sized is already the subject; or leave it, since
Coord.* has the same shape and the symmetry is worth something.

Deliberately not done as part of the rename: a rename that also reorganises the
tree is two changes wearing one commit message, and this one is not forced.
close_reason: Done in commit 96cfd54 on worktree-rename-grid-sized. src/Grid/Sized/Grid/Grid.hs -> src/Data/Grid/Sized/Grid.hs, so the module is Data.Grid.Sized.Grid with Class, Focused and Unsafe still beneath it -- the same shape Coord already had. One file moved, not four: the corrected analysis in the comments showed this restores symmetry with Coord rather than breaking it. Build clean, 334 tests still passing. The residual repetition (Grid at positions 2 and 4) is NOT fixed here and is filed as sized-grid-zxz, because that one needs the head module to absorb the type's export list rather than just a file move.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Correction to the description's "Options" paragraph, which framed this wrong.

I wrote it as "flatten the Grid.* layer, OR leave it for symmetry with Coord.*".
That is a false trade. Look at what Coord actually does:

  Grid.Sized.Coord            <- the module for the type
  Grid.Sized.Coord.Class
  Grid.Sized.Coord.Clamped
  Grid.Sized.Coord.Periodic

A module 'A.B' and modules beneath 'A.B.*' coexist perfectly well -- this is the
Data.Vector / Data.Vector.Mutable shape and it is thoroughly idiomatic. Coord
already has it. Grid does not, because the type's module is 'Grid.Sized.Grid.Grid'
and there is no 'Grid.Sized.Grid' at all:

  src/Grid/Sized/Coord.hs        EXISTS
  src/Grid/Sized/Grid.hs         DOES NOT EXIST
  src/Grid/Sized/Grid/Grid.hs    the type lives here instead

So collapsing Grid.Sized.Grid.Grid -> Grid.Sized.Grid does not BREAK symmetry
with Coord, it RESTORES it. Grid is currently the odd one out. The fix is a
single file move, src/Grid/Sized/Grid/Grid.hs -> src/Grid/Sized/Grid.hs, with
Class, Focused and Unsafe staying exactly where they are beneath it.

That also makes this smaller than filed: one module renamed, not four, and the
"leave it alone" option loses the argument that was supporting it.

Independent of the Data.* prefix question: adding or removing a 'Data.' at the
front does not touch this, since Data.Grid.Sized.Grid.Grid stutters identically.

title: axisSteps rescans its candidate list per candidate: the real neighbourhood cost, 67% of it
description:
sized-grid-5uq moved the stepsWithin fold into an IsCoordList method, which is
correct and unrolls, and it was worth 9% of the allocation. The remaining cost
is one function below it, in axisSteps, and it is most of the benchmark.

MEASURED, both sides in one session, on 'extend neighbourSum 50x50':

  HEAD before 5uq                      6.84 ms / 25.71 MB
  after 5uq (the fold as a method)     6.46 ms / 23.42 MB
  with the dedup scan skipped          2.24 ms / 12 MB     (67% less than HEAD)

So the fold was ~9% and this is the rest.

WHAT IT IS. axisSteps builds 'reachable' and then, per element, scans that whole
list again with 'any (beats (d, v)) reachable' --- quadratic in the number of
candidates, with a closure allocated per element. The scan exists to drop
duplicates: on a torus axis with 2*r >= n two offsets reach the same value, and
the one that took fewer steps has to win so that the recorded distance is the
true distance.

THE EXPERIMENT that produced the 2.24 ms was a guard skipping the scan when it
cannot fire:

    axisSteps r c
        | 2 * r + 1 <= ordinalSize @(CoordNat x) = [(abs d, v) | (d, v) <- reachable]
        | otherwise = <the scan as it is now>

Sound for the library's own axes. On a bounded axis the surviving values are at
position i + d and so are distinct for distinct d whatever r is; on Periodic
they are (i + d) mod n, distinct exactly when 2*r + 1 <= n. When every key is
distinct no element beats another --- 'beats' requires key equality, and an
element never beats itself --- so the fast path is elementwise equal to the
scan, order included.

THE DECISION TO MAKE, and why this was not landed with 5uq. The argument above
is about what offsetIsCoord does, not about what the class promises. A
third-party IsCoord with a reflecting boundary --- offset +1 from the top edge
coming back to n-2 --- would satisfy the stated law relating offsetIsCoord to
(.+^) and still produce duplicates under the guard. Either the guard is right
and IsCoord should say that offsetIsCoord is injective in d where it is Just,
or the dedup has to stay unconditional and get cheaper another way (scan the
candidates in (abs d, d) order keeping the first per key, which is the same
answer without the per-element rescan). That is a call about the class contract,
so it is filed rather than assumed.

VERIFY WITH 'extend neighbourSum 50x50' in bench/Main.hs, measuring both sides
now per that file's header. Do not read against the recorded CSV. The 334 tests
in tests/Test/Neighbours.hs already cover the torus cases the scan is for ---
'vonNeumannNeighbours 2' on a 3-cycle, 'mooreNeighbours 2' on a 4-torus --- so
they are the check on whatever replaces it.
notes:
RESOLVED BY MEASUREMENT, NOT BY THE DECISION THIS ISSUE ASKED FOR.

The premise was wrong. The cost was not the quadratic dedup scan; it was that
axisSteps is out of line and so folds nothing it calls. One INLINE pragma:

  extend neighbourSum 50x50   6.51 ms / 22 MB  ->  2.12 ms / 9.9 MB  (67% less)

Every other benchmark in the suite unmoved, measured both sides in one session.
All 334 tests plus the downstream and readme suites pass.

WHY THE SCAN WAS NOT THE CAUSE. The neighbourhood functions run at r = 1, so
reachable has three elements and the scan is nine comparisons. Out of line each
one paid a dictionary. Before-Core of $waxisSteps:

  offsetIsCoord $dIsCoord $dKnownNat irred (eta `cast` ...) ds

per candidate, boxing a fresh ds = I# x1, and per inner element of the scan:

  asOrdinal $dIsCoord $fProfunctorFUN $fFunctorConst (lvl10 `cast` ...) (v' `cast` ...)

After-Core at '[Clamped 50, Clamped 50]: reachable is a go loop over Int# whose
body is ># x (-# 49# y) and <# x (negateInt# y), the bounds check against a
literal with no Natural anywhere; the scan is a joinrec, so no closure per
element; key is case v `cast` ... of I# x, asOrdinal reduced to a coercion; and
the (abs d', d') < (abs d, d) tuple comparison is branches on Int# with no
tuples built. No axisSteps, offsetIsCoord, npStepsWithin, integerFromNatural or
dictionary argument survives in the benchmark's Core.

THE CONTRACT DECISION IS DECLINED, and does not need making. The guard measured
2.24 ms / 12 MB -- slower than the INLINE -- so the injectivity law would have
bought nothing. It would also have cost: a reflecting boundary reaches the same
value from +d and -d at an edge, satisfies every law IsCoord currently states,
and is precisely what the fork's thesis (the coordinate type is the boundary
policy, sized-grid-85n) exists to admit. Narrowing the class to buy speed the
compiler gives away for free is the wrong trade.

Commit 66d50ee. Doc note added at axisSteps; the stale claim in the
offsetByPosition note that the residue was the fold above it is corrected.
close_reason: Closed

title: README does not mention the example executables
description:
There are now five demo packages -- gameOfLife, sudoko, ising-example, automata, maze -- and README.md names none of them. It uses 'gameOfLife' as an identifier in its tutorial code and that is the only occurrence of any of the five.

After sized-grid-nnww they are the best evidence the library has for its own thesis, and each one now exists to make a specific point: gameOfLife that a wrapping neighbourhood needs no bounds check, sudoko that grid-slicing is type-level, automata that Stencil is an engine rather than a Life loop and that a walker is the other shape, maze that FocusedGrid carries a position so the algorithm does not have to. A short section listing them with their flags and one line each on what each demonstrates would cost a paragraph.

Note README.lhs is a symlink to README.md and is the readme test-suite's main-is, so any code fence added has to compile.

title: The gloss windows have not been looked at since the nnww rewrite
description:
sized-grid-nnww rewrote gameOfLife's window and added three more (sudoko --gloss, automata, maze). Every one of them was verified by its logic -- the event streams, the rules, the maze invariants -- and none of them was seen rendered. The machine the work was done on has no Screen Recording permission, so screencapture returned 'could not create image from display'; the windows do open and run (a foreground launch blocked until killed), they were simply never looked at.

So the parts a screenshot would have caught are still open: whether the HUD text overruns its window at the widths chosen, whether the sudoku digit glyph is actually centred in its cell (translate (-15) (-15) at scale 0.3 is derived from GLUT stroke metrics of about 104x100 units, not measured), whether the maze's cycled distance colouring reads as bands or as noise, and whether the Wireworld amber/blue/violet is legible on the dark background.

The arithmetic was checked on paper for all four -- every HUD line and every board fits inside its window with the text scales used -- so this is a polish pass, not a suspected bug.
close_reason: Superseded by sized-grid-23y3, which had to solve this to make progress. All four gloss windows have now been captured and looked at: gameOfLife, sudoko --gloss, automata --wireworld/--torus and maze. The technique is on 23y3's notes -- switch play to playIO and glReadPixels the front buffer into a PPM from inside the draw action, since screencapture cannot work on this machine. Two findings that came out of actually looking: the Wireworld board was far too large for its circuits (fixed, Clamped 46 -> 28), and the sudoku digit centring derived from GLUT stroke metrics was correct.

title: Add the separable policies that fit today: Reflective and Reflect101
description:
Three boundary policies from the transcript catalogue are separable, so they
are ordinary `IsCoord` instances with no new machinery -- the same shape as
Clamped.hs, which is 93 lines including its Haddock.

REFLECTIVE (billiard bounce)
    Stepping past an edge reflects back inside. Index -1 becomes 0, -2 becomes
    1; past the top, size-1 becomes size-1, size becomes size-2.

    bounceAxis size x dx = go (x + dx) where
      go i | i < 0     = go (negate i - 1)
           | i >= size = go (2 * size - 1 - i)
           | otherwise = i

    Note `go` recurses: a displacement larger than 2*size bounces repeatedly.
    Worth doing in closed form (divMod by 2*size, then a conditional mirror) so
    it is O(1) and matches the no-allocation standard the other axis types now
    meet -- see the measured notes on Clamped's (.+^).

REFLECT101 (mirror without edge duplication)
    The image-processing variant: reflects AROUND the boundary cell rather than
    across the wall, so -1 becomes 1, not 0. Standard for Sobel/Laplacian
    kernels, where Reflective double-weights the edge cell. Distinct enough
    from Reflective to be its own type.

CONSTANT / padding
    Out of range yields a fixed value. This one does NOT fit `IsCoord`: the
    policy needs a VALUE, and a coordinate type has no place to put one. It is
    a property of a lookup, not of an axis. Probably belongs as a function over
    the existing `Ordinal` axis (`indexOr :: a -> Grid cs a -> ... -> a`)
    rather than a coord type at all. Filed here to record that it was
    considered and why it is different.

FIT WITH THE THESIS

Reflective and Reflect101 are total, like Clamped, and they destroy information
the same way -- so, like Clamped, they are honest only because the caller named
them. `offsetIsCoord` should still report leaving the axis; the reflection
belongs in (.+^) alone. That is exactly the split Clamped documents at
Coord/Clamped.hs:19-22 and the new types should copy it verbatim.

ONE INTERACTION worth flagging: a bouncing walker has REVERSED VELOCITY after
the bounce, which is a frame transform, which is the seam rule. So Reflective
is the cheapest possible motivation for that work -- a separable policy that
still wants the frame to change. Build it, and the seam-rule question becomes
concrete instead of speculative.

ALSO: `axisDistanceIsCoord` must be overridden. The default measures straight,
which is right; but check whether a reflective axis wants reflected distance
(it probably does not -- distance is a property of the space, and the space is
still bounded). Decide deliberately and test it, the way Periodic's override is
tested.
close_reason: Reflective and Reflect101 IsCoord instances implemented, tested (closed-form vs. issue's own recursive reference, offsetIsCoord/axisDistance/axisBoundary default-preservation, AffineSpace/IsCoord/Aeson laws), and wired into the public API. CONSTANT/padding confirmed not an IsCoord fit, as the issue predicted.

title: foldAxis' with a product accumulator costs 9.7x on unboxed grids
description:
Found while measuring sized-grid-7qbi, and the one place the recommended loop loses badly.

foldAxis' holds its accumulator in an argument, which is free for a scalar and re-allocated every step for a product: folding Int into (Int, Int) -- a min/max pair -- over a 300x300 UGrid costs 1716 us and allocates 12.2 MB, where the input-driven variant that keeps its accumulators in the unboxed output vector costs 177 us and allocates 4.9 KB. 9.7x and 2,500x. -O2 does not change it (1572 against 177). Boxed, neither shape wins: 1855 against 2280.

This matters because min/max, mean-and-count, and running (sum, sumOfSquares) are exactly the row/column statistics sized-grid-7qbi names as the motivation.

Both loops are in spike/7qbi-foldaxis ('foldAxisNonEmpty' and 'foldAxisSweep'), checked against the same reference, with the numbers in its two CSVs.
design:
The fix is not obvious, which is why this is filed rather than designed. Choosing the input-driven loop wholesale is wrong: it writes every output cell axisSize times, and on a boxed vector each write allocates, costing 1.4 MB per fold and 1.6-2.4x on every boxed benchmark. Choosing between them needs to know whether 'v y' is unboxed, and 'VG.Vector v y' does not say.

Options to weigh: (a) a second exported function, foldAxisSweep', documented for unboxed accumulator types, which is two names for one operation; (b) a class distinguishing the two representations, which reaches further than this problem; (c) a RULE firing at v ~ U.Vector, in the shape of the 'collapseGrid/boxed' rules in Internal.Grid.Core, which is the cheapest if it fires reliably; (d) nothing, and document the two-pass workaround (fold each component separately, each with a scalar accumulator).

Blocked on foldAxis' landing first -- there is nothing to fix until there is something to fix.

title: Unexplained 1.2-1.3x between two identical contiguous scan loops (scanSeqMut vs scanSeqStrip)
description:
In spike/utxm-paraxis, scanSeqMut and scanSeqStrip run line-for-line the same inner loop on the contiguous axis, allocate within 1 KB of each other, and neither forks anything. scanSeqStrip is consistently faster:

- 90,000 cells (300x300) axis 1, -N1: 48.4 us vs 37.1 us
- 4,000,000 cells (2000x2000) axis 1, -N1: 2.02 ms vs 1.63 ms

Reproduces on every stride-1 shape and in both cache regimes. Three explanations were tested and ELIMINATED:
- Chunk count: scanSeqStrip at one chunk is a single sequential loop and measures the same as at 32.
- Forking: scanSeqStrip is scanParStrip's code with sequence_ in place of fork/join. It is the fastest arm at -N1.
- Construction: scanSeqFreeze holds the loop fixed and swaps VG.create for runST + unsafeNew/unsafeFreeze. 48.3 us vs scanSeqMut's 48.4 us. Not VG.create.

What is left is the monad (ST under VG.create vs IO under unsafePerformIO) and the loop being reached through a list of chunk ranges rather than called directly. Neither confirmed. Needs Core inspection.

Worth chasing: it is comparable to what four cores contribute to the same operation and costs no threads. Depends on sized-grid-utxm's first follow-up landing, since it stacks on top of it.

title: Export the coordinate distance axisSteps already computes
description:
Inspiration: `Data.Manifold.Riemannian`'s `Geodesic` class, which asks a manifold for the
path between two points rather than leaving the caller to reconstruct it.

But the real point of this issue is smaller and cheaper than that: SIZED-GRID ALREADY
COMPUTES THE DISTANCE AND THEN THROWS IT AWAY.

    src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:398  axisSteps   :: IsCoordLifted x => Int -> x -> [(Int, x)]
    src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:423  stepsWithin :: All IsCoordLifted cs
                                            => Int -> Coord cs -> [(Int, Coord cs)]

`axisSteps` computes the TRUE per-axis distance, and its own documentation
(Coord.hs:386-397) explains that this is the hard part:

    "Where two offsets reach the same value --- which a torus axis does as soon as
     2 * r >= n --- the one that took fewer steps wins, so the recorded distance is the
     true distance on that axis rather than whichever offset the enumeration happened to
     try first."

`stepsWithin` sums that across axes. And then both consumers discard the `Int`:

    mooreNeighbours      r c = [n | (s, n) <- stepsWithin r c, s > 0]           -- :454
    vonNeumannNeighbours r c = [n | (s, n) <- stepsWithin r c, s > 0, s <= r]   -- :471

Neither `axisSteps` nor `stepsWithin` is exported --- check the export list at
Coord.hs:6-39. So the library contains a correct, wrap-aware, mixed-boundary-policy
distance function that no caller can reach.

PROPOSAL

1. Export the distance directly. Both metrics fall out of the same per-axis numbers:

     coordDistance     :: All IsCoordLifted cs => Coord cs -> Coord cs -> Int  -- L-infinity
     coordManhattan    :: All IsCoordLifted cs => Coord cs -> Coord cs -> Int  -- L-1

   Note these must NOT be built on `stepsWithin`, which is radius-bounded and enumerates
   the whole neighbourhood --- that would be O(r^d) to answer a question that is O(d).
   Factor the per-axis "shorter route wins" rule out of `axisSteps` into a scalar
   `axisDistance :: IsCoordLifted x => x -> x -> Int` and build all three on it.

2. Export `stepsWithin` itself. It is the general primitive (every coord within radius r,
   paired with its true distance), both neighbourhood functions are one-liners over it,
   and BFS-shaped consumers want the distances.

WHY THIS IS THE CHEAPEST ITEM IN THE SET

The semantics are already written, reviewed and covered by the neighbourhood tests. The
work is factoring a scalar out of a list comprehension and adding names to an export
list. No type-level machinery, no breaking change --- purely additive.

CORRECTNESS NOTE

`coordDistance` on a mixed `'[HardWrap 5, Periodic 5]` coord must use each axis's own
policy: the bounded axis measures straight, the torus axis takes the shorter way round.
That is the behaviour `axisSteps` already has and is exactly what a caller cannot easily
write by hand, which is the argument for exporting it.
design: Factor the per-axis 'shorter route wins' rule out of axisSteps into a scalar axisDistance, then build coordDistance, coordManhattan and axisSteps on it. Do NOT implement distance via stepsWithin: that is radius-bounded and O(r^d) for an O(d) question.
acceptance_criteria: coordDistance and coordManhattan are exported and correct on mixed '[HardWrap 5, Periodic 5] coords (torus axis takes the shorter way round); stepsWithin is exported; mooreNeighbours and vonNeumannNeighbours are unchanged in behaviour.
notes:
DONE in df9575d.

DESIGN DEVIATION from this issue, deliberate: the issue said to build all three
on axisDistance, INCLUDING axisSteps. I left axisSteps alone. Rebuilding it on
axisDistance would have to enumerate allCoordLike to find what is within r,
which is two regressions at once:
  - cost goes from O(r) to O(n) per axis regardless of r. 'neighbours' (r=1) on
    a 300-wide axis would go from 3 offsets to 300, in the hot loop of every
    cellular-automaton consumer.
  - ordering changes. axisSteps is documented to order 'by the surviving
    offset, ascending, so the centre sits in the middle'; enumerating values
    would order by value, which on a Periodic axis is a DIFFERENT order and
    would break the 'a torus axis is ordered by offset, not by value' test.
That collides with this issue's own acceptance criterion that moore/vonNeumann
be unchanged in behaviour. So axisDistance is a SECOND implementation of the
'shorter route wins' rule, and the drift risk is handled by a test instead --
see below.

SHIPPED
  axisDistanceIsCoord   new IsCoord method, bounded default, Periodic override
  axisDistance          lifted scalar
  axisDistances         per-axis breakdown (the honest primitive)
  coordDistance         Chebyshev / L-inf
  coordManhattan        L-1
  axisSteps, stepsWithin  now exported
  ChangeLog entry.

Periodic's override needed an InstanceSig to bring n into scope for ordinalSize
(the instance head is 'IsCoord Periodic', so n lives only in the method's
forall). It drops the class's '1 <= n', which the body does not use.

TESTS (24 new, in tests/Test/Neighbours.hs)
  - axisDistance == the distance axisSteps records, checked EXHAUSTIVELY over
    Clamped 5, Periodic 5, Ordinal 5, Periodic 4, Periodic 3. Exhaustive rather
    than QuickCheck because the axes are 5 wide and because Ordinal has no
    Arbitrary instance. This is the anti-drift test.
  - mooreNeighbours r is exactly the coordDistance ball, vonNeumannNeighbours r
    exactly the coordManhattan ball, each on bounded / torus / MIXED axes.
    Strongest available evidence, since the neighbourhoods were already covered.
  - metric laws: identity, symmetry, triangle inequality, Chebyshev <= Manhattan.
  - the mixed-policy acceptance case explicitly:
      axisDistances (mixc 0 0) (mixc 4 4) == [4, 1]   bounded straight, torus wraps
      coordDistance  == 4, coordManhattan == 5

MUTATION-CHECKED: replacing Periodic's 'min d (size - d)' with the naive
straight-line distance fails 12 of the new tests across every group, so they are
not vacuous.

VERIFIED: cabal test -- all 201 pass, both suites. Build clean, no new warnings.
All 8 ../aoc SizedGrid modules still type-check, confirming 'purely additive'.

SPUN OUT: sized-grid-b8f (ChangeLog claims GHC 9.8; base >=4.20 and tested-with
both say 9.10). Noticed because the new code uses Prelude's foldl', which is
base 4.20+ -- fine under the real bound, not under the claimed one.
close_reason: Closed

title: Research missing library concepts: checked offsets and safe neighbourhood moves
description: Research whether the library is missing any core concepts relative to its design thesis that the coordinate type is the boundary policy. The strongest concrete gap is a checked, Maybe-returning movement concept: the library exposes total `. +^` / affine-space movement that clamps or wraps, but not a safe "offset by a delta, or fail if that leaves the space" API. The design note at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-11-safe-neighbour-offset-design.md documents this exact omission and cites downstream users in ../aoc that rebuild the pattern by widening coordinates, using explicit bounds checks, or filtering the result afterward. That suggests the public API is missing a first-class concept for boundary-aware movement and neighbourhood generation that does not silently clamp. A broader research pass should inventory other candidate gaps: safe edge traversal, explicit radius-checked neighbourhoods, and whether the public API should expose a boundary-aware movement primitive rather than requiring callers to reconstruct it.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Review the library design thesis and public API against the boundary-policy model. 2. Confirm at least one concrete missing concept with evidence from code or docs. 3. Document whether it is an API omission, an intentional omission, or a design decision that should be formalized. 4. Recommend the appropriate next step: add API, add docs, or close as intentionally unsupported.
notes:
Research complete 2026-08-30. Full report: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-30-boundary-policy-audit.md.

Criterion 2/3 -- the concept this issue named is no longer missing. sized-grid-7gs landed it and sized-grid-i0ob.2 and sized-grid-c0s9 finished it: offsetIsCoord (Coord/Class/Axis.hs:87), offsetCoord (Coord/Neighbourhood.hs:31), mooreNeighbours/vonNeumannNeighbours/neighbours/stepsWithin/axisSteps, coordRay/offsetCoordUpTo/OffGrid/Path/walkPath, and traceOffset/tracePath/walkEverywhere at the grid layer. All three sub-questions this issue listed -- safe edge traversal, radius-checked neighbourhoods, a boundary-aware movement primitive -- are answered by code that exists. Indexing checked movement by MapStep rather than the affine MapDiff is what reaches Ordinal, and so reaches inside a window.

Sweep of the remaining public surface found no new violation of the thesis rule at the coordinate layer. Clean and worth recording: gridFromVector/gridFromList return Maybe; coordFromPosition and the _Position/_Weakened/_Strengthened prisms are checked; translated (Optics/Coordinate.hs:147) is gated on All Boundaryless cs, which is the sharpest instance of the rule in the library; every restriction returns the narrowed axis as Ordinal; no axis type has a Num instance, so no fromInteger truncates silently; the unsafe routes are named.

What the sweep did turn up, now filed:
- sized-grid-8hgl (P3): offsetIsCoord is the only IsCoord method with a Type-kinded use and no lifted wrapper. axisBoundary, axisDistance and axisFrameFlips all have one; axisSteps covers only the radius form.
- sized-grid-gfbc (P3): Coord.Boundary enumerates interiorCoords but has no boundaryCoords, so the module named for boundaries returns everything except the boundary.
- sized-grid-eca4 (P2): ../aoc/src/2018/18.hs:70-80 is the fourth call site in the 7gs design table and the only one never migrated. Still the 11-line hand-roll with an explicit nr >= 0 && nr < nVal check, rebuilt through toEnum on a Clamped axis -- the throwing path in sized-grid-tgmj.

Already tracked, no duplicate filed: tgmj (toEnum), qbal (checked movement through FocusedGrid/Walker), pc93 (stepWalker frame flip), azdr (Reflective/Reflect101 range laws).

Two behaviours that look like gaps and are decisions, both documented where a reader meets them: Clamped's offsetIsCoord refuses at the edge rather than clamping (7gs design note); Reflective and Reflect101 also refuse despite their types saying how to come back, because the law at Coord/Class/Axis.hs:119-124 fixes offsetCoord as 'move without hitting a wall' and transportCoord as the total bouncing counterpart (sized-grid-c0s9).

Criterion 4 -- no new library concept. Close this; the three issues above carry the remaining work.
close_reason: Research done. The checked-movement concept this issue named was a real omission when filed and is now first-class (sized-grid-7gs, i0ob.2, c0s9); the broader sweep found no further violation of the boundary-policy rule at the coordinate layer. Three unfiled findings became sized-grid-8hgl, sized-grid-gfbc and sized-grid-eca4. Report in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-30-boundary-policy-audit.md. Recommendation: no new library concept.

title: Provide list-free stencil rule variant to avoid per-cell neighbor list allocation
description: stencilGrid (src/Data/Grid/Sized/Stencil.hs around L191-L202, gatherRow around L290) builds a boxed [a] list of neighbor values per cell for the rule function, which allocates a cons cell per neighbor. stencilFoldGrid (L223-233) avoids this by folding directly and measures ~3x faster / 5x less allocation on a 50x50 grid (283us/2.4MB vs 92us/479KB per bench/README.md and bench/Main.hs L102-131), but it only supports fold-shaped rules. Consider a third variant (e.g. stencilTraverseGrid or a CPS-style neighbor visitor) that lets rule authors avoid intermediate list allocation while still receiving neighbors one at a time, for rules that need more than a simple fold (e.g. early exit, multiple accumulators).
acceptance_criteria: A design is proposed (and ideally implemented) for a list-free stencil API for non-fold use cases, benchmarked against both stencilGrid and stencilFoldGrid to confirm it avoids the list allocation cost.

title: [epic] Sokoban on a Mobius strip: a game where the topology IS the puzzle
description:
A real game, not another demo, built so that the library's central claim is the thing the player is actually fighting.

WHY THIS ONE. grid-atlas already carries Mobius, Klein, Projective and CubeMap and NOTHING in the repo exercises them -- the five examples all sit on grid-sized's separable policies. grid-atlas's own synopsis says it is 'explicitly the layer for the policies that thesis cannot express (non-separable topologies: a Mobius seam, a cube map)', and that layer currently has no consumer at all.

Sokoban is the right game for it. Its whole vocabulary is 'step' and 'push one cell in the direction I am facing', and Data.Grid.Atlas.Mobius already provides exactly that primitive:

    mobiusStep :: AtlasCoord '[Clamped w, Clamped h] 1
               -> Heading
               -> Maybe (AtlasCoord '[Clamped w, Clamped h] 1, Heading)

Position AND transformed heading out, Maybe for the Straight edge that genuinely ends.
