Crossing the Wrapped seam flips you -- crossMobiusEdge returns True for exactly those two cases -- so pushing a crate off the right edge brings it back on the left INVERTED, and 'up' is no longer up. That is not a special case anyone has to write. It is what the seam table already says.

The result is a puzzle game whose difficulty comes from geometry rather than from content volume, which is the only way a small project ships a game with levels. And it is an honest test of the atlas API: if writing Sokoban on it is awkward, that is a finding about the API worth more than the game.

SCOPE. Deliberately small. One surface (Mobius) done properly beats four done thinly; Klein and Projective are follow-ons once the shape is right, and the cube map is a different game.

NOT A DEMO. The five example packages exist to illustrate one API each. This is allowed to be a game: a title screen, levels, undo, a win condition, and something worth showing someone who does not write Haskell.
design:
OPEN QUESTIONS, to settle before writing much:

1. RENDERING A NON-ORIENTABLE SURFACE HONESTLY. A Mobius strip drawn as a flat rectangle is a lie the player has to hold in their head, and the whole game rests on them believing the seam. Options: (a) flat rectangle with the seam edges marked and a ghost strip showing the mirrored continuation past each edge; (b) a scrolling view centred on the player, so crossing the seam visibly rotates the world; (c) an actual 3D twisted band. (b) is probably the honest one and the least work, but it should be prototyped before the level design is committed to, because it changes what a solvable puzzle looks like.

2. WHETHER THE PLAYER'S HEADING IS VISIBLE AT ALL. Sokoban traditionally has no facing -- you push by moving into a crate. But on this surface heading is load-bearing, because it is what the seam transforms. Either the sprite shows facing, or the player cannot predict a push across the seam, which would make it luck. Leaning: show it.

3. UNDO. Non-negotiable for a Sokoban, and easy here -- the state is a grid plus a walker, so undo is a stack of previous states rather than an inverse-move function, and an inverse move across a flipping seam is exactly the thing not to have to reason about.

4. LEVEL FORMAT. Reuse the shape sudoko's parser landed on: a picture of itself in text, one character per cell, everything unrecognised ignored. It reads as the level in the source, and the same parser takes a file.

PRIOR ART IN THIS REPO WORTH COPYING: the maze example's structure is the closest match -- a lazy stream of moves folded into a picture, layout in a fixed design space scaled to the window (sized-grid-23y3), and a Model/Generate/Solve/Render module split. And the ant example is the precedent for a walker carrying a heading through a seam that transforms it.

TRAP ALREADY PAID FOR ONCE: never use (.-.) to get a cell's index for drawing. On a wrapping axis it is the shortest signed route, not a position. coordPosition/divMod. See sized-grid-23y3.
close_reason: All eight children done. The game ships: rules on three surfaces, ten levels each verified to need a half turn, undo, a solver, three views including the strip drawn as a band, a title screen, a level screen and a way out. What writing it found out about the atlas API is in lopy.4, and two more findings are filed as sized-grid-d0sc and sized-grid-c54t.

title: Sokoban: prototype the Mobius view before committing to level design
description:
The one question that changes everything downstream: how do you draw a non-orientable surface so a player can actually plan a push across the seam?

A flat rectangle with the seam unmarked is unplayable -- the player cannot see that pushing right will bring the crate back mirrored, so every seam crossing is a surprise rather than a plan. Puzzles designed against an unplayable view are wasted work, which is why this comes first.

Three candidates, in rough order of expected honesty:

(a) PLAYER-CENTRED SCROLLING VIEW. The camera follows the walker and the world rotates as the seam is crossed. Locally always 'normal', globally impossible -- which is the actual experience of living on a Mobius strip. Least drawing work. Risk: the player loses the global picture, which Sokoban usually needs.

(b) FLAT RECTANGLE WITH GHOST CONTINUATIONS. Draw the strip flat, mark the two Wrapped edges, and past each edge draw a dimmed mirrored copy of what is on the far side. The player sees the consequence of a push before making it. Keeps the whole level visible. Risk: two ghost strips is a lot of screen for a small board.

(c) 3D TWISTED BAND. Honest and pretty; by far the most work, and gloss is 2D so it would mean projecting by hand or leaving gloss.

DELIVERABLE: a throwaway prototype -- a walker, a couple of crates, no puzzle -- rendering the same level under at least two of these, with a recommendation. Verify by framebuffer capture, not by reasoning: switch play to playIO and glReadPixels the front buffer (see sized-grid-23y3's notes; screencapture does not work on this machine).

ACCEPTANCE: a recommendation with a reason, and a note on what it implies for level size -- (a) and (b) can afford very different boards.
close_reason:
RECOMMENDATION: the flat rectangle with ghost continuations, candidate (b). Both were built and both were photographed; (b) wins, and (a) is worth keeping as a second view because of what it demonstrates, not because anyone should play in it.

Verified by framebuffer capture as the issue asked, not by reasoning: sokoban-shot runs the game under playIO and calls glReadPixels on the front buffer from inside the draw action. Regenerate any shot with

  cabal run sokoban:exe:sokoban-shot -- --out x.ppm --level 2 --view flat --keys lll

then convert the PPM. Reads the viewport, not the window: the framebuffer came back 1800x1400 for a 900x700 window, so the HiDPI point/pixel gap from sized-grid-23y3 is still live and the viewport is the number in the units glReadPixels wants.

WHY (b) WINS, in one picture. Level 2, three pushes in, the crate at the last column of its row: past the seam, in the dimmed continuation, is the goal, two cells further along. The player can see that three more pushes finish the level BEFORE making the first move through the seam. That is the whole job of the view and it does it.

WHY (a) LOSES, also in one picture, and it is not a bug. Level 2 at move 0 and at move 4 -- a crate has crossed the seam in between -- are the same image. 1896 differing bytes out of 5,076,000 in the board area, 0.04 per cent, and the difference is antialiasing. In the player's frame nothing happened, because in the player's frame nothing DID happen: the crate is one cell to the right before the crossing and one cell to the right after it. A Sokoban is a game of planning several pushes ahead, and a view that cannot distinguish a seam crossing from an ordinary step cannot be planned in.

(a) IS STILL WORTH HAVING, on the 'v' key, for one thing it shows that nothing else does: at radius 5 on a 6-wide strip, the same crate appears twice -- once beside the player and once up and to the left, reached the long way round through the seam. That is the surface's non-orientability on screen in a single frame, and it is the best argument the game has for why it exists. As a thing to look at, not to play in.

(c), the 3D twisted band, was not built. Filed separately.

WHAT MADE (b) READABLE, and it was not the ghosts alone. Three things, in order of how much they helped:

 1. COLOURED TABS PAIRING THE ROWS. A tab on each row at both edges, coloured by which row the seam joins it to, so row y and row h-1-y carry the same colour on both sides. Cheap, and it turns 'the seam mirrors' from a sentence in the level note into something read off the picture. This was the single biggest improvement and it was not in the issue's list of candidates.
 2. THE GHOST COLUMNS themselves, three each side, dimmed by laying 62% background over the finished cell picture -- gloss has no opacity for a Picture and the cells set their own colours, so a 'color' wrapper does not reach them.
 3. DISTINGUISHING THE TWO KINDS OF EDGE. Left and right are seams and are loud; top and bottom are the strip's genuine boundary and are a plain grey line. Sokoban.Rules keeps OffTheStrip and BlockedByWall apart for the same reason.

WHAT IT IMPLIES FOR LEVEL SIZE, which is what lopy.3 needs:

 * Screen: the flat view draws w + 6 columns, so the ghosts cost as much width as a 6-wide board. At the current design space that is comfortable to about 20 around and 12 across before tiles get small. Not the binding constraint.
 * The binding constraint is the PUZZLE. A crate needs w pushes to reach the mirrored row and 2w to come home. At w = 6 a lap is a plan; at w = 20 it is typing. Keep levels 5 to 12 around.
 * Height wants to be small, 3 to 7, because every row across is a row the mirror pairs, and a player can hold four or five pairings in their head, not ten.
 * ODD HEIGHT IS A DIFFERENT GAME FROM EVEN. An odd strip has a middle row the mirror fixes -- the one loop that closes in a single lap -- and an even strip has none. Built-in level 1 is the first, level 3 the second, and they teach different things. lopy.3 should treat that as a difficulty axis rather than an accident.
 * A one-row strip works and is the best possible tutorial: the whole level is a ring, there is no mirror to explain yet, and stepping across is OffTheStrip everywhere. Built-in level 1 is 7x1.

ALSO SETTLED, the issue's open question 2 (whether the player's heading is visible): yes, as a wedge on the player's disc, and it is drawn in the frame the view is drawing in -- which is why Play now carries a Heading rather than the Dir that was pressed. See the commit.

title: Sokoban: the rules on a Mobius strip -- move, push, undo, win
description:
The game logic, independent of how it is drawn.

State is a Grid of cells (wall, floor, goal), a set of crate positions, and a Walker carrying the player's heading. Every move goes through Data.Grid.Atlas.Mobius.mobiusStep, which returns the new AtlasCoord AND the transformed Heading, so the seam's flip is never something this module computes -- it consults.

A push is two mobiusStep calls, and the subtlety is that they are NOT the same step applied twice: the crate is one cell ahead of the player, so it crosses the seam one move earlier and its heading transforms before the player's does. Getting that wrong is the most likely bug in the whole game, and it is exactly the case a test should pin.

Rules to implement:
  * move: step if the target is floor and crate-free
  * push: step if the target holds a crate and the cell beyond it is floor and crate-free; both move
  * blocked: Nothing from mobiusStep (the Straight edge) or a wall
  * win: every goal cell holds a crate
  * undo: a stack of previous states, not an inverse move -- inverting a move across a flipping seam is precisely what not to reason about

ACCEPTANCE: a pure module with no gloss in it, plus tests. At minimum: a crate pushed all the way around the Wrapped axis returns to its starting cell with the strip's orientation reversed relative to the player, and twice around restores it; a push into the Straight edge is refused; undo restores exactly.

Reference implementation for the seam behaviour, so the tests assert against something independent: the ant demo's edge check in sized-grid-nnww.8 established that stepWalker at a wall gives Periodic 100->0 heading unchanged, Clamped stays heading unchanged, Reflective stays with heading reversed. The Mobius seam is the atlas-level analogue and deserves the same treatment.
close_reason:
Done, with tests. Sokoban.Rules is pure and gloss-free; Sokoban.Board holds the surface; 38 tests pass.

THE PUSH, which was the risk the issue named: it is two steps, and the way to keep them in the same frame is to step the PLAYER first and feed the heading that comes back into the crate's step. 'stepSpot here heading' returns the cell the crate is standing in AND the heading in that cell's frame, so 'stepSpot ahead ahead'' asks the surface the second question in the frame it is now in. There is no case for the seam in the rules module. The test 'a push with the pair straddling the seam moves both' pins the case the issue was worried about: player at column 4 of row 3 on a 6x5 strip, crate at column 5, push right -- the crate crosses to (0, 1) while the player is still at (5, 3), so their rows are mirror images and no displacement relates them; the next push takes the player through onto the cell the crate has just left.

ACCEPTANCE, against what the issue asked for:
 * 'a crate pushed all the way around returns to its starting cell with the orientation reversed, and twice around restores it' -- the first half of that is only true on the row the mirror fixes, which is the middle row of an odd-height strip, and the tests say so both ways. On any other row one lap lands the crate in row h-1-v and two bring it home. Two tests: 'a crate pushed a full lap arrives in the mirrored row' (middle row, so back to its own cell, player upside down) and 'a lap off the middle row lands in the row the mirror sends it to' ((2,3) -> (2,1) -> (2,3)).
 * 'a push into the Straight edge is refused' -- yes, and separately from a wall. Outcome distinguishes OffTheStrip from BlockedByWall from BlockedByCrate, because a player looking at the boundary of a rectangle cannot otherwise tell that the left and right edges are not edges at all.
 * 'undo restores exactly' -- a stack of Play values, not an inverse move. Property test: any run of moves, undone, is the start again, counters included.

WHAT THE SEAM ACTUALLY DOES, which is not quite what the epic said. mobiusStep never returns a changed Heading on this surface: the mirror fixes the wrapped axis and reverses the other, so a walker crossing sideways keeps its direction of travel, and a walker moving across the strip never reaches the seam. The whole of the twist a caller sees is in the landing coordinate. The frame flip -- 'up is no longer up' -- is real but invisible in the API's answer, so Play carries a parity bit and Board.crossesSeam reconstructs it with a bounds test. Filed as sized-grid-lopy.5.

BEYOND SCOPE BUT DONE, because the alternative was hand-built grids in every test: the level format and parser (a picture of itself, traditional character set, size read out of the picture and reified), and a BFS solver. lopy.3 keeps the level ramp and the design work; it now has a parser and a solver to do it with.

title: Sokoban: levels, a level format, and a way to tell a good puzzle from a gimmick
description:
A game needs levels, and levels are where this either becomes a real puzzle game or stays a tech demo.

The test for every level: would it still be interesting on a flat torus? If yes, the topology is decoration and the level is not earning its place. The good ones should be unsolvable-looking until you notice you can send a crate around the seam and have it come back mirrored into a position you could not otherwise reach.

FORMAT: reuse the shape sudoko's parser landed on -- a picture of itself in text, one character per cell (# wall, . floor, $ crate, * crate on goal, @ player, + player on goal, following the traditional Sokoban character set), everything unrecognised ignored so decorated layouts and comments read. Levels live in a file, with a handful built in so the game runs with no arguments.

ACCEPTANCE: at least six levels in a deliberate difficulty ramp, each one verified solvable by a solver (a plain BFS over states is fine at this size and doubles as a regression test that the rules module has not changed under you), and each one annotated with the single insight it is teaching. Plus at least one level that is genuinely unsolvable on a flat board of the same shape -- that one is the game's thesis statement.
close_reason:
Eight levels, all verified, seven of them needing the half turn. The format and the solver landed early with lopy.2; what this issue actually produced was the STANDARD, and it is worth more than the levels.

THE STANDARD, and why it had to be mechanical. The issue's test -- 'would it still be interesting on a flat torus' -- cannot be applied by eye. A level can look as though it needs the seam and have an ordinary solution nobody noticed. My own 'Twice around' from the previous commit was exactly that: nine pushes on the strip, three on a cylinder, and it shipped with a note claiming the second lap was necessary. So Sokoban.Flat plays the same layout on the two flat surfaces of the same shape and the verdict is a fact, not a claim:

  * solvable on a plain rectangle -> neither the wrap nor the twist is doing anything
  * solvable on a cylinder but not a rectangle -> the wrap is load bearing, the twist is not
  * neither -> the answer is the half turn

'sokoban --check' prints it for every level; the test suite asserts it. Flat is written out again rather than reusing the rules, deliberately: Solve plays through Sokoban.Rules so a rule change surfaces as a level that stops having a solution, and Flat is forty lines of Int arithmetic that has never heard of grid-sized, so agreement between them is evidence rather than a tautology. A test walls off both seam columns -- which makes the strip literally the rectangle of the same shape -- and requires the two to agree.

THE STRUCTURAL FINDING, which is the transferable part and the answer to this issue's title. THE TWIST BUYS EXACTLY ONE THING: ACCESS TO THE MIRRORED ROW. Within a single row a cylinder is strictly MORE connected than a strip -- on a cylinder the two ends of a row are adjacent, on a strip they are not, since leaving one end lands you in the other row. So no level can require the twist for a within-row journey, and every genuine Mobius puzzle is one where something has to reach row h-1-v. The variety is entirely in WHAT has to get there and WHY that is hard:

  * a crate that cannot turn, because there is nowhere to stand to push it (levels 2, 5)
  * a player who cannot get behind a crate that is already on the far deck (level 3)
  * a wall in the crate's own row, so the way past it is out through the seam (level 4)
  * two or three crates in a one-wide corridor, where the order is the puzzle (6, 7, 8)

That list is the level set. It is also the checklist for the next one.

THE RAMP, ordered by idea and not by size, each level teaching one thing:

  1. No edge to stop at    7x1  3 pushes, 4 states     [cylinder, on purpose]
  2. The other row         5x4  6 pushes, 46 states    MOBIUS
  3. Go yourself           6x4  2 pushes, 9 states     MOBIUS
  4. The long way          7x4  5 pushes, 27 states    MOBIUS
  5. The far row           6x5  6 pushes, 61 states    MOBIUS
  6. One stays, one goes   6x4  7 pushes, 207 states   MOBIUS
  7. Both at once          7x4  10 pushes, 764 states  MOBIUS
  8. Three                 7x4  15 pushes, 3772 states MOBIUS

Level 1 is the deliberate exception the issue's acceptance did not ask for and should have: a player who has not yet believed that the two ends of the picture are the same place cannot be taught anything else, and the honest way to teach that is a level where the wrap is all that matters. It is asserted to be cylinder-solvable, so a change that makes it need the twist fails the tests rather than quietly contradicting its own note.

Level 3 is two pushes long and that is the design. The idea is the whole level; padding it would bury it.

Sizes follow lopy.1's note: 5 to 7 around, 1 to 5 across. Nothing wanted to be bigger. The state counts say the ramp is real -- 4 to 3772 -- and the test asserts the first level is the smallest search and the last the largest, which is weak on purpose so that editing a middle level does not break it.

WHAT DID NOT SURVIVE: 'Twice around' as a distinct lesson. A crate returning to the row it left is a within-row journey, and by the finding above the cylinder always does it in fewer pushes. It is a real thing that happens on the strip and it is not a thing a level can REQUIRE. Anyone tempted to write it again should read the finding first.

FORMAT NOTE: the level separator is a line of three or more equals signs, not a blank line and not a rule of hyphens. Both of those were tried and both are pictures: an all-floor row is written either as nothing at all or as a run of hyphens, and the first draft of the built-in levels was silently cut in half by its own scenery.

title: Sokoban: report back on what writing a game found out about the atlas API
description:
The epic's second purpose. grid-atlas has had no consumer at all until now, and a game is a harsher reader of an API than a demo is: it calls the same few functions thousands of times, in combinations nobody designing the API pictured.

Write up what was awkward, with the call site that made it awkward. Candidate things to watch for while building lopy.1-3:

  * Is AtlasCoord pleasant to carry in game state, or does it want wrapping?
  * mobiusStep answers in Maybe for the Straight edge. Is Maybe the right answer for a caller that wants to distinguish 'off the edge' from 'blocked by a wall', or does it flatten two different refusals into one?
  * Heading is (Axis, Extremum). Is that the right shape for a caller that thinks in up/down/left/right, or is every call site translating?
  * Does anything force index arithmetic the atlas was supposed to hide?
  * Does the two-step push (crate crosses the seam a move before the player) reveal a missing primitive -- something like 'step this coord and this heading, twice, keeping them in the same frame'?

ACCEPTANCE: findings on this issue's design field, with follow-up issues filed for anything that should change in grid-atlas or atlas-topology. A finding of 'nothing, it fitted' is a perfectly good result and worth recording as such -- it is evidence the API is right, which nothing currently supplies.

BLOCKED BY lopy.2 in practice: there is nothing to report until the rules are written against the real API.
close_reason:
Report written. Short version: the API fitted, in the places the issue was most worried about, and failed in one place the issue did not ask about. Four follow-ups filed.

The game is sokoban/. Roughly 1200 lines against grid-atlas, called some thousands of times per solve, which is the harsher reading the issue wanted.

== THE HEADLINE, and the one real defect

MOBIUS STEP COMPUTES WHETHER THE SEAM WAS CROSSED AND THROWS IT AWAY. Filed as sized-grid-lopy.5. SeamTable's crossing returns (chart, boundary, Bool) with the Bool meaning 'the frame is reversed'; crossMobiusEdge returns True for exactly the two wrapped half-edges; rectStep consumes it to mirror the free coordinate; mobiusStep returns only a position and a heading. A caller carrying a frame of its own -- which is any caller on a non-orientable surface, since that is what non-orientable MEANS -- has to reconstruct it, and Sokoban.Board.crossesSeam does so with a bounds test against ordinalSize. That is the arithmetic grid-sized exists to remove, in the one package whose job is the topology.

Note the trap that rules out the obvious workaround: you cannot recover the bit by comparing the positions. On a strip one cell wide, every sideways step crosses the seam and the column does not change.

== THE ISSUE'S FIVE QUESTIONS, answered

1. IS AtlasCoord PLEASANT TO CARRY IN GAME STATE? Adequately. It is a tuple, so Eq/Ord/Show come free, which is what let crate sets be a Set keyed straight off it. The friction is that at k = 1 the chart component is always minBound: every construction writes it, every consumer drops it, and the game keys its sets on the Coord alone so equality does not compare a component that cannot differ. Filed as sized-grid-3rpp, at P3, because the honest answer is 'one word of noise per call site'.

2. IS Maybe THE RIGHT ANSWER FOR THE STRAIGHT EDGE, OR DOES IT FLATTEN TWO REFUSALS? It does not flatten anything, and the shape is right. The game distinguishes three refusals -- OffTheStrip, BlockedByWall, BlockedByCrate -- and they come from three different places: Nothing from mobiusStep, a Tile lookup, and a Set membership. The atlas owns exactly one of them and answers about exactly that one. A caller that wanted the other two out of mobiusStep would be asking it about terrain, which it has no business knowing. NOTHING TO CHANGE.

3. IS Heading = (Axis, Extremum) THE RIGHT SHAPE, OR IS EVERY CALL SITE TRANSLATING? Right shape, and this is the finding I expected to go the other way. Yes, the game translates -- Board.headingFor turns a key press into a Heading -- but that translation is load bearing rather than boilerplate: it is exactly where the player's own frame gets applied, and it is the only place in the game that knows the seam reverses one axis and fixes the other. Had Heading been an up/down/left/right sum, that code would still have to exist AND the seam table would need a separate vocabulary for its boundary labels, because a boundary is (axis, end) whatever the walker calls it. Rect's own comment says it: 'a step that leaves the chart IS the half-edge it leaves through'. That is correct and it is why the type is right. NOTHING TO CHANGE.

4. DOES ANYTHING FORCE INDEX ARITHMETIC THE ATLAS WAS SUPPOSED TO HIDE? Two things.
   * crossesSeam, above. That one is grid-atlas's and is lopy.5.
   * Getting a cell's column and row at all. That one is grid-sized's, it is older than this game, and it turns out all four demos hand-roll it and disagree -- sudoko unwraps with a pattern, maze uses divMod against a hardcoded literal, sokoban unwraps three layers of boundary policy, and gameOfLife and ising-example used (.-.) and were wrong, which was sized-grid-23y3. Filed as sized-grid-bzzy at P2, because the bug that issue fixed was possible precisely because the obvious question has no obvious answer in the API.
   And one thing that is not arithmetic but is the same kind of gap: there is no way to turn a runtime size into an axis type, so a level read from a file needs a hand-written cmpNat/OrderingI dance before it can become a Grid at all. reifyOrdinal is the identical three lines with different bounds. Filed as sized-grid-q8ig at P2. Every consumer whose data is not a literal hits this before it can build anything; the five examples all missed it by hardcoding their sizes.

5. DOES THE TWO-STEP PUSH REVEAL A MISSING PRIMITIVE? NO, AND THIS IS THE BEST RESULT IN THE REPORT. The epic called this 'the most likely bug in the whole game'. It is two lines:

     (ahead,  ahead') <- stepSpot here  heading
     (beyond, _)      <- stepSpot ahead ahead'

   and it is correct because mobiusStep returns the heading IN THE FRAME IT LANDED IN. Step the player first; the cell it lands on is the crate's cell and the heading it lands with is the heading in that cell's frame; ask the surface again. There is no case for the seam anywhere in Sokoban.Rules, and the test that pins the hard case -- player and crate straddling the seam, their rows mirror images, no displacement relating them -- passes with no special handling because there is none to have. The returned-heading design is what makes this work, and a 'step twice keeping them in the same frame' primitive would only be the >>= that is already there.

== ONE CORRECTION TO THE EPIC'S PREMISE

The epic says crossing the seam means 'up is no longer up. That is not a special case anyone has to write.' Half right, and the half that is wrong is lopy.5. mobiusStep NEVER returns a changed heading on a Mobius strip: the mirror fixes the wrapped axis and reverses the other, so a walker crossing sideways keeps its direction of travel, and a walker moving across the strip never reaches the seam. Every visible consequence of the twist is in the landing COORDINATE. The frame flip is real and the API is silent about it.

== WHAT THE GAME PROVED ABOUT THE SURFACE, which is grid-atlas's actual claim

The strip behaves. Verified by test and by an independent implementation, not by reading the source:
  * one lap lands in row h-1-v and two land home, for every starting cell (property test, 100 cases)
  * the middle row of an odd strip is the one lap that closes
  * the straight axis is a genuine edge in both directions and the wrapped axis never is
  * a full-width wall never separates a Mobius strip -- three levels are built on that and their solutions are the proof

And separately, Sokoban.Flat plays the same layouts on a cylinder and a plain rectangle with forty lines of Int arithmetic that has never heard of grid-sized. Where the two surfaces coincide -- a strip with both seam columns walled off -- the two implementations agree on the push count. That is the strongest evidence in the repo that the atlas's Mobius strip is the surface it says it is, and it exists because a game needed a solver and a solver needed a control.

== VERDICT

Four issues filed, one of them a defect (lopy.5), two of them gaps in grid-sized that this game found because it is the first consumer whose data does not live in a type synonym (q8ig, bzzy), one an observation on layering (3rpp). Set against that: three of the issue's five questions came back 'nothing, it fitted', and the one the epic feared most -- the push across the seam -- came back as two lines with no special case. The issue asked for that result to be recorded as a real one, and it is.

title: mobiusStep drops the seam's orientation bit, so a walker with a frame has to reconstruct it
description:
Found by writing sized-grid-lopy.2 against the real API, which is what the epic said a game would be good for.

A Mobius strip is non-orientable, so a walker on it carries an orientation: after an odd number of seam crossings the direction the walker calls 'up' is the chart's down. Any caller that reads direction keys in the walker's own frame -- which is any caller drawing a player-centred view, and is candidate (a) of sized-grid-lopy.1 -- has to track that bit.

The bit exists. Data.Atlas.Topology.Seam.SeamTable's crossing returns it: '(chart, boundary, Bool)' where the Bool is 'the along-the-seam direction is reversed'. crossMobiusEdge returns True for exactly the two Wrapped half-edges and False for the Straight ones. rectStep consumes it to mirror the free coordinate, and returns '(chart, (Int, Int), Heading)'. mobiusStep then returns '(AtlasCoord, Heading)'. The bit is computed and thrown away at every layer.

So Sokoban.Board.crossesSeam reconstructs it:

    crossesSeam spot (Heading along end) =
        case (along, end) of
            (Wrapped, AtMax) -> x == ordinalSize @w - 1
            (Wrapped, AtMin) -> x == 0
            (Straight, _)    -> False

which is a bounds test written against a size -- precisely the thing grid-sized exists so that callers do not write, and lopy.4 asks after by name ('does anything force index arithmetic the atlas was supposed to hide').

NOTE THE TRAP, because it rules out the obvious workaround: you cannot recover the bit by comparing the positions before and after. On a strip of width 1 every sideways step crosses the seam and the column does not change, so 'the column moved by more than one' reports no crossing where there was one. The test 'crossesSeam agrees with what the step actually did' in sokoban/tests/Test/Seam.hs pins the equivalence for w=6; at w=1 only the source-cell form is right.

ALSO NOTE what is NOT the problem: the heading mobiusStep returns is correct. A step along Wrapped that crosses comes back with the same heading, which is right -- the seam's mirror fixes the wrapped axis and reverses the other one, so a walker travelling around the strip keeps travelling around it. And a step along Straight never reaches the seam. So on this surface the returned Heading never changes at a crossing, and the whole of the twist that a caller can see is in the landing coordinate. The epic's 'crossing the Wrapped seam flips you... up is no longer up. That is not a special case anyone has to write' is half right: the position mirror is free, the frame flip is not.

FIX, roughly in order of how much they change:
 1. Return it. 'mobiusStep :: ... -> Maybe (AtlasCoord cs 1, Heading, Bool)', or a small record, or a 'Crossing' sum that also distinguishes 'stayed in the chart' from 'crossed a seam'. Cheapest, and it is information the function already has in hand.
 2. Return the frame transform rather than a bit, which is what generalises: a cube map's crossings permute the axes, and a Bool cannot say that. grid-sized already has a name for this shape -- transportCoord and axisFrameFlips in Data.Grid.Sized.Coord -- so there is a vocabulary to match rather than invent.
 3. Offer a walker that carries its own frame, so no caller writes the bookkeeping twice. Only worth it if a second consumer appears.

Whichever, the same question wants answering for CubeMap and Klein, since they call rectStep too and drop the same bit.
close_reason:
Fixed in grid-atlas, and the fix reads out all four surfaces correctly from tables nobody had to change.

WHAT LANDED. rectStep returns a Landing record carrying a Crossing -- Interior, Seam or MirroredSeam -- with crossedSeam and reversedFrame to read it. mobiusStep, kleinStep, cubeStep and projectiveStep each return it as a third component. Sokoban.Board.crossesSeam is deleted and Sokoban.Rules takes the player's parity straight off the step that moved them.

THE THING THIS ISSUE GOT WRONG, and it matters. I wrote that 'the bit exists' in the seam table and is merely dropped. It does not. The table's Bool says whether the two edges of a seam run the same way along the coordinate they share. Whether the WALKER comes back mirrored depends on the heading as well, because a walker's left lies on the increasing side of that coordinate for some headings and the decreasing side for others, and a crossing can change which. The frame survives exactly when the two disagreements cancel:

    mirrored = reversed /= (leftHandIncreases heading /= leftHandIncreases heading')

where leftHandIncreases (Heading a s) = (a == U) == (s == AtMax), a quarter turn anticlockwise in the frame where U is drawn rightwards.

So a caller could not have recovered this from the table even with the table in hand. That strengthens the case for fixing it here rather than exposing more of the table, and it is why the cube map -- whose table says 'not reversed' on all 24 half-edges -- still needed the computation to confirm that none of its crossings mirrors anything.

OPTION 2 IS NOT NEEDED. This issue suggested returning a frame transform rather than a bit, on the grounds that a cube map's crossings permute the axes and a Bool cannot say that. The heading already carries the permutation -- rectStep has always returned the transformed heading. What is left over is handedness, and for a frame on a square lattice with the forward direction already fixed there are exactly two possibilities. So (heading, handedness) is the complete transform and a Bool's worth is all that was missing.

OPTION 3, a walker that carries its own frame, is still not worth it: one consumer, and the accumulation is a single xor at the call site.

NEW CAPABILITY, which was the unexpected part. With the bit returned, orientability becomes something the package can state and test rather than something its documentation asserts. grid-atlas/tests/Test/Frames.hs:

  * a cube map never mirrors a walker -- all 24 half-edges at every position along them, every interior step Interior, and every closed 4n belt walk from every cell and heading returning the walker as it was
  * a Mobius strip mirrors on every wrapped crossing, and one lap of the middle row of an odd-height strip CLOSES -- same cell, same heading -- with exactly one mirroring. That is the shortest proof of non-orientability the package can state, and it is now a test.
  * a Klein bottle mirrors on Twisted and not on Rolled, which is exactly what makes it a bottle rather than a torus
  * a projective plane mirrors on both, which is what makes it not a bottle

Those four sit alongside the existing vertexCycleLengths tests and say a different thing: vertex cycles distinguish surfaces by their cone points, crossings distinguish them by orientability, and a torus and a Klein bottle -- which vertexCycleLengths reports identically, as its own haddock notes -- are now told apart by the second.

STILL OPEN, deliberately: nothing. The issue's closing line asked whether CubeMap and Klein wanted the same treatment. They got it in the same change, because they all go through rectStep and the fix is in rectStep.

31 tests in grid-atlas, 51 in sokoban, all six suites in the repo green.

title: Sokoban: a third view, the strip drawn as an actual twisted band
description:
Candidate (c) of sized-grid-lopy.1, not built there because (b) answered the question and (c) is by far the most work.

Worth doing anyway, for the reason (a) turned out to be worth keeping: the game's whole claim is about a surface, and the only thing on screen that says so is a colour convention. A band with a half twist in it says it without a legend.

gloss is 2D, so this means projecting by hand: parametrise the strip, place each cell as a quad, sort back to front and draw with 'polygon'. Perhaps 40 lines. No new dependency and no leaving gloss, which is the version worth trying first -- reach for a 3D library only if hand projection is genuinely unreadable.

NOT the view to play in. It is a title screen, a between-levels animation, and the picture that goes at the top of the README. The playable view is settled: sized-grid-lopy.1 recommends the flat rectangle with ghost continuations, and nothing here should replace it.

Check it the way lopy.1 checked the others: sokoban-shot, glReadPixels, look at the PPM.
close_reason: Sokoban.Band draws the strip as a twisted band with its one edge in one colour; a third View in the window, Test.Band ties the parametrisation to the game's own walker, and sokoban-shot grew --view band/--spin/--girth/--tilt/--dist to choose its proportions by looking. Commit 36a474d.

title: Sokoban: the surface is hardcoded to Mobius, so a Klein or projective level cannot exist
description:
Sokoban.Board names mobiusStep directly and Sokoban.Rules is written against Board. Everything above the step -- move, push, undo, win, the solver, the level format, both views -- is already indifferent to which surface it is on, because none of them says anything about the seam. The only Mobius-specific code in the game is:

  * Board.stepSpot = mobiusStep
  * Board.crossesSeam, which knows the seam is on the Wrapped axis
  * Board.headingFor / dirOf, which know the mirror fixes u and reverses v
  * Render's pairColour and the ghost columns, which know row y joins row h-1-y

That is a small surface, and grid-atlas already carries Klein and Projective and CubeMap with nobody calling them at all. A 'Surface' record of those four things, chosen per level, would give the game three more topologies for about the cost of the abstraction -- and would be a far harsher test of grid-atlas than one surface is, which was half the point of the epic (sized-grid-lopy.4).

A Klein bottle is the interesting one: both axes glued, one with a flip, so there is no genuine edge anywhere and OffTheStrip stops existing. Whether the rules read the same with no partiality at all is worth knowing.

DO NOT do this before sized-grid-lopy.3. One surface with good levels beats four with thin ones, and the level format would have to name the surface, which is a decision better made once there is a level pack to migrate.

DEPENDS on sized-grid-lopy.5 in spirit: if mobiusStep learns to return the crossing, three of the four Mobius-specific pieces above go away by themselves.
close_reason: Surface is a record chosen per level; Mobius, Klein and projective all play. Found two things: the walker's frame needs two bits not one (projective's seams mirror different axes), and level 3 was torus-solvable, which led to comparison sets that depend on the level's own surface. spotBeyond generalised both flat views' ghosts and tabs; band stays Mobius via surfaceIsBand; two coda levels ship; Test.Surface asserts the cross-surface claims. Follow-ups sized-grid-d0sc and sized-grid-c54t. Commit 834118a.

title: Sokoban: it plays like a game and does not open like one -- no title, no progress, no way to leave
description:
The epic's own words: 'This is allowed to be a game: a title screen, levels, undo, a win condition, and something worth showing someone who does not write Haskell.' Levels, undo and the win condition are done (sized-grid-lopy.2, lopy.3). The rest of that sentence is not, and what is missing is the part a person who does not write Haskell meets first.

WHAT THE WINDOW DOES NOW. Opens directly on level 1. Solving a level changes one word in a readout and nothing else -- no pause, no acknowledgement, and the next level only arrives if the player happens to press n. There is no title, no indication that there are eight levels or which one you are on beyond a number, and no way to quit except closing the window. A player who solves the last level is left sitting on it.

WHAT IT NEEDS, in the order it would be missed:

  1. SOMETHING ON SOLVING. A moment, and then the next level. The board is already there to animate: the crates are on the goals, and the seam tabs are the game's own iconography.
  2. A TITLE SCREEN. The place to say what a Mobius strip is, in a sentence, to someone who has not met one -- which the levels cannot do, because by the time a level is on screen it is too late to explain. The strip drawn as an actual twisted band would earn its keep here more than anywhere (sized-grid-lopy.6).
  3. PROGRESS. Which levels are done. Eight is few enough to show all of them at once, and their pictures are small enough to draw as thumbnails, which doubles as a level-select.
  4. QUIT, and probably pause. gloss's play gives no exit; the window's close button is the only way out, and that is not obvious in a full-window game.

NOT IN SCOPE HERE: a hint button, though the solver would give one for free (Sokoban.Solve.solveFrom already takes a game in progress rather than a level, for exactly that reason). Deadlock detection likewise -- the solver can tell you a position is lost, and telling the player so is a design decision, not a missing feature.

DEPENDS ON NOTHING, but reads better after sized-grid-lopy.6.
close_reason: Four screens (Title, Levels, Playing, Cleared) in a new Sokoban.Shell split out of Render; q leaves from anywhere via playIO with onEvent still pure; a victory lap walked with the game's own step; Test.Shell asserts the stage machine and the lap; sokoban-shot grew --stage. Also fixed EOF at the terminal's solved prompt. Commit 23fad70.

title: Ixed and a 'cell' Lens' for GridOf: the one element access the class hierarchy is missing
description:
From the sized-grid-90f survey. Verified against the tree, not guessed.

== Why

Grid already carries FunctorWithIndex, FoldableWithIndex and
TraversableWithIndex at Coord cs (Internal/Grid.hs:234-246) and is
Representable with Rep = Coord cs (Internal/Grid.hs:217). The one thing a
consumer cannot do is focus a single cell. There is no single-cell update
function anywhere in the public API either: the export list of
Data.Grid.Sized has gridFromVector, mapGrid, imapGrid, zipWithGrid and so on,
but nothing that writes one coordinate. Today that costs an imap over the
whole grid with an equality test per cell.

== What to add

  type instance Index   (GridOf v cs a) = Coord cs
  type instance IxValue (GridOf v cs a) = a
  instance (VG.Vector v a, IsCoordList cs) => Ixed (GridOf v cs a)

Note the instance head: GridOf, not Grid. indexGrid is already written at
GridOf with a VG.Vector constraint (Internal/Grid.hs:138), so the unboxed
grids in Data.Grid.Sized.Unboxed get this for the same code. Do not narrow it
to the boxed Grid.

Alongside it, export the honest optic:

  cell :: (VG.Vector v a, IsCoordList cs) => Coord cs -> Lens' (GridOf v cs a) a

lens fixes ix :: Index m -> Traversal' m (IxValue m) (confirmed in
lens-5.3.6, Control.Lens.At), which throws away the fact that here it can
never miss: every Coord cs indexes a cell by construction, so this is a
genuine Lens'. 'ix' is what the class demands and what generic code calls;
'cell' is what a consumer should reach for, and only the exported Lens' lets
them use it as a getter without a Monoid.

== Do NOT add At, and do not add Contains

At implies insert and delete, which a fixed shape cannot do. lens's own
Haddock for At says it outright: "Map-like containers form a reasonable
instance, but not Array-like ones, where you cannot satisfy the Lens laws."

Contains is the same mistake in the other direction: contains :: Index m ->
Lens' m Bool would have to be a constant-True getter with no lawful setter.

== Cost

None. lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Implemented Ixed and cell Lens' for GridOf, with focused getter/setter tests; full grid-sized test suite passes.

title: Restrictions keep the source's boundary policy, so a window invents a seam that is not there
description:
A sub-grid taken out of a grid keeps the source's coordinate constructor, so its boundary policy describes walls and seams that do not exist in the space it is a view of. This is a silent wrong answer, which is the failure mode the library organises its types against.

Evidence (source [1..9], window of 3 at offset 1, one step left of the window's first cell):

  Periodic 9 -> Periodic 3: window cell 0 step left = 4; the same step in the source = 1
  Clamped  9 -> Clamped  3: window cell 0 step left = 2; the same step in the source = 1

Periodicity is a property of a whole axis, and a proper sub-window of a periodic axis is not periodic. Clamped means stepping off the edge stays at the edge, and the window's edge is not the source's edge.

The API also disagrees with itself about this. shrinkGrid's instance head is ShrinkableGrid (c x ': cs) (c y ': as) (c z ': bs), so it FORCES the window's policy to equal the source's. gridWindows and gridTiles relate small and big only through CoordNat, so they leave it entirely FREE -- gridWindows @(Clamped 3) over a Grid '[Periodic 9] compiles, and is what produced the right-hand column above.

The rule, derived from the thesis in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-26-grid-view-design.md: a restriction destroys the boundary policy, a pointing preserves it. Every proper sub-grid should land on Ordinal, the policy-free axis the library already has.

The same rule fixes the offsets. shrinkGrid's offset into a Periodic 9 source windowed to 3 has type Coord '[Periodic 7]: the 7 is the offset count and Periodic is meaningless there, and worse, <> on that coordinate wraps offset 6 <> offset 3 round to offset 2.
design:
Two halves.

Docs-only half, worth landing on its own: state the rule in Internal.Grid.Windows's module header, on permuteGrid, and in the README's boundary-policy section.

Breaking half: shrinkGrid, gridWindows and gridTiles return Ordinal-axed grids, and shrinkGrid's offset becomes an Ordinal coordinate. Pre-1.0, and the status quo is a silent wrong answer, so the break is the cheap part.

Test.Windows's law -- gridWindows agrees with shrinkGrid at every offset -- is currently only statable at the policy-preserving instantiation, and uses Ordinal for both. Under the rule it becomes statable everywhere. Add a property that a window's off-edge step returns Nothing rather than a source-policy answer.
close_reason: Closed

title: Neighbourhood decomposition: split a window into focus and neighbours
description:
Prior art: Chris Penner's 'grids' has

  partitionFocus :: (Centered window, IsGrid window)
                 => Grid window a -> (a, Grid window (Maybe a))

splitting a window into its centre value and the same window with a hole where
the centre was. That is the shape Conway actually wants -- the rule is a
function of the cell AND its neighbours, and today a caller of 'neighbours'
has to carry the centre separately or re-index for it.

WHAT IT IS, precisely. Not a comonad. Grid window is Representable over
Coord window, and 'Centered window' names a basepoint c0, so the honest
statement is the splitting of a representable functor over a pointed index:

  (I -> a)  ~=  a * (I \ {i0} -> a)

The Maybe encodes the puncture in place rather than in the index type.

It IS the shape of a cofree-comonad step, though. For any comonad w,
'extract &&& duplicate' has type 'w a -> (a, w (w a))', which is one unfolding
of 'Cofree w a = a :< w (Cofree w a)'. partitionFocus is that shape with the
recursive position truncated to 'Maybe a': it keeps the values and marks the
hole instead of recursing. So it is a shadow of Store, which this library
already has via FocusedGrid's ComonadStore instance -- worth knowing so we do
not reinvent a comonad we already own.

DESIGN NOTE, and the reason not to copy it verbatim. The codomain
'(a, Grid window (Maybe a))' is strictly larger than the thing it represents:
it admits Nothing at any cell and Just at the centre, neither of which the
function can produce. The type does not say where the hole is. That is the
same species of imprecision the boundary thesis rejects -- the type should
say it, not the documentation.

Options for our version, to be decided when this is picked up:
  (a) a punctured coordinate type, so the hole lives in the index and the
      Maybe disappears;
  (b) return the neighbours as a sized vector of length 'Size window - 1',
      which is precise and cheap but discards the window's shape;
  (c) keep the shape and accept the Maybe, documenting the invariant --
      cheapest, and the option the thesis argues against.

Wants the odd-extent precondition to be expressible with a readable error,
which is sized-grid-0kq.
close_reason: Implemented as option (a), PuncturedCoord cs: a newtype over Ordinal (MaxCoordSize cs - 1), the punctured-coordinate index type. puncturedToCoord :: PuncturedCoord cs -> Coord cs is total (skips centreCoord's flat position). allPunctured enumerates them in allCoord order minus the centre. partitionFocus :: Grid cs a -> (a, PuncturedCoord cs -> a) in Focused.hs, per user's choice of the function-returning form. The 1<=MaxCoordSize cs proof needed for KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs - 1) is recovered at runtime via cmpNat, mirroring reifyOrdinal's own pattern, kept private (coordSpaceNonEmpty, unexported). Tests added in Test/Neighbours.hs and Test/Focused.hs; full suite (424 tests) and gameOfLife/ising-example/sudoko all build clean.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Follow-on from the comonad question, and a trap to avoid.

There IS a comonad structure available on Grid window without asking for it.
Grid window is Representable over Coord window, and for any MONOID m the
functor (m -> a) is the Traced comonad:

  extract f   = f mempty
  duplicate f = \i j -> f (i <> j)

Coord cs is a Monoid whenever every axis is, and both Clamped and Periodic are.
So the instance would typecheck today.

Do not add it blind. On Periodic axes it is sound: Periodic is a group, (<>) is
modular addition, and the comonad laws hold on the nose. On Clamped axes (<>)
is SATURATING addition, so duplicate composes offsets by clamping -- meaning
'move right 3, then right 3' and 'move right 6' agree near an edge when they
should not, and the comonad's own associativity is doing the silent clamping
the boundary thesis exists to forbid. The structure would be well-typed and
quietly wrong, which is the worst failure mode this library has.

If a Traced-style instance is ever wanted, it belongs behind a constraint that
admits only axes whose monoid is a group -- i.e. Periodic, and whatever later
axis types satisfy it -- not 'All Monoid cs'. Ordinal has no Monoid at all and
is fine by construction.

Recorded here rather than as its own issue because it is a decision not to
build something; promote it if someone proposes the instance.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Precision fix to the previous comment, which understated the problem.

Saturating addition on [0, n-1] IS associative, so Clamped's Monoid is lawful,
and the Traced comonad laws that follow from it hold on the nose. Nothing would
fail. A law-checking test suite would pass.

That makes the case against the instance stronger, not weaker: it would be
lawful AND semantically wrong for this library. duplicate composes displacements
by clamping, so near an edge 'right 3 then right 3' equals 'right 6' -- the
distinction between a move that fit and one that did not is erased by the
comonad's own composition, and no law says otherwise.

This is the sharpest example so far of why the thesis is stated in terms of what
the library refuses rather than what it proves: lawfulness does not imply the
boundary is being respected. Worth putting in the README if the thesis section
is ever expanded with a worked example.

title: FromJSON (Grid cs a) does not validate length, silently builds a Grid whose vector is the wrong size
description:
CONFIRMED empirically.

src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:145-151

    instance (All IsCoordLifted cs, FromJSON a) => FromJSON (Grid cs a) where
      parseJSON v = case (shape :: Shape cs) of
        ShapeNil -> Grid . V.singleton <$> parseJSON v
        ShapeCons _ -> do
          a :: [Grid (Tail cs) a] <- parseJSON v
          return $ Grid $ foldMap unGrid a

Nothing checks that the outer list has exactly CoordNat (Head cs) elements.

Probe result:
    decode "[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]" :: Maybe (Grid '[Ordinal 3, Ordinal 3] Int)
    => Just, with unGrid length 6 (type promises 9)

The whole point of the library is that the type pins the size. A decoded Grid that
breaks the invariant makes every downstream operation unsound:
  - index/gridIndex do 'v V.! coordPosition c' -> out-of-bounds exception at runtime
  - Applicative (<*>) is V.zipWith -> silently truncates
  - collapseGrid produces a ragged result

Contrast with gridFromList (src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:121-132), which DOES check
'length cg == natVal (Proxy @(CoordNat (Head cs)))' and returns Nothing. FromJSON
should reuse exactly that logic.

Note the constraints are also asymmetric: ToJSON needs AllGridSizeKnown + SListI,
FromJSON needs All IsCoordLifted. FromJSON needs the KnownNat evidence to validate,
so aligning them on AllGridSizeKnown is part of the fix.

Why the test suite misses it: aesonLaws only round-trips well-formed values.
Add a negative test decoding a short/long array and asserting Nothing.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
FIXED. FromJSON now validates the length at every dimension and 'fail's otherwise, so a decoded Grid always satisfies the size invariant. Constraints aligned with ToJSON (AllGridSizeKnown cs, SListI cs), which is what supplies the KnownNat evidence needed to check.

Ragged input is rejected by the recursion: the outer list length is checked at each level. All three negative tests (too few rows / too many rows / ragged rows) now pass.

title: Opt-in parallel stencil table build, threshold 1024 cells
description:
sized-grid-kb38 measured this at 2.6x on top of sized-grid-fup0's bounded build
(4.9x against today's stencilFor) at -N4 on a 90,000-cell grid, and settled the
threshold. What it did not settle is whether the library should do it without
being asked -- hence "opt-in" in the title, and hence this being a separate
issue from fup0, which has none of the same questions.

WHAT WORKS (spike/kb38-parstencil, tableParBounded):
  Both the width pass and the fill split by index range. Workers write disjoint
  slices of one mutable vector, join before freeze, and propagate the first
  exception any of them raised, so the result is a function of the arguments
  alone. Static split via forkOn, one chunk per capability; the chunk count
  does not matter (one per capability and eight per capability measure within
  2% at 90,000 cells) so there is no work queue to build.

THRESHOLD, decided:
  - coordSpaceSize >= 1024, and getNumCapabilities > 1.
  - Break-even is ~100 cells; the dispatch costs ~20-30 us of fork/join. 1024
    has an order of magnitude of margin either side and is a >= on a number the
    type already knows. Below it, or on a consumer not linked -threaded, the
    sequential path costs nothing extra.
  - Do NOT go past -N4 expecting more: parBounded on 90,000 cells measures
    29.9 / 16.2 / 11.7 / 14.6 ms at -N1/2/4/8. It is slower at eight than at
    four. The build is allocation-bound, so past a few cores it competes for
    memory bandwidth and GC rather than arithmetic.

THE DECISION THIS ISSUE HAS TO MAKE. Not whether it is faster -- it is -- but
whether a pure function in this library should contain unsafePerformIO + forkOn
and take a consumer's cores without being asked:
  - The purity argument is sound as far as it goes: disjoint writes to a vector
    nothing else can see, joined before freezing, exceptions propagated. But
    this library has spent real effort removing its last unsafeCoerce
    (sized-grid-wrc) and its asserts (adr.14), and an unsafePerformIO is a
    step back across that line even when it is defensible.
  - The win only exists for a consumer linked -threaded and running -N. For
    everyone else the code is dead weight.
  - Turning -N on costs the SEQUENTIAL path 7-38% (stencilFor: 57.0 ms at -N1,
    61.2 at -N4, 78.9 at -N8, unchanged code, parallel GC on a single-threaded
    mutator). So the fallback below the threshold is a path that -N has already
    made slower, which is an argument for the threshold being low rather than
    high.
  - A separate entry point (parMooreStencil, or a Build/Strategy argument)
    keeps the choice visible in the consumer's code, which is the same argument
    the module Haddock already makes for Stencil being a value rather than an
    argument to stencilGrid.

Do fup0 first: it is where most of the win is, it carries none of these
questions, and it changes the sequential baseline this would be measured
against.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- Decide and record the API shape (opt-in entry point vs internal dispatch).
- If it lands: threshold as above, and the sequential path must be unchanged
  below it.
- Test.Stencil states that the parallel build agrees exactly -- width and
  positions -- with the sequential one over mixed-policy axis lists.
- Benchmarks run with --time-mode wall (see bench/README.md) or they measure
  nothing.

title: _FocusedGrid Iso and a focus Lens: the ComonadStore methods do not compose
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier A: an Iso, plus the field lenses
that should come with it.

  data FocusedGrid cs a = FocusedGrid
      { focusedGrid         :: Grid cs a
      , focusedGridPosition :: Coord cs
      }                                                  Focused.hs:26

A product of exactly two fields, both public, no invariant relating them --
every `Coord cs` is a valid focus by construction. So:

  _FocusedGrid :: Iso' (FocusedGrid cs a) (Grid cs a, Coord cs)
  _FocusedGrid = iso (\(FocusedGrid g p) -> (g, p)) (uncurry FocusedGrid)

  focus     :: Lens' (FocusedGrid cs a) (Coord cs)
  unfocused :: Lens (FocusedGrid cs a) (FocusedGrid cs b) (Grid cs a) (Grid cs b)

The two record accessors are already exported (`FocusedGrid(..)`,
Focused.hs:3), so the getters are free; the lenses add the setters, which
today have to be written as a record update.

`focus` is the interesting one. `ComonadStore` gives `pos`/`seek`/`seeks`
(Focused.hs:52-58) which is get/set/modify on exactly this field under three
names -- `focus` is the fourth, but it is the one that COMPOSES: `focus . _1`
moves along the first axis of the focus (Field1 for Coord already exists,
Coord.hs:351), and `over focus (.+^ d)` is a step. Neither is expressible
through the ComonadStore methods without naming an intermediate.

Do this issue together with the asFocusedGrid law bug, which is about the
same type and whose honest fix probably IS this Iso: a `Grid` has no focus to
store, so the conversion between the two cannot be a `Lens'` in that
direction, but it can be an Iso to a pair.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Fixed together: dropped the unlawful asFocusedGrid Lens from IsGrid, added _FocusedGrid/focus/unfocused to FocusedGrid, wired law tests. See commit c0bc2df.

title: ../aoc 2025/04 calls moorePoints, removed in 0.3.0.0
description:
../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:62 does not compile against sized-grid 0.3.0.0:

    neighs = experiment (filter (/= coord) . nubOrd . moorePoints 1) g

    src/2025/04.hs:62:55: error: [GHC-88464]
        Variable not in scope:
          moorePoints :: t0 -> Coord [Clamped n, Clamped n] -> [Coord [Clamped n, Clamped n]]

'moorePoints' was REMOVED in the 0.3.0.0 neighbourhood replacement (see ChangeLog).
Removal rather than deprecation was deliberate: the behaviour changed under an
otherwise compatible signature.

This call site is the exact idiom the ChangeLog migration note predicts -- it
works around both of the old API's defects at once, including the centre
('filter (/= coord)') and the duplicates the clamping '(.+^)' produced
('nubOrd'). The replacement does neither.

MIGRATION

    neighs = experiment neighbours g

'neighbours' is the Moore neighbourhood at radius one, already excluding the
centre and already duplicate-free. Both the 'filter' and the 'nubOrd' go. Check
whether 'nubOrd' (Data.Containers.ListUtils) is still used elsewhere in the file;
if not, drop the import or -Wall will flag it.

DISCOVERED how: type-checking aoc during sized-grid-7d1 (HardWrap -> Clamped).
This is NOT caused by that rename -- the rename diff to this file is purely the
type name, and the error names 'moorePoints'. Note the error text shows
'Coord [Clamped n, Clamped n]' resolving correctly.

SIBLING of sized-grid-bb5, which covers the OTHER pre-existing aoc breakage
(the sealed-Grid reach-through at 2018/11.hs:31). aoc needs both before it builds.

CANNOT BE VERIFIED BY 'cabal build' in this environment: aoc depends on
hmatrix-0.20.2, whose configure step fails with 'Missing (or bad) C libraries:
blas, lapack'. Type-check individual modules instead -- see the
sized-grid-aoc-cannot-be-cabal-built memory for the exact recipe.
acceptance_criteria: ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs type-checks against sized-grid 0.3.0.0 with no reference to moorePoints, and no unused-import warning.
notes:
RESOLVED, but NOT by the migration this issue prescribed. The prescribed 'experiment neighbours g' is behaviour-preserving -- verified -- but it preserves a BUG.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG

experiment f w = fmap (peek w) (f (pos w)), so the neighbourhood is centred on
'pos g', NOT on 'coord'. In forklift, 'pos g' is the parse-time focus (0,0) and
never moves, while 'coord' varies over every cell. So forklift inspected the
corner's neighbourhood for all 100 cells. On the example that region is
{(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)} holding 2 Paper, so 'papers < 4' was always True and
forklift was degenerately constant.

Sibling call sites confirm the intended idiom: 2015/18.hs:51 and 2018/18.hs:67
both wrote 'filter (/= pos fg)', excluding the point experiment actually centres
on. 2025/04 wrote 'filter (/= coord)' -- a mis-adaptation.

PROVENANCE: it is a regression, with the original in git.
  d050263 (first commit): neighs = filter (/= coord) (nubOrd $ moorePoints 1 coord)
                          peek p g over that list -- centred on coord, CORRECT
                          doctest: '>>> solve example' == 13
  3278a32 ('2025 day 6'): refactored to experiment (...) g, which silently
                          re-centred on pos g, AND updated the doctest 13 -> 71
                          to match the newly-broken output. partTwo's 43 was
                          left alone and has been failing ever since.

MEASURED (probe against live 0.3.0.0, all four variants):
  doctest expects      solve=71  partTwo=43
  A current aoc code   solve=71  partTwo=71   <- partTwo already failing
  B this issue's fix   solve=71  partTwo=71   <- identical to A, bug preserved
  C centred on coord   solve=13  partTwo=43   <- both match d050263's originals

APPLIED (variant C):
  neighs = experiment neighbours (seek coord g)
  + 'seek' added to the Control.Comonad.Store import
  - 'import Data.Containers.ListUtils (nubOrd)' dropped
  doctest '>>> solve example' restored 71 -> 13

Both call sites needed no change: solve passes 'coord', partTwo passes 'pos c',
and seek overrides the focus in both.

VERIFIED: ghc -Wall -fno-code clean, no warnings; compiled and ran the edited
file -- solve example = 13, partTwo example = 43.
close_reason: Closed

title: [epic] Demos: improve UX and broaden showcase coverage
description: Reviewed gameOfLife, sudoko and ising-example. gameOfLife has a gloss UI but only click-to-toggle and a 't' pause key, no HUD, no presets, and the window title is still the leftover debug string "floatMe". sudoko is a pure stdout dump of one hardcoded board with no interactivity and no visualisation of the backtracking search it runs. Both undersell what the library actually does (typed boundary policies, stencils, grid-slicing) compared to ising-example's animated presentation. This epic tracks concrete UX fixes to the existing demos, a look at non-gloss UI options for headless/CI-friendly showcases, and new demos that exercise parts of the API (walker/path semantics, generic Rule/Stencil reuse) the current three don't touch.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Existing demo UX issues below are triaged and either fixed or explicitly deferred. 2. A decision is recorded on whether a terminal-based (non-gloss) UI is worth adding. 3. At least one new demo idea is scoped with a concrete acceptance criteria.
close_reason: All eight children closed. Acceptance criteria met: (1) every existing-demo UX issue fixed, not deferred -- gameOfLife has a HUD, presets, randomise/clear/speed keys and runtime-selectable rule and neighbourhood, and both leftover 'floatMe' titles are gone; sudoko's search is now animated and it takes a board from a file or stdin. (2) The terminal-UI decision is recorded on nnww.6 with measured dependency counts and shipped as sudoko --ansi (raw escape codes, zero new dependencies). (3) Two new demos rather than one scoped idea: 'automata' (Wireworld on the same Stencil engine, Langton's ant on Walker with the topology as a flag) and 'maze' (FocusedGrid-focused carving plus BFS on Clamped axes). Follow-ups filed: sized-grid-scja (the demos have no automated check; reference values for one are on its design field), sized-grid-kvpb (the four gloss windows were verified by logic, never seen rendered -- no Screen Recording permission on this machine), sized-grid-kqm8 (README names none of the five demos).

title: gameOfLife: fix leftover debug window title "floatMe"
description: Main.hs's play call opens the window with (InWindow "floatMe" (1100, 1100) (1, 1)), an obvious copy-paste leftover from another gloss example. Cosmetic but visible the moment the demo runs.
acceptance_criteria: Window title reflects the demo, e.g. "Game of Life".
close_reason: Closed

title: gameOfLife: add HUD, presets and speed/reset controls
description: Currently the only interaction is click-to-toggle a cell and 't' to pause/resume; there is no feedback on generation count, tick rate, or how to reset/randomize the board. Compare to ising-example, which at least streams a running simulation. Add: (1) an on-screen HUD showing generation count, ticking/paused state and tick interval; (2) a randomize-board key; (3) a clear-board key; (4) keys to speed up/slow down the tick interval; (5) at least one classic-pattern preset (glider, glider gun) loadable at start or via keypress, to make the periodic topology's wrap-around visible without having to draw one by hand.
acceptance_criteria: Running the demo shows generation count and tick rate on screen. 'r' randomizes, 'c' clears, +/- change speed, and a preset (e.g. glider) can be loaded and observed wrapping around the Periodic 60x60 board.
close_reason: Closed

title: gameOfLife: runtime-selectable rule and neighbourhood
description: applyRule is already parameterised over Rule n and Stencil cs, and Rule/Stencil are generic enough to express other 2-state totalistic automata (HighLife, Seeds) or a different neighbourhood (von Neumann instead of Moore radius 1). Right now gameOfLife bakes in gameOfLife :: Rule 2 and mooreStencil 1 at startup with no way to change them. Exposing a keypress to cycle between a couple of prebuilt Rule/Stencil pairs would demonstrate that the engine is generic, not just a Game-of-Life-specific loop.
acceptance_criteria: At least one alternate rule (e.g. HighLife) and one alternate neighbourhood (von Neumann) are selectable at runtime without recompiling, and the WorldState/applyRule plumbing needs no change beyond swapping the value.
close_reason: Closed

title: sudoko: visualise the backtracking solve step-by-step with gloss
description: sudoko's Main.hs only prints the given board and the final solved board to stdout; the backtracking search in solveBoard runs invisibly. This is the driver example for grid-slicing (gridTiles/zipLowerDim) but currently reads like a pure console script, not a showcase. Add a gloss (or equivalent) animated view that steps solveBoard's search one placement/backtrack at a time, colouring given clues, tentatively placed symbols, and backtracked cells differently, mirroring the visual style already used by gameOfLife and ising-example.
acceptance_criteria: Running the demo opens a window showing the 9x9 board updating live as the backtracking search proceeds, with distinct colours for given/placed/backtracked cells, and terminates showing the solved board.
close_reason: Closed

title: sudoko: accept a custom board instead of one hardcoded example
description: exampleGrid in sudoko/src/Main.hs is the only board the demo can ever solve; there is no CLI argument or file input. Accept a 9x9 board from a file path argument or stdin (e.g. 9 lines of 9 digits, 0 for blank, matching the existing literal-list shape already used for exampleGrid) so the demo can be pointed at other puzzles, including ones with no solution or multiple givens removed, without editing and recompiling.
acceptance_criteria: Running the executable with a file path argument solves that board; running with no argument falls back to the existing exampleGrid so the default demo still works.
close_reason: Closed

title: Research: terminal (non-gloss) UI option for demos
description: All three demos with visuals (gameOfLife, ising-example) depend on gloss, which needs a display/window and doesn't run headless or over SSH; sudoko has no visuals at all. Research whether a terminal-rendered alternative (ansi-terminal raw ASCII redraw, or a full TUI framework like brick/vty) is worth adding as a second front-end for one of the demos, so the library's grid output can be watched in a plain terminal/CI log without a GUI. Compare effort of a minimal ANSI redraw loop vs adopting brick, and note packaging/dependency cost.
design:
RESULT: raw ANSI redraw, no new dependency, prototyped for sudoko.
Shipped as sudoko/src/Sudoku/Render/Ansi.hs behind --ansi.

WHAT A GRID DEMO ACTUALLY NEEDS FROM A TERMINAL FRONT END
Move the cursor to the top-left, write a rectangle of characters, tint a
few of them, reset. That is the whole requirement. There is no layout to
negotiate, no scrolling viewport, no focus ring, no text entry, no mouse.
The shipped module's entire vocabulary is ESC[H, ESC[2J, ESC[?25l/h and
ESC[Nm -- four escape sequences, and the module is about 140 lines
including the board drawing and the degradation path.

DEPENDENCY COST, MEASURED (cabal build --dry-run, GHC 9.12.3, this store)
  bare escape codes   0 new packages
  ansi-terminal       3 (ansi-terminal, ansi-terminal-types, colour)
  vty 6.6             8 (blaze-builder, microlens, microlens-mtl,
                         microlens-th, utf8-string, vty, vty-unix,
                         vty-crossplatform)
  brick 2.13         18 (the eight above plus bimap, case-insensitive,
                         config-ini, data-clist, megaparsec,
                         parser-combinators, text-zipper, unix-compat,
                         word-wrap, and brick itself)

EFFORT
Raw ANSI: one afternoon, and most of it was the board layout and the
non-tty degradation, neither of which brick would have removed. brick:
the widget/attr/EventM scaffolding is not hard, but it is a new
programming model in a demo whose point is a grid library, and the
demo's own code would get smaller by roughly nothing. brick earns its
keep on scrolling lists, forms, resizable panes and mouse -- none of
which any of these three demos has or wants.

BOUNDS -- and the one place brick looks BETTER than what is already here
brick 2.13 declares base < 4.23 and containers with no upper bound, so
it does not carry the trap sized-grid-8hx records in cabal.project,
where the whole gloss stack caps containers < 0.8 and has no GHC 9.14
release. If a future demo genuinely needs a TUI, brick is not the
9.14 liability gloss is. That is a reason not to rule it out, not a
reason to adopt it now.

WHY SUDOKO AND NOT GAMEOFLIFE
sudoko had no visuals at all and its search is a sequence of small
discrete edits -- exactly what a character grid shows well, and what
reads fine in a scrollback or a log. gameOfLife's gloss front end
already does its job, and its interaction is mouse-driven cell editing,
which is the part a terminal cannot reproduce. A 60x60 board of
half-block characters would be legible; the editing would not.

DEGRADATION, which is the actual headless win
When stdout is not a terminal the escape codes and the frame delay are
both dropped and frames are appended instead of redrawn. So
`sudoko --ansi --rate 5000 board.txt | tail` works in a pipe and in a CI
log, which is the case gloss cannot serve at all -- it needs a window.
acceptance_criteria: A short writeup comparing at least two approaches (raw ANSI redraw vs a TUI library) with a recommendation, and a decision on whether to prototype one for sudoko or gameOfLife.
close_reason: Decision: raw ANSI redraw, zero new dependencies, prototyped for sudoko as Sudoku.Render.Ansi behind --ansi. Comparison of bare escape codes / ansi-terminal / vty / brick with measured dependency counts (0 / 3 / 8 / 18 packages on GHC 9.12.3) is on the design field, along with why sudoko and not gameOfLife and the one point in brick's favour (it does not carry gloss's containers<0.8 GHC 9.14 trap, sized-grid-8hx).

title: New demo: maze generation + pathfinding to showcase FocusedGrid/walker semantics
description: The three existing demos (gameOfLife, sudoko, ising-example) exercise stencils, grid-slicing and bulk grid ops, but none exercise FocusedGrid, Comonad/ComonadStore, or boundary-aware walking, which is a design area under active research (sized-grid-ylhl, sized-grid-i0ob). A maze-generation (e.g. randomized DFS/Wilson's) plus pathfinding (BFS/A*) demo on a Grid '[Clamped n, Clamped n] naturally needs stepping a focus through the grid and reacting to walls/edges, giving that part of the API a concrete showcase. Visualise generation and solve steps with gloss.
acceptance_criteria: A new executable generates a maze on a Clamped grid, finds a path between two points, and animates both generation and solve, using FocusedGrid/walker-style movement rather than raw index arithmetic.
close_reason: New 'maze' executable: randomised depth-first carving then BFS on Grid '[Clamped 61, Clamped 61], animated with gloss. The carving head is a FocusedGrid's focus (pos/seek/gridIndex), candidate directions are a two-step Path traced from it, and neither phase contains a bounds test or index arithmetic -- offsetCoord returning Nothing on a Clamped axis is the only wall test. Verified: perfect maze (spanning tree, 900 cells / 899 opened walls), solid border, route (1,1)-(59,59) with every step adjacent and no repeats.

title: New demo: additional cellular automaton reusing gameOfLife's generic Rule/Stencil engine
description: gameOfLife's Rule n / applyRule / Stencil plumbing is already generic enough to run other totalistic or non-totalistic automata (e.g. Wireworld, which needs 4 states and asymmetric transition logic, or Langton's Ant, which needs a single stateful walker instead of a bulk rule). Adding a second, visually distinct automaton as its own small executable (sharing the Rule/Stencil approach where it fits, diverging where it doesn't, e.g. Langton's Ant needs a walker not a stencil) would demonstrate the engine isn't Game-of-Life-specific and would give the walker-semantics research another concrete data point.
acceptance_criteria: A new executable runs and visualises at least one automaton other than Conway's Game of Life (Wireworld or Langton's Ant), reusing UGrid/Stencil/Rule machinery where applicable.
close_reason: New 'automata' executable. Wireworld runs on the same Stencil/stencilGrid machinery as gameOfLife (four states, non-totalistic transition, Clamped axes) proving the engine is not Life-specific; Langton's ant runs on Walker/FocusedGrid/stepWalker because a stencil cannot express a single walker with a heading, and its topology (Periodic/Clamped/Reflective) is a CLI flag since stepWalker delegates the edge to the axis type. Both checked against independent reference implementations.

title: Retune the benchmark gate threshold once CI has run history
description:
sized-grid-adr.11 shipped the gate at --fail-if-slower 25, the value that issue proposed, with no CI data to set it from.

The one measurement taken is not reassuring. Same machine, same binary, same baseline CSV, aarch64-darwin/9.12.3: with an unrelated build running alongside, 17 of 48 benchmarks failed at 26-71% slower and the suite took 405s. Once the machine was quiet, none failed and it took 132s. The failures were not a property of the code -- they clustered in time and hit the small benchmarks hardest, where 'extract 50x50' is 10ns and one rescheduled thread is the whole measurement.

A GitHub shared runner is permanently in something like the first condition. If PRs start going red for reasons nobody can reproduce, the gate gets switched off, which is the failure mode sized-grid-adr.11 was explicitly trying to avoid.

After a few weeks of runs, look at the bench job's history and either tighten 25 (if the runner turns out steadier than feared) or raise it. The per-run CSVs are uploaded as artifacts on every run, pass or fail, so the spread is recoverable. If loosening the single global threshold would blunt it too much, note that tasty-bench takes FailIfSlower via localOption/adjustOption per benchmark or bgroup -- the nanosecond-scale ones could carry a looser bound than the millisecond-scale ones instead of everything moving together.

title: Seam rule: boundary resolution returns a coordinate AND a frame transform
description:
The unifying shape for every non-separable policy, from the Gemini transcript
and worth keeping because it is correct:

    type Policy = Coord -> (Coord, Needle -> Needle)

Resolving an out-of-range position returns the canonical in-range coordinate
AND a transform to apply to the walker's own direction. That second component
is the seam rule, and it is the whole content of the idea.

On a Mobius strip, crossing the seam an odd number of times flips the y axis.
The coordinate lands somewhere legal either way; what distinguishes Mobius from
a plain torus is that your notion of "up" is now different. A policy that
returns only a coordinate cannot express that.

WHAT THIS SUBSUMES

  Torus       -> (wrap c, id)
  Reflective  -> (bounce c, negate on the reflected axis)   <- note: bounce is
