title: CI never runs the atlas-topology or grid-atlas test suites
description:
Neither CI job executes the 21 tests in atlas-topology and grid-atlas. They only ever run on a developer's machine via an explicit 'cabal test all'.

Where it goes wrong:

1. flake-check job runs 'nix build .#checks.$system.ghc912 .#checks.$system.ghc914'. flake.nix's checks are mkPackage, and mkPackage is 'doCheck (hsPkgs.callCabal2nix "grid-sized" src {})' -- cabal2nix on the repo root picks up grid-sized.cabal, the only .cabal there. The derivation's checkPhase therefore runs grid-sized's three suites (tests, downstream, readme) and nothing else. grid-sized does not depend on grid-atlas, so the atlas packages are never in the build graph at all. flake.nix's own comment, 'nix flake check builds the library and runs the tasty suite on both', is accurate but easy to read as covering more than it does.

2. cabal matrix job runs 'cabal build all --enable-tests --enable-benchmarks'. Its comment states outright that 'This matrix builds only', deferring execution to nix flake check -- which, per (1), does not cover these packages. The two jobs each assume the other runs them.

3. bench job runs grid-sized:bench:benchmarks only.

Uncovered: Test.Seam (8 tests, incl. the vertex-cycle law), Test.CubeMap, Test.Klein, Test.Mobius, Test.Projective, Test.Tiles (13 tests). All currently pass locally, so this is a gap in the safety net rather than a hidden red -- but the projective atlas landed in fe5a76a with tests that CI has never executed, and sized-grid-5gm7 is a confirmed defect in exactly this uncovered code.
design:
Cheapest fix: change the cabal matrix job's build step to 'cabal test all --enable-tests' (or add a 'cabal test all' step after the build). That covers every package across the whole 9.10/9.12/9.14 matrix and needs no flake changes; the suites are fast (about 17s total, dominated by grid-sized).

Alternative: add atlas-topology and grid-atlas to flake.nix as their own callCabal2nix derivations under checks, so nix flake check covers them too. More faithful to the current structure but more moving parts, and it needs the ghc-typelits plugin overrides threaded through for grid-atlas.

Whichever is chosen, correct the two stale comments in ci.yml and flake.nix that describe the current coverage.
close_reason: Closed

title: Periodic's Enum wraps modulo n-1, so toEnum 2 :: Periodic 3 is 0
description:
src/SizedGrid/Coord/Periodic.hs:42-44

    toEnum x = Periodic $ fromJust $ numToOrdinal $
        (fromIntegral x) `mod` (maxCoordSize (Proxy @(Periodic n)))

'maxCoordSize' is natVal - 1, not natVal, so the period is one short. Every
other operation in the module uses 'maxCoordSize + 1' correctly, so it is the
only place with the off-by-one.

Consequences: fromEnum . toEnum is not the identity on the type's own range
(toEnum 4 :: Periodic 5 == 0), and toEnum 3,4,5 :: Periodic 3 gives [1,0,1]
rather than [0,1,2]. Not caught before because the coordinate enumeration path
('allCoordLike') goes through Ordinal's Enum, not Periodic's, and HardWrap's is
derived from Ordinal's.

Found while rewriting these lines for sized-grid-upo.
acceptance_criteria: fromEnum . toEnum == id on [0, n); toEnum wraps with period n. Regression test in tests/Test/Ordinal.hs.
close_reason: Fixed in commit 'Make Ordinal a newtype over Int' on branch worktree-ordinal-int; 100 tests pass, zero warnings

title: -O2 on the library silently strips unsafeOrdinal's assert unless -fno-ignore-asserts is restated after it
description:
Measured under sized-grid-adr.6. Adding -O2 to the library re-enables -fignore-asserts, because -O implies it and the last flag on the command line wins. The library's deliberate -fno-ignore-asserts (sized-grid-6os) is written before any optimisation flag cabal appends, so a naive 'ghc-options: -O2' silently defeats it.

Evidence: a downstream consumer calling 'unsafeOrdinal 99 :: Ordinal 5' and forcing it:
  base (-O1, -fno-ignore-asserts)          -> ASSERT FIRED
  -O2 appended after                       -> NO ASSERT: got 99
  -fexpose-all-unfoldings only             -> ASSERT FIRED
  -O2 + unfolding flags appended after     -> NO ASSERT: got 99
  -O2 with -fno-ignore-asserts restated last -> ASSERT FIRED

Fix: whenever an optimisation flag is added to the library stanza, -fno-ignore-asserts must come after it. Anyone adding -O2 later in a cabal.project 'package grid-sized' stanza reintroduces the bug, since project ghc-options are appended after the .cabal's.
close_reason: Closed

title: (BUG) The readme test-suite does not compile: README.md still uses asFocusedGrid
description:
c0bc2df dropped asFocusedGrid from IsGrid (sized-grid-3au) but left README.md:144 using it:

  applyRule rule = over asFocusedGrid $
      extend $ \fg -> rule (extract fg) $ map (\p -> peek p fg) $
          neighbours $ pos fg

README.lhs is a symlink to README.md and is the readme test-suite's main-is,
so this is a build failure, not a stale doc:

  README.lhs:144:23: error: [GHC-88464] Variable not in scope: asFocusedGrid

CI's matrix job runs 'cabal build all --enable-tests --enable-benchmarks'
(.github/workflows/ci.yml:146), so master is red on this today. Found while
working sized-grid-djh; nothing in that change touches it, and the failure
reproduces on c0bc2df alone.

applyRule is polymorphic over 'grid cs' via IsGrid, so the replacement has to
go through asGrid, which survived: focus the grid, extend, take the grid back.
The working tree at the time this was filed had an uncommitted
'focusedAtZero :: IsCoordList cs => Grid cs a -> FocusedGrid cs a' in
Focused.hs, which is what that rewrite wants:

  applyRule rule = over asGrid (focusedGrid . extend step . focusedAtZero)

Whether focusedAtZero ships is the open question -- it is the same 'focus at
the origin because there is nowhere else to start' that asFocusedGrid was
criticised for hiding, but as a named function rather than a lens it is
honest about it.
close_reason: i fixed it

title: toEnum honours the boundary policy only for Periodic; Clamped/Reflective/Reflect101 throw
description:
The library's thesis is that the coordinate type IS the boundary policy. Every other operation upholds it -- .+^ clamps on Clamped, <> clamps, .+^ reflects on Reflective. toEnum is the one escape hatch that does not.

Clamped, Reflective and Reflect101 all get Enum via 'deriving newtype' from Ordinal (Coord/Clamped.hs:29, Reflective.hs:33, Reflect101.hs:32). Ordinal's own toEnum (Ordinal.hs:232) calls 'error' when numToOrdinal returns Nothing. Only Periodic writes a real instance (Coord/Periodic.hs:37).

Observed:

  toEnum 12   :: Clamped 10    = EXCEPTION: toEnum: 12 is out of range for Ordinal 10
  toEnum (-1) :: Clamped 10    = EXCEPTION: toEnum: -1 is out of range for Ordinal 10
  toEnum 12   :: Reflective 10 = EXCEPTION: toEnum: 12 is out of range for Ordinal 10
  toEnum 12   :: Periodic 10   = 2
  toEnum (-1) :: Periodic 10   = 9

Clamped should give 9 and 0; Reflective should give 7.

What makes this more than a curiosity: enumRangeLaws was added in 3ffd0b9 specifically to assert that toEnum stays in range, and tests/Main.hs:361 applies it to Periodic alone -- the only one of the four that passes. The three that would fail are silently excluded, so the property reads as covering the invariant when it covers a quarter of it.

Partiality is at least undocumented either way: Ordinal's toEnum error is not mentioned in the Haddock of the derived instances.
design:
Decide first whether toEnum is meant to be policy-honouring or partial-and-Ordinal-like.

If policy-honouring (consistent with the library's thesis, and with what Periodic already does): give Clamped, Reflective and Reflect101 hand-written Enum instances routing toEnum through the same normalisation their .+^ uses, then extend enumRangeLaws to all four in tests/Main.hs.

If deliberately partial: say so in Haddock on each derived instance, and either drop enumRangeLaws or restate it as a Periodic-specific property so it does not read as a general law. Note that this reading makes Periodic the odd one out instead.

title: Property-test that zeroPosition agrees with mempty/zeroV where both exist
description:
Surfaced while answering a question about whether a standard "zero"
typeclass (Monoid, AdditiveGroup, etc.) could replace IsCoord.zeroPosition.

IsCoord.zeroPosition is the only zero-like operation every axis type
(Clamped, Periodic, Reflective, Reflect101, Ordinal) honestly implements.
Monoid's mempty only exists for Clamped and Periodic; AdditiveGroup's
zeroV only exists for Periodic (deliberately -- Clamped saturates instead
of wrapping, so it has no additive inverse and would be dishonest as a
group, the same reason asFocusedGrid was unlawful, sized-grid-3au).

Coord/Class.hs documents the relationship with a default:

    zeroPosition :: (1 <= n, KnownNat n) => c n
    default zeroPosition :: Monoid (c n) => c n
    zeroPosition = mempty

but nothing checks that an instance which defines zeroPosition
explicitly (or picks up a Monoid default) actually agrees with mempty
and zeroV on the axes where more than one of these is defined:

  - Clamped n: has both zeroPosition and Monoid -- check zeroPosition == mempty
  - Periodic n: has zeroPosition, Monoid, and AdditiveGroup -- check
    zeroPosition == mempty == zeroV

This is a cheap addition to isCoordLaws in Test/Utils.hs (or a sibling
helper it's composed with), gated on the relevant Monoid/AdditiveGroup
constraints so it only runs where applicable.
close_reason: Closed

title: Is the atlas/seam layer a general discrete-manifold library, not a grid-specific one?
description:
sized-grid-fh2 (atlas: charts glued by seam transitions), sized-grid-o1n (seam
rule: boundary resolution returns a coordinate AND a frame transform) and
sized-grid-1bm (space-group framing: grid space = Z^n/G) together describe
something that doesn't actually mention cell contents anywhere load-bearing:

  * ChartId + Coord cs is a coordinate on a discrete space built from charts.
  * A seam is a transition (ChartId, Coord) -> (ChartId, Coord) plus a frame
    transform, i.e. an element of a groupoid of chart-gluings.
  * Z^n/G (sized-grid-1bm) already states the single-chart case as a quotient
    by a group; the multi-chart atlas is the same idea one level up -- a
    manifold built from charts and transition functions, which is exactly the
    textbook definition of a manifold's atlas, just discrete.

None of that needs `Grid cs a` specifically. A chart could be any
Representable/indexed structure, or nothing at all (bare coordinate topology
with no payload, useful for pathfinding/graph problems). grid-atlas v1 is
being built AS a grid-specific instantiation on purpose -- concrete and
checkable beats an abstracted-too-early library -- but the question is real:
once there's a second concrete consumer (the cube map, or something from
../aoc), does the ChartId/Seam/transition-table machinery want to be pulled
out into its own package with no grid-sized dependency, something like a
'manifold' or 'atlas-topology' library that grid-atlas (and potentially
non-grid consumers) depend on?

NOT to be resolved now. Revisit once grid-atlas has at least two concrete
atlases built (the degenerate/tiled one and the cube map) -- that is the
minimum evidence needed to see which parts of the design are actually
grid-independent versus which only look that way with one example.
close_reason: Resolved via decision sized-grid-jtt: evidence bar met (two atlases exist), but no real non-grid consumer exists to drive an extraction, so machinery stays in grid-atlas until one does.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
The second data point this issue asked for now exists: sized-grid-68j (cube map, Data.Grid.Atlas.CubeMap) shipped alongside grid-atlas v1's tiled atlas. Both are grid-specific instantiations, so the extraction question can now actually be compared against two real designs instead of one:

- Tiled atlas (fh2): AtlasCoord = (Ordinal k, Coord cs), transitions are all identity, atlasOffsetHead only ever moves the head axis.
- Cube map (68j): AtlasCoord = (Ordinal 6, Coord cs) with cs fixed to '[Ordinal n, Ordinal n], transitions are a hand-written 24-entry table keyed on Face/Axis/Extremum, cubeStep applies a coordinate remap AND a heading frame transform.

What's grid-independent in the cube map's design, on this evidence: Face/Axis/Extremum/Heading and cubeSeam's shape (source seam -> destination seam + orientation bit) don't mention Grid or cell contents anywhere load-bearing -- a chart could be any Representable, or nothing. What's still grid-specific: cubeAtlas and cubeStep both hard-code cs = '[Ordinal n, Ordinal n] and go through Atlas/AtlasCoord.

Not resolving the extraction question itself here -- that's still a real design decision (new package vs. staying put) worth deciding deliberately rather than as a side effect of closing 68j. Flagging that the evidence bar this issue set is now met.

title: Grid is boxed-vector only; no unboxed/storable representation for numeric grids
description:
src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:40 hardcodes Data.Vector (boxed).

For the numeric workloads this library is aimed at, that is the wrong default:
  - ising-example/src/Main.hs is a Monte Carlo spin simulation
  - gameOfLife/src/Main.hs is a cellular automaton
  - ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs builds a 300x300 Int summed-area table
All of these want Data.Vector.Unboxed and get boxed Ints with a pointer chase each.

The complication: Functor/Applicative/Monad/Representable/Traversable all require the
element type to be unconstrained, so Grid cannot simply switch to Unboxed.

Options:
  1. Parameterise over the vector type:
       newtype GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a = GridOf (v a)
       type Grid = GridOf V.Vector
     Keep the current instances for the boxed version; give the unboxed version the
     instances it can support (Foldable-like ops via a Vector.Generic constraint,
     no Functor). Costs an extra type parameter in every signature.
  2. Leave Grid boxed and add a separate SizedGrid.Grid.Unboxed with a monomorphic
     API (map/zipWith/fold/index taking Unbox constraints). Less elegant, far less
     disruptive, and covers the actual use cases.

Recommend option 2 first -- it is additive and non-breaking. Revisit 1 only if the
duplication becomes painful.

Prerequisite either way: benchmarks, so the win is measured rather than assumed.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Baseline landed (sized-grid-amf). Relevant figure for the unboxed-Grid case: a 300x300
Grid of Int costs 93 MB of allocation to build via tabulate and 72 MB to read back via
index over allCoord, against a true payload under 1 MB. Most of that is Ordinal and
Coord boxing rather than the vector itself, so sized-grid-upo should land first --
switching the vector to unboxed cannot help while every element access still constructs
a boxed Coord. Benchmarks to watch: 'tabulate 300x300', 'index x90000' and 'fmap
300x300' in bench/Main.hs.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Unblocked in principle by the sized-grid-upo work: Ordinal is now a newtype over
Int, so a Coord's components are machine words rather than GADTs carrying
dictionaries. That was the stated prerequisite for an unboxed or storable Grid.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Measure-first spike (bench-spike/, branch worktree-up6-measure-unboxed, ghc 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin).
Minimal UGrid over Data.Vector.Unboxed vs the real Grid, same shapes, same workloads, both
sides through coordPosition/allCoord so the coord machinery cancels.

  operation (300x300 Int)   boxed              unboxed            delta
  tabulate                  14.2 ms / 20 MB    1.90 ms / 9.6 MB   7.5x faster
  index x90000              765 us  / 26 B     751 us  / 41 B     none
  map then sum              1.52 ms / 4.1 MB   92.5 us / 18 B     16x faster
  foldl'                    312 us             86.8 us            3.6x faster
  row prefix scanl1         1.68 ms / 4.2 MB   845 us  / 5.5 MB   2x faster
  transpose                 14.6 ms / 18 MB    2.24 ms / 9.6 MB   6.5x faster
  SAT build (2018/11)       57.3 ms / 64 MB    13.3 ms / 40 MB    4.3x faster
  SAT solve, 360k reads     35.2 ms / 157 MB   36.4 ms / 157 MB   none

Conclusion: the win is real but it is NOT where up6's description assumed. It is entirely in
BULK operations that touch the vector wholesale (3.6x-16x). Per-coordinate access wins exactly
nothing -- 'index' and the SAT solve are identical to within noise, because their cost is the
Coord arithmetic and not the vector read.

That settles the API shape: an unboxed grid wants map/zipWith/fold/scanl1/tabulate/transpose,
and there is no point optimising an indexed read path.

Caveat on the fmap row: part of that 16x is fusion U.map/U.foldl' get and the derived
Functor/Foldable on Grid do not, so read the SAT build (4.3x on a whole real workload) as the
honest headline. Caveat on index: both benchmarks walk row-major, which is the prefetch-friendly
best case for boxed. The consumer's real access patterns are also near-sequential, so this is
representative rather than flattering.

Separate finding, filed as its own issue: the SAT solve burns 157 MB for 360,000 reads (~436 B
per read) and that is all coordinate arithmetic ((.+^) over allCoord), not the grid.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
From the sized-grid-zzj evaluation (closed): if this lands on vector-sized rather than raw Data.Vector.Unboxed, note that vector-sized 1.6.1 indexes with Data.Finite's Integer-backed alias, not an Int-backed one:

    index (Vector v) (Finite i) = v `VG.unsafeIndex` fromIntegral i
    generate f = Vector (VG.generate i (f . Finite . fromIntegral))

So an Ordinal -> Finite conversion at that boundary allocates an Integer per index, and that cost is inherent to vector-sized rather than to Ordinal -- switching Ordinal's representation would not avoid it. Given the spike above already showed per-coordinate access wins nothing and the whole win is in bulk operations, the cheap route is to keep the bulk API off the index path entirely (map/zipWith/fold/scanl1/tabulate/transpose over the underlying vector) and not route reads through Finite at all. Raw Data.Vector.Unboxed, as the spike used, sidesteps the question.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Ordering: sized-grid-0tj should land first. Decomposing the solve loop showed (.+^) is 93% of
it, with a 14.8x ceiling, against up6's 4.3x on the build. On ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs as a whole
(1 build + 17 solves) up6 alone is 1.04x, 0tj alone is 6.6x, both together 11.6x. up6 is still
worth doing -- it is most of what is left once 0tj lands -- but it is the second half, not the
first. Full numbers and root cause on sized-grid-0tj.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Follow-up: evaluated forking vector-sized. Recommendation is DON'T -- and don't
depend on it either. Use raw Data.Vector.Unboxed, as the spike above did.

Maintenance status (checked 2026-08-13): dormant, not dead.
  - Last commit 2024-02-01 (~2.5 years ago); not archived; 6 open issues, 2 open PRs.
  - Last release 1.6.1 uploaded 2024-02-07 by koz_ross, not the author (expipiplus1).
  - Last FEATURE release was 1.6.0, January 2022 (~4.5 years ago). The two releases
    since were life support -- bounds bumps and foldl' future-proofing contributed by
    Bodigrim, i.e. an ecosystem caretaker keeping it compiling.
  - tested-with maxes at GHC 9.2.1.
  - BUT it builds fine on GHC 9.12.3 -- verified by compiling against it; 1.6.1 is
    already in the nix GHC package set. The presburger lesson recorded in
    sized-grid.cabal is that the risk is a dep that stops BUILDING on a GHC we need,
    not one that stops adding features. vector-sized is not there.

The strong version of the fork idea does work, and deserves credit: fork it and swap
Finite n for our own Ordinal n, and finite-typelits disappears along with the
KnownIntegral/Limited constraint wall documented in sized-grid-zzj. That would give an
Int-backed index under plain KnownNat, the vocabulary the rest of the library speaks.
So the fork genuinely can solve the representation problem.

It fails on three other counts:

1. It duplicates a size proof we already have. Grid is
   'newtype Grid (cs :: [Type]) a = Grid (V.Vector a)' -- a flat vector carrying our
   own type-level size machinery (cs, Coord, Ordinal, AllGridSizeKnown). A type-level
   size tag IS vector-sized's whole value proposition. Adopting it puts a
   Vector (product-of-cs) a inside a Grid cs a: two independent size proofs to keep in
   agreement, plus the product constraint relating them. AllGridSizeKnown already
   carries KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs) as a superclass, and sized-grid-oxb is open work
   to REMOVE a KnownNat (n * n) from signatures. Same direction as the finite-typelits
   migration, same reason to decline.

2. Cost: 9,521 lines across 12 modules, with deps on adjunctions, comonad,
   distributive, binary and primitive -- owned forever, on our GHC upgrade schedule.
   Ordinal.hs is ~200 lines.

3. It buys nothing the spike above needs. All measured wins (7.5x tabulate, 16x
   map/sum, 4.3x SAT build) are bulk operations over the underlying vector, which never
   touch an index type. The spike also found per-coordinate access wins nothing --
   and the indexed read path is exactly the surface vector-sized would provide.

A fork would be justified if we wanted to EXPOSE a size-tagged vector in the public
API, or if vector-sized broke on a GHC we need and upstream stayed silent. Neither
holds. If the second ever does, the proportionate fix is a bounds-bump PR or a Hackage
revision -- which is precisely what the last two releases were.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Re-priced after sized-grid-czf landed, on the real consumer rather than by projection.

WHOLE PROGRAM, ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs (1 SAT build + 17 solves), same binary shape
both sides, aoc's nix devshell, GHC 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin:

  against master (pre-0tj, pre-czf)   0.72 s   2.91 GB allocated   MUT 0.645 s
  against 0tj + czf                   0.28 s   1.07 GB allocated   MUT 0.207 s

2.6x end to end. That is the coordinate work finished; up6 is what is left.

WHERE THE REMAINING 207 ms GOES. Split by re-benchmarking the two halves of that
program separately (scratch package, code copied unchanged from 11.hs):

  makeSAT 300x300, the build          78.5 ms
  solve 3, one solve of 360k offsets   8.02 ms
  solve 3 with 'corners' hoisted       4.12 ms

1 build + 17 solves = 78.5 + 17x8.02 = 215 ms, against 207 ms measured. The model
is the program.

So the shares are: build 36 percent, solves 64 percent. And of a solve, only
~2.0 ms is the library's offset path (the 'four corner reads' benchmark, now
2.02 ms / 53 B per 360,000 offsets) -- the other ~6 ms is the caller rebuilding
its four-element 'corners' list inside squareSum, once per position, 90,000 times
a solve. Hoisting it halves the solve. Filed separately.

WHAT up6 IS NOW WORTH HERE. The build is bulk operations over the whole grid --
tabulate, scanl1Grid, mapLowerDim, transposeGrid -- which is exactly the shape
the spike above measured at 4.3x for the SAT build and 7.5x for tabulate. At
that ratio the build goes 78.5 -> ~18 ms, i.e. ~28 percent off the program, 1.4x.
It does NOT help the solves: the spike measured per-coordinate index reads as
unchanged (765 us boxed vs 751 us unboxed), and this split confirms the solve
half is caller-side list building rather than element access.

So: still worth doing, and now the largest library-side item left for this
workload, but as a 1.4x on the build half and not a rewrite of the hot loop. The
stronger cases remain ising-example and gameOfLife, which are bulk map/zip over
numeric grids end to end -- 16x on map/sum in the spike -- rather than
offset-and-read like 11.hs.

Recommendation unchanged: option 2, an additive SizedGrid.Grid.Unboxed with a
monomorphic API, non-breaking.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Option 1 re-evaluated and now RECOMMENDED, reversing the earlier call for option 2. Compiled a
crux module (worktree-up6-generic-grid) against the three things that were not obviously possible.
All three work.

  newtype GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a = GridOf (v a)
  type Grid = GridOf V.Vector          -- zero-arity, so 'Grid cs' stays partially applicable

1. MIXED REPRESENTATION. The objection that killed option 1 on paper was nested grids: a grid is
   never Unbox, so 'splitGrid :: Grid (c ': cs) a -> Grid '[c] (Grid cs a)' cannot be uniform in v.
   It does not have to be -- the outer vector is always boxed, and that is statable:

     splitGrid   :: (VG.Vector v a, AllSizedKnown cs)
                 => GridOf v (c ': cs) a -> GridOf V.Vector '[c] (GridOf v cs a)
     combineGrid :: VG.Vector v a
                 => GridOf V.Vector '[c] (GridOf v cs a) -> GridOf v (c ': cs) a

   Compiles, and combineGrid . splitGrid roundtrips at v ~ U.Vector. mapLowerDim generalises the
   same way -- it already chunks through a LIST of vectors, so only the element constraint changes.

2. THE BOXED INSTANCE SET SURVIVES, as concrete instances at 'GridOf V.Vector cs'. Functor,
   Foldable, Applicative, Distributive and Representable all carry over with bodies unchanged
   ('deriving newtype' for the first two). Only Traversable needs writing out by hand: GND coerces
   under the applicative m, whose role it must assume nominal. One line.

3. THE PROOFS STILL DISCHARGE through the extra parameter. The ShrinkableGrid instance -- windowFits,
   reifyCoord's existential, sliceGrid's 'off + len <= m' -- typechecks unchanged, and natnormalise
   still fires. GHC additionally reports 'VG.Vector v a' as REDUNDANT on the window helper, which is
   the useful surprise: shrinkGrid only ever moves whole sub-grids, so the shape algebra is
   element-agnostic and does not even need the element constraint.

WHY THIS REVERSES THE RECOMMENDATION. Option 2's cost was mis-stated as 'less elegant'. Its real
cost is that the unboxed module needs its own dropGrid/takeGrid/sliceGrid/splitGrid/combineGrid/
splitHigherDim/mapLowerDim/gridTiles/ShrinkableGrid/collapseGrid -- i.e. the whole shape algebra,
including the windowFits proof and the 'off + len <= m' restatement that took all of sized-grid-wrc
to get right. Two copies of this library's hardest and most safety-critical code, guaranteed to
drift. Under option 1 that code exists once and both representations get all of it.

Option 1's cost is one genuinely ambiguous signature -- gridFromList, whose v is determined by
nothing -- fixed by exporting it monomorphised at V.Vector from Data.Grid.Sized. Every other
function takes a grid as an argument, so v is inferred. That is far cheaper than the original
'an extra type parameter in every signature' framing assumed.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED on branch worktree-up6-generic-grid (commit d921a80), as option 1. All 431 tests
pass (16 new), hlint clean, readme and downstream suites green.

SHAPE. 'newtype GridOf v (cs :: [Type]) a = Grid (v a)', with 'type Grid = GridOf V.Vector' and a
new Data.Grid.Sized.Unboxed giving 'type UGrid = GridOf U.Vector'. The synonym takes no parameters
of its own so 'Grid cs' stays partially applicable; no existing signature in the tree changed. The
constructor is still spelled 'Grid' (different namespace from the synonym), so internal pattern
matches and derived Show output are unchanged.

The Unboxed module is ~30 lines and almost all documentation. That is the result: the shape algebra
is not duplicated, it is shared.

WHAT DOES NOT GENERALISE, and all of it is element-polymorphic by nature: Functor/Foldable/
Traversable are given as 'Functor v => Functor (GridOf v cs)' so any boxed-like vector gets them;
Applicative/Monad/Distributive/Representable are given concretely at GridOf V.Vector. Replacements
exported from Data.Grid.Sized and usable at either representation: tabulateGrid, indexGrid, mapGrid,
imapGrid, zipWithGrid, foldlGrid'. FocusedGrid and Comonad stay boxed-only -- duplicate builds a
grid OF grids.

MEASURED (bench group 'boxed vs unboxed', 300x300 Int, ghc 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin):

  operation             boxed      unboxed   speedup
  tabulateGrid          6.36 ms    1.93 ms     3.3x
  mapGrid then sum       318 us    92.1 us     3.5x
  foldlGrid'             312 us    88.7 us     3.5x
  transposeGrid         5.06 ms    2.15 ms     2.4x
  summed-area build     28.1 ms    13.1 ms     2.1x
  indexGrid x90000       751 us     793 us     none

THE SPIKE'S NUMBERS DID NOT REPRODUCE. It reported 7.5x/16x/6.5x/4.3x on those rows. It compared a
hand-written monomorphic unboxed loop against the library's boxed path, so it credited
specialisation to the representation. Both sides here are the same generic code. The honest ratio
is 2-3.5x, and the 'no change on indexed reads' finding stands exactly as the spike had it -- that
one was right and is the load-bearing one for deciding when to reach for UGrid.

PRAGMAS ARE LOAD-BEARING, and this was the surprise. Without INLINE/INLINABLE nothing specialises
through the VG.Vector dictionary: the summed-area build runs 53.6 ms rather than 13.1 ms. They help
the BOXED path at least as much, since it is the same code -- against e7d6340, tabulate is 60%
faster and fmap 78% faster (mapGrid and a following fold now fuse). So the library was leaving that
speedup on the table before it had a vector parameter at all.

TWO REGRESSIONS, both at conversion boundaries. The four operations that recurse down the axis list
-- collapseGrid, gridFromList, toJSON, parseJSON -- cannot specialise through a recursive call at a
changing cs, so their vector primitives stayed behind a dictionary and ran 60-300% slower. Fixed by
making the recursion monomorphic over a boxed vector with a local splitBoxedBySize; the exported
generic splitVectorBySize inside a polymorphically-recursive function never reduces to its O(1)
slice, and that single helper was most of the gap. What remains is one VG.convert per call:
collapseGrid +9%, toJSON +19%, gridFromList and parseJSON level. Two alternative shapes were
measured and cost more (list recursion: collapseGrid +83%, toJSON +68%; passing vector ops as
arguments: fixes the plain functions, but JSON goes to +74%/+56% because an instance method does not
specialise at its call site the way an INLINABLE function does). The module header records all
three.

Every other benchmark is level with baseline.

HOUSEKEEPING. bench-spike/ is deleted -- its own comment said to remove it once this decision was
made, and it had begun breaking 'cabal build all --enable-benchmarks' by depending on the old
upstream sized-grid from Hackage. Its workloads are folded into bench/Main.hs against the real
implementation. Test.Unboxed runs each operation at both representations and compares, so they
cannot drift. Baseline CSV refreshed.

title: Ordinal's GADT representation costs a KnownNat dictionary + someNatVal allocation per arithmetic op
description:
The central performance problem.

src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:31-32

    data Ordinal m where
      Ordinal :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat m, n + 1 <= m) => Proxy n -> Ordinal m

Every Ordinal value carries a type-level Nat and its dictionary. Consequences:

  - ordinalToNum goes Proxy -> natVal -> Integer -> fromIntegral. Integer, not Int.
  - numToOrdinal (src/SizedGrid/Ordinal.hs:50-61) calls someNatVal (allocates a
    SomeNat, builds a KnownNat dictionary via unsafeCoerce) plus cmpNat, on EVERY
    construction.
  - toEnum = fromJust . numToOrdinal, so enumerating an axis allocates one Nat
    dictionary per element.
  - Periodic's (<>), negateV, (.+^), (.-.) and HardWrap's equivalents all round-trip
    through numToOrdinal. A single coordinate addition allocates a type-level natural.

Observed cost in practice: ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs works on Grid '[HardWrap 300, HardWrap 300]
and iterates 'allCoord' (90,000 coords), each one an NP of two GADTs carrying dictionaries.

Proposal: make it a newtype over Int with a smart constructor.

    newtype Ordinal (m :: Nat) = UnsafeOrdinal { ordinalToInt :: Int }

The only thing the GADT buys at runtime is asSizeProxy (src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:48-53),
which recovers 'Proxy m' with 'm + 1 <= n'. That is used in exactly one place
(shrinkGrid, src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:248-254). Reconstruct the evidence there via
someNatVal at that single call site instead of paying for it on every value.

Expected: coordinate arithmetic becomes machine-word Int ops; Ordinal becomes
unboxable, which unblocks the unboxed-Grid work.

Do this behind the existing _Ordinal prism / numToOrdinal / ordinalToNum API so
most call sites are unaffected. Benchmark first (see the criterion issue).
close_reason: Fixed in commit 'Make Ordinal a newtype over Int' on branch worktree-ordinal-int; 100 tests pass, zero warnings

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Dependency on sized-grid-h56 removed. h56 was retested on 2026-08-09 and deferred --
ghc-tcplugins-extra has no GHC 9.14 release on Hackage, so natnormalise and knownnat
cannot be adopted without dropping 9.14 support. Leaving this blocked on it would block
it indefinitely on an upstream event. The manual Nat plumbing in Ordinal.hs:61/68/79
therefore has to be handled by this refactor itself rather than dissolved by a plugin
first. Still blocked on sized-grid-amf, which is the right gate: benchmark before
rewriting the representation.

Also note sized-grid-j23 (fromJust in Ordinal construction) now depends on this issue --
the seven fromJust call sites collapse into one checked constructor once Ordinal is a
newtype over Int, so they should be fixed here rather than patched separately.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Baseline landed (sized-grid-amf), so this is now measurable rather than speculative.

The strongest single number: 'tabulate' on a 300x300 grid of Int allocates 93 MB and
takes 23.6 ms. The payload of that grid is 90,000 boxed Ints, well under 1 MB. Roughly
1 KB of allocation per cell is exactly the someNatVal / KnownNat-dictionary traffic this
issue describes -- every Ordinal construction builds a type-level natural.

Supporting figures, all GHC 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin -O1:
    index x90000, 300x300      13.8 ms,  72 MB   (153 ns and ~800 B per index)
    ifoldl' 300x300            19.5 ms, 107 MB
    extend neighbourSum 50x50  5.42 ms,  29 MB   (2.2 us per cell, 9 peeks each)
    (.+^) Periodic             157 ns/op, 1.1 KB/op
    toEnum/fromEnum HardWrap    24 ns/op

Compare 'fmap 300x300' at 758 us / 4.1 MB, which touches every cell but constructs no
Ordinals. That is the target the newtype-over-Int representation should be aiming at.

Re-run 'cabal run bench:benchmarks' and diff against
bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv to judge the refactor.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Done in commit "Make Ordinal a newtype over Int" (branch worktree-ordinal-int).

Shipped as proposed: newtype over Int with a nominal role, constructor not
exported, numToOrdinal as the checked entry point and unsafeOrdinal as the one
unchecked one (assert-guarded). asSizeProxy's evidence is rebuilt on demand by
reifyOrdinal at the single call site (shrinkGrid) instead of being carried in
every value. Signatures that gained a constraint the GADT used to smuggle in:
asSizeProxy (KnownNat n), ShrinkableGrid (KnownNat x), maxCoord (1 <= n).

Result, A/B measured in one session:

    (.+^) Periodic 300x300      2.07x faster, 49% less allocated
    toEnum/fromEnum HardWrap    2.50x faster, 61% less allocated
    extend neighbourSum         1.12x faster, 11% less allocated
    (.-.) HardWrap              1.22x faster,  5% less allocated
    tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl' unchanged to within 1%

The estimate in this issue's earlier comment -- that tabulate's 93 MB was
someNatVal/KnownNat traffic -- was wrong, and the benchmark says so plainly.
allCoord shares 600 Ordinals across 90,000 coords, so per-value representation
never dominated the grid-wide operations. The remaining cost is NP allocation
plus coordPosition's Integer arithmetic; both belong to sized-grid-uvd, which
now has the numbers on it.

Also note the measurement trap hit on the way: the recorded baseline CSV was
1.9x off because the machine was busier than when it was written, which made a
2x win read as a 2x regression. bench/Main.hs now documents measuring both
sides in one session.

title: Perf research: parallel axis operations (mapAxis/scanAxis)
description: Investigate multicore parallelism for axis-wise operations in `src/Data/Grid/Sized/Internal/Grid.hs`, especially `mapAxisStrided` and possibly `scanAxisStrided`. `mapAxis` has independent fibres that can run in parallel; `scanAxis` has serial dependency within each fibre but independent fibres across blocks.
acceptance_criteria:
- Prototype parallelization of independent fibres/blocks for `mapAxisStrided` and assess viability for `scanAxisStrided` (parallel across fibres, sequential within fibre).
- Maintain current memory-safety/invariant assumptions and no public API breakage.
- Benchmark axis-0 and axis-1 workloads from bench/Main.hs with +RTS -N1/-N4/-N8, boxed and unboxed.
- Report cache/stride effects and determine when parallel execution helps vs hurts.
- If `scanAxis` is not worthwhile, document evidence and close with rationale.
notes:
ANSWERED in spike/utxm-paraxis (README.md has the full write-up; results-*.csv and results-huge-*.csv are the eight runs).

HEADLINE: the axis operations do parallelise, but most of what is available here is sequential, and the thresholds are in FIBRES not cells.

1. The unit of parallelism is the fibre (len/axisSize), not the cell. A 4x22500 grid has 90,000 cells and FOUR fibres along its inner axis. Crossover ~100 fibres, unambiguous by 200. A cell-count threshold would fork eight workers for four units of work.

2. CACHE DECIDED THE ANSWER, and the first pass measured the wrong regime. Every shape up to 90,000 cells (720 KB) is resident in this machine's 16 MB L2, where a strided walk and an in-order walk are indistinguishable (75.8 vs 75.7 us). Added a 2000x2000 shape (32 MB): the same two arms are 3.05 ms vs 23.14 ms, 7.6x. The library's Haddock claim was right and unreproducible on the shape it names (see sized-grid-erwx).

3. mapAxis parallelises cleanly (its sequential path already walks fibres): 2.5x at -N4 in cache, 3.2x out of it, above ~200 fibres.

4. scanAxis: parallelise by STRIP (contiguous offset range, in-order walk preserved), never by fibre. The fibre split reinstates the walk scanAxisStrided rejected, and out of cache four cores running it are STILL 2.4x slower than one core running the in-order pass. The strip split wins 1.61x at -N4 on the strided axis.

5. The chunk multiplier MATTERS here, unlike kb38/49hi, because the fibre count bounds it: 32 chunks/capability at -N8 measured 8.3x worse than 1. Use one chunk per capability.

6. Sparks lose everywhere except one out-of-cache case where the win is really the memory layout (sized-grid-12sa).

7. kb38's -N-costs-the-sequential-path finding transferred: 15-25% on untouched library code.

BIGGEST WIN HAS NO THREADS IN IT: filling the contiguous scan directly instead of concatenating per-fibre vectors is 1.52x in cache, 1.99x out of it, and halves allocation (sized-grid-oyih, P1). A second sequential 1.2-1.3x is real but unexplained after eliminating chunk count, forking and VG.create (sized-grid-l63s).

Follow-ups: sized-grid-oyih (P1, do this one), sized-grid-l63s, sized-grid-12sa, sized-grid-erwx, sized-grid-xmhm (the parallelism itself, blocked on the sequential work since it moves the baseline).
close_reason: Closed

title: allCoord is rebuilt from scratch on every imap/ifoldMap/itraverse/tabulate
description:
src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:67-75

    imap func (Grid v)      = Grid $ V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v
    ifoldMap func (Grid v)  = foldMap id $ V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v
    itraverse func (Grid v) = Grid <$> sequenceA (V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v)

and src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:64

    tabulate func = Grid $ V.fromList $ map func allCoord

'allCoord' (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:206-212) builds the full coordinate list through
the list monad over an NP, then V.fromList copies it into a vector. This happens on
every single indexed traversal, and each element is a heap-allocated NP I cs whose
components each carry a KnownNat dictionary.

For Grid '[HardWrap 300, HardWrap 300] that is 90,000 NP allocations per imap.

Also src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:220-237: coordPosition recomputes the per-axis size
product ('sizeOfList') on every call, in Integer, and index calls coordPosition for
every access.

Options, roughly in order of payoff:
  1. Cache the coordinate vector per type in a CAF: 'allCoordVector :: V.Vector (Coord cs)'
     bound at top level so GHC shares it across calls. Needs care to actually float.
  2. Precompute the axis strides once (a small [Int]) rather than folding sizes each
     time in coordPosition.
  3. Better: make imap/ifoldMap/itraverse iterate positions as Int and only
     materialise a Coord when the user function demands one. Most callers use
     fromEnum on the result anyway -- see ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs:40
     '(fromEnum -> r) :| (fromEnum -> c) :| _'.

Depends on the Ordinal representation change for the biggest win.
close_reason: Fixed on branch worktree-allcoord. coordPosition is a single Int pass (was Integer with a per-axis re-traversal); tabulate uses V.fromListN coordSpaceSize; ifoldr/ifoldl' given outright. allCoord itself was not the problem - the V.fromList in the traversals fuses. 24-49% less allocation across tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl'/extend, 110 tests pass, zero warnings. Remainder tracked as sized-grid-0vl.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Quantified by sized-grid-amf's baseline (GHC 9.12.3, aarch64-darwin, -O1). The
benchmark pairs each allCoord-using operation with the closest operation that does not
use it, so the difference is attributable:

    tabulate 300x300  23.6 ms,  93 MB   vs   pure 300x300  206 us, 704 KB   -> 115x, 132x alloc
    imap     300x300  17.7 ms,  80 MB   vs   fmap 300x300  758 us, 4.1 MB   ->  23x,  20x alloc

allCoord is not overhead on indexed traversal, it is essentially the entire cost. Re-run
'cabal run bench:benchmarks' after any caching change and compare against
bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv.

Note there is no standalone allCoord benchmark and it is not an oversight: at a fixed
type allCoord is a CAF and the optimiser shares it, so a direct measurement reports ~2 ns
for 90,000 coordinates. Details in the comment in bench/Main.hs.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Measured correction from the sized-grid-upo work (commit "Make Ordinal a newtype
over Int"). The Ordinal representation is NOT what tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl'
are paying for. A/B with both sides measured in one session:

    (.+^) Periodic          2.07x faster, 49% less allocated
    toEnum/fromEnum         2.50x faster, 61% less allocated
    tabulate 300x300        unchanged: 97,580,033 -> 97,421,177 bytes
    imap 300x300            unchanged: 83,502,208 -> 83,502,303 bytes
    index x90000            unchanged: 75,581,477 -> 75,581,480 bytes
    ifoldl' 300x300         unchanged: 112,040,243 -> 111,881,769 bytes

Why: allCoord is a cartesian product over the per-axis lists, so for a 300x300
grid it constructs 600 Ordinals and shares them across all 90,000 NPs. Ordinal
construction was never the per-cell cost. What is left, and what this issue now
owns in full, is:

  1. the 90,000 NP I cs allocations themselves, rebuilt per traversal, and
  2. coordPosition, which is called per cell and does its arithmetic in Integer
     -- ordinalToNum boxes an Integer per axis, and sizeOfList recomputes the
     stride product per call.

(2) is now a clean win to take: ordinalToInt gives the axis value as an Int
directly, so coordPosition can be Int throughout with the strides precomputed
once. That did not exist before the newtype.

Judge any change here by the allocation columns, not the times -- see the note
added to bench/Main.hs about cross-session drift.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Done. The issue's premise was wrong in an instructive way, so the result is recorded here in full.

allCoord is NOT rebuilt in the sense meant. 'V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v' fuses: the coordinates are produced and consumed one at a time and never all exist at once. Its real cost is about 67 bytes a cell. I confirmed this by breaking it -- building the coordinate vector from a recursive function, and separately by putting the same list under V.fromListN -- and both made imap 23% more allocation and 59% slower, with ifoldl' copying jumping from 48KB to 18MB. The fused form is now commented as such in SizedGrid.Grid.Grid so it does not get "fixed" again.

What the benchmark gap actually measured was coordPosition, which tabulate/imap/ifoldl' are all handed as their per-cell function: ~800 bytes per call. The old version recomputed the axis-size product with a separate traversal per axis, in Integer.

Changes:
  - coordPosition is one Int pass; the stride of an axis is the size of the axes below it, which comes back up the recursion.
  - tabulate uses V.fromListN coordSpaceSize (its result is a vector regardless, so the exact length just avoids growth doubling).
  - ifoldr/ifoldl' given outright rather than derived from ifoldMap through an Endo chain.
  - New API: coordSpaceSize (MaxCoordSize as a value, needing only All IsCoordLifted) and coordFromPosition (checked inverse of coordPosition).
  - 10 new tests pinning the position/coordinate bijection and that imap/ifoldMap/ifoldr/ifoldl' agree with tabulate and with each other. Mutation-checked: a wrong stride fails 6 of them.

Allocated, before -> after (the deterministic column):
  tabulate 300x300    97,421,177 ->  73,740,888   -24%
  imap 300x300        83,502,303 ->  62,641,438   -25%
  index x90000        75,581,480 ->  54,720,335   -28%
  ifoldl' 300x300    111,881,769 ->  57,600,340   -49%
  extend 50x50        27,045,702 ->  21,808,586   -19%
  extract 50x50              808 ->         608   -25%
  itraverse 100x100   unchanged; everything else unchanged

Times, both sides measured in one session:
  tabulate 47.0ms -> 33.4ms, imap 33.9 -> 22.8, index 27.0 -> 15.0,
  ifoldl' 38.0 -> 15.1, extend 9.39ms -> 6.23ms, extract 298ns -> 167ns

Baseline CSV re-recorded. The "allCoord overhead" benchmark group is renamed to "indexed vs unindexed (the gap is coordPosition, not allCoord)" -- its old name and its pairing are what pointed this issue at the wrong thing.

What is left is sized-grid-0vl: coordPosition's remaining ~550 bytes a call is dictionary plumbing (peeling IsCoordLifted out of All, natVal boxing an Integer, the Iso call for asOrdinal), not arithmetic.

title: INLINE rather than INLINABLE on stencilGrid and stencilFoldGrid
description:
sized-grid-49hi measured this as the largest single win available to the stencil kernels, and it is a one-word diff per function with no API change, no threads and no threshold.

INLINABLE exposes an unfolding for GHC to SPECIALISE on the types; it does not oblige GHC to INLINE the body. When GHC declines, the rule stays a lambda-bound variable inside the fill, so stencilFoldGrid's accumulator is a boxed Int that step re-boxes once per neighbour, and the neighbour it folds in is boxed on the way out of the unboxed vector as well. The Core tell is an inner loop reading 'case acc of acc1 { I# ipv7 -> ... step acc1 (I# ds8) }' where a specialised one reads 'jump $wgo1 (+# ww8 1#) (+# ww9 ds5)'.

MEASURED IN THE LIBRARY, not only in the spike: changing only the two pragmas and rebuilding nothing else, on 90,000 unboxed cells at -N1, stencilFoldGrid went 1.03 ms / 13 MB -> 430 us / 703 KB and stencilGrid went 6.28 ms / 92 MB -> 4.47 ms / 82 MB. In the spike's own matrix the same change is 780 us / 13 MB -> 448 us / 703 KB: 1.74x and 19x less allocated.

The gather kernel gains far less than the fold kernel because stencilGrid builds a list per cell, so a boxed accumulator is a small part of what it already allocates. stencilFoldGrid exists so as not to build that list, and boxing was most of what it had left.

TO DO
- Flip both pragmas, run bench/Main.hs against the laptop baseline, and regenerate the baseline in its own commit if it moves.
- Measure the code-size cost at call sites, which the spike did NOT measure: INLINE on a kernel this size will grow every consumer. gameOfLife, ising-example and sudoko are the call sites in tree.
- Update the module Haddock's measured numbers, which quote the current kernels.

Evidence: spike/49hi-parexec, README section 'The largest win is sequential, and it is a pragma'.
close_reason:
Both pragmas flipped to INLINE (7ee9dda), laptop baseline regenerated (d42591a).

Measured old baseline vs a fresh idle-machine run, 50x50, GHC 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin:
  stencilFoldStep one pass, table built  48.3 us / 479 KB -> 42.5 us / 215 KB
  stencilFoldStep x100 boxed             19.3 ms /  47 MB -> 17.7 ms /  21 MB
  stencilFoldStep x100 unboxed           10.3 ms / 149 MB -> 1.38 ms / 1.9 MB
  stencilStep one pass, table built       148 us / 2.4 MB ->  133 us / 2.1 MB
  stencilStep x100 boxed                 33.2 ms / 237 MB -> 31.0 ms / 210 MB
  stencilStep x100 unboxed               12.9 ms / 249 MB -> 12.9 ms / 221 MB

Untouched benchmarks in the same two runs agree within 3% (imapGrid over neighbours x100: 77.9 -> 77.5 ms), which is what licenses reading the above as the pragma. Allocation is byte-identical across repeat runs of a binary, so it is the trustworthy column; times drift tens of percent with thermal state (two earlier runs were polluted by a video call and were discarded).

The unboxed fold loop: 1.9 MB across 100 generations of 2,500 cells is 100*2500*8 bytes -- the result vectors and nothing else. Everything above that was boxing.

CODE SIZE, which the spike did not measure: it got SMALLER, not larger. Stencil.o 50,112 -> 48,648 bytes; gameOfLife Main.o 86,824 -> 85,368; bench Main.o 432,344 -> 422,400. ising-example and sudoko are byte-identical (ising uses stencilAt, sudoko no stencil at all), so the three in-tree call sites are gameOfLife and the bench. The specialised loop drops boxing, the generic vector dictionary and dead sentinel arithmetic, and that outweighs the body it inlines.

Haddock updated: module header figures restated from the new baseline, a new section 'Why both kernels are INLINE and not INLINABLE' with the Core tell and the code-size measurement, stencilFoldGrid's own measured numbers restated, and a note at each pragma so it is not weakened back without re-benchmarking. ChangeLog entry added.

All 821 tests, the downstream suite and the readme suite pass. No API, signature or semantic change.

title: Two obstacles to instantiating PseudoAffine: an orphan on Int, and MapDiff idempotence
description:
Both hit while building the sized-grid-8nz proof of concept. Neither is fatal;
both need a decision. Only relevant if 8nz goes ahead.

== 1. manifolds-core has no Semimanifold Int

It derives Semimanifold/PseudoAffine for Double and Rational only (a CPP
'deriveAffine' macro applied twice). Int is not a manifold as far as it is
concerned, which is defensible -- a Needle is meant to be a vector space over
R, and Int is not one.

Every Diff in this library is an Int, so the instances do not typecheck without
supplying it:

    instance Semimanifold Int where
      type Needle Int = Int
      (.+~^) = (+)
    instance PseudoAffine Int where
      a .-~. b = pure (a - b)
      (.-~!) = (-)

That is an orphan instance on a base type. It is the thing that would make a
grid-sized-manifolds *separate package* (option (b) in 8nz) attractive: the
orphan is then confined to a package a consumer opts into, and cannot collide
in the main library's own dependency cone. ../aoc defining the same orphan
would be an overlap error, so check there before choosing.

Worth asking upstream whether Semimanifold Int is wanted in manifolds-core
before committing to carrying an orphan indefinitely.

== 2. MapDiff (MapDiff cs) ~ MapDiff cs

Semimanifold's semimanifoldWitness default needs
Needle (Needle x) ~ Needle x, and PseudoAffine's needs PseudoAffine (Needle x).
At Coord cs with Needle (Coord cs) = Coord (MapDiff cs), that is

    MapDiff (MapDiff cs) ~ MapDiff cs
    AffineCoordList (MapDiff cs)
    All AdditiveGroup (MapDiff (MapDiff cs))

True -- MapDiff sends every coord to Int and Diff Int = Int, so it is
idempotent -- but GHC cannot see it without induction over the axis list. The
proof of concept punted by writing all four as instance constraints, which
compiles but pushes them onto every downstream signature.

The clean fix is an inductive class over cs that discharges them once, the same
shape as AffineCoordList and IsCoordList already have (and the same shape the
existing note about Nat-indexed class recursion warns about: a fundep, not an
associated type family, or GHC rejects overlapping instances as conflicting).

At a concrete axis list -- which is most code, including ../aoc -- MapDiff
reduces and none of this is visible. It is only polymorphic code that pays.
notes:
Obstacle 2 (MapDiff (MapDiff cs) ~ MapDiff cs) is dissolved by sized-grid-adr.16, not by the inductive class this issue proposes.

adr.16 splits the displacement out of Coord: Diff (Coord cs) stops being
Coord (MapDiff cs) and becomes Delta (MapDiff cs), where Delta is a type of
its own. A vector space is its own needle, so Needle (Delta ds) = Delta ds and

    Needle (Needle (Coord cs)) = Needle (Delta (MapDiff cs))
                               = Delta (MapDiff cs)
                               = Needle (Coord cs)

holds definitionally. No induction over the axis list, no inductive class, and
nothing pushed onto downstream signatures. The four constraints the 8nz proof
of concept carried as instance constraints go away with it.

Obstacle 1 (the Semimanifold Int orphan) is untouched by adr.16 and is still
the open question here.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text: Interoperability research (2026-08-23): verified against the locally fetched manifolds-core-0.6.1.1 source. The original proof-of-concept remains mechanically viable after Delta: Needle (Coord cs) can be Delta (MapDiff cs), so nested-Needle idempotence is now definitionally solved. The remaining blocker is exclusively the orphan Semimanifold Int/PseudoAffine Int instance. Package metadata also shows manifolds-core is GPL-3, while grid-sized is MIT; a direct main-library dependency should therefore be rejected unless the licensing outcome is explicitly accepted. A separate opt-in adapter package can confine the orphan and license boundary, but must first audit real consumers for a conflicting Int instance and establish that a GPL component is acceptable. This strengthens option (b) from sized-grid-8nz; it does not justify reopening a direct core dependency.

title: windowFits is an asserted axiom; try ghc-typelits-presburger to discharge it
description:
`SizedGrid.Internal.Type.windowFits` is the only `unsafeCoerce` in the library:

    windowFits :: forall n y z. Dict (n <= y, z <= (y - n))
    windowFits = unsafeCoerce (Dict :: Dict (0 <= 0, 0 <= 0))

It supplies the two facts `shrinkGrid` needs to call `dropGrid` then `takeGrid`.
Soundness rests entirely on the `x + z <= y + 1` constraint on the
`ShrinkableGrid` instance, which is checked at every call site -- so the axiom is
believed true, but it is asserted rather than derived, and an `unsafeCoerce`
producing a `Dict` is the single place where a mistake in that reasoning would
be silent.

The module comment already names the candidate fix and nobody has tried it:

> That wanted is a `<=` goal from `<=` givens over a truncating subtraction,
> which needs ghc-typelits-presburger; it stays an asserted axiom.

This is a bounded spike, not a redesign. Add `ghc-typelits-presburger` to the
`common lang` plugin list next to `natnormalise` and `knownnat`, delete
`windowFits`, and see whether the `shrinkGrid` call site still compiles.

Two acceptable outcomes, and both are worth having:

- It works: the library's last asserted axiom goes away, and
  `SizedGrid.Internal.Type` shrinks to just `requiring`.
- It does not: the comment gets upgraded from "needs presburger" (a guess) to a
  record of what was actually tried and how it failed, so the next reader does
  not re-run this spike.

Note the constraint that sank sized-grid-h56 applies here too: `-fplugin` is not
transitive. A plugin enabled for this library says nothing about a downstream
consumer. That is fine for `windowFits` specifically, because the goal is solved
*inside* this library at the `shrinkGrid` definition rather than being re-emitted
into a consumer's context -- but confirm that before concluding, because it is
exactly the assumption that made h56 look like a fix when it was not.
design:
The arithmetic the axiom stands in for, from the module comment:

At the use site the window offset `n` comes from `reifyCoord` on a coord of size
`x`, so `n + 1 <= x`, and the `ShrinkableGrid` instance requires
`x + z <= y + 1`. Together:

    n + 1 + z <= x + z <= y + 1        so   n + z <= y

which gives both `n <= y` (drop stays in range) and `z <= y - n` (the window fits
in what is left).

The first conjunct is ordinary linear arithmetic. The second mentions `y - n`,
GHC's *truncating* subtraction on Nat, over an existential `n` -- that is what
natnormalise will not do. Presburger arithmetic can express truncating
subtraction by case analysis on `n <= y`, and here the `n <= y` case is exactly
what the first conjunct establishes, which is the reason to expect this to work.

Verify rather than assume: check that ghc-typelits-presburger's current release
supports GHC 9.10/9.12/9.14 before adding it, since its GHC support has
historically lagged. If it only covers part of the tested-with range that is a
reason to reject, and should be recorded as such.
acceptance_criteria: Either windowFits is deleted and SizedGrid.Internal.Type exports only 'requiring', with the full test suite green on the tested-with GHCs; or the module comment records the concrete presburger attempt and why it failed, so the spike is not repeated.
close_reason:
Done, but not the way the issue predicted -- no plugin was added.

Presburger was tried first and it DOES discharge the goal: commit ae643ea has the
working change, all suites green on 9.12.3. It was rejected on the criterion this
issue's own design section set out. ghc-typelits-presburger 0.7.4.2 is bounded
'ghc <9.13', as is the ghc-tcplugins-extra 0.5 beneath it, with no 9.14 branch
upstream (last release supports 9.12). With it in build-depends GHC 9.14.1 fails
to resolve outright, [Cabal-7107] -- verified against a real 9.14.1 compiler, and
verified that removing that one dependency is what makes 9.14 resolve again. That
is precisely the trap that left h56 deferred; natnormalise and knownnat escaped it
by moving to ghc-tcplugin-api, and presburger has not moved.

The axiom turned out not to need a solver at all (commit 7bf7531). Probing
natnormalise showed the real limitation is broader than the issue assumed: it is
not just the truncating subtraction, it will not chain two '<=' givens at all and
fails on a bare 'a <= b, b <= c => a <= c'. But it does cancel constants from both
sides. So:

  - 'sliceGrid off len' replaces 'takeGrid len . dropGrid off', stating the bound
    as 'off + len <= m' rather than 'len <= m - off'. The truncating subtraction
    never appears. It is also V.slice's own precondition, so that bounds check
    cannot fire. Same elements: [off, off+len).
  - 'windowFits' keeps its name but is derived, not asserted, from plusMonotone1
    and leTrans in Data.Constraint.Nat. 'constraints' was already a dependency.

Net result: no unsafeCoerce in src/, no new dependency, GHC 9.14 kept.

Honest limit on the claim: plusMonotone1 and leTrans are themselves unsafeCoerce
inside 'constraints'. What changed is that the reasoning is machine-checked --
those are general lemmas about + and <=, where windowFits was a bespoke
three-variable claim about this library's window invariant, asserted whole. GHC
now verifies the composition yields 'n + z <= y' from the givens.

Verified on GHC 9.12.3 with -fforce-recomp: library, three examples and benchmarks
warning-free; 315 tasty tests, readme suite and the plugin-free downstream suite
all pass. The downstream suite passing is what shows the goal is solved at the
definition rather than re-emitted into a consumer's context.

Filed sized-grid-ior: tests/Main.hs and README.lhs have 8 pre-existing warnings
that only show on a cold build (confirmed present at c697f1b, so not from this
work).

'sliceGrid' is exported from SizedGrid.Internal.Grid but NOT added to the public
SizedGrid.Grid.Grid list -- deliberately left out of scope; worth deciding
separately, since dropGrid and takeGrid are both public and this is the more
useful primitive.

title: _CoordCons and _DeltaCons: cons/uncons as an Iso, and why lens's Cons class does not fit
description:
From the sized-grid-31z optics survey. Tier A: a genuine Iso, and a note on
why lens's own class does not fit.

  coordSplit  :: Coord (c ': cs) -> (c, Coord cs)     Coord.hs:182
  appendCoord :: c -> Coord cs -> Coord (c ': cs)     Coord.hs:339
  deltaSplit  :: Delta (d ': ds) -> (d, Delta ds)     Delta.hs:89
  appendDelta :: a -> Delta as -> Delta (a ': as)     Delta.hs:203

  _CoordCons :: (IsCoordLifted c, IsCoordList cs)
             => Iso' (Coord (c ': cs)) (c, Coord cs)
  _CoordCons = iso coordSplit (uncurry appendCoord)

  _DeltaCons :: Iso' (Delta (d ': ds)) (d, Delta ds)

And the two degenerate ends, which complete the family:

  _SingleCoord :: IsCoordLifted c => Iso' (Coord '[c]) c
  _EmptyCoord  :: Iso' (Coord '[]) ()

== Do NOT instantiate lens's `Cons` for these

`Cons s t a b` gives `_Cons :: Prism s t (a, s) (b, t)` -- the tail has the
SAME type as the whole. A `Coord (c ': cs)`'s tail is a `Coord cs`, a
different type, so the class simply does not typecheck here.

That is a feature, not an obstacle. `Cons` is a Prism because a list can be
empty and the match can fail; `Coord (c ': cs)` has a head and a tail by
construction, so the bespoke version is an Iso -- strictly stronger. Same for
`Snoc`, which additionally has no cheap implementation: the last axis is the
least significant digit, so uncons is a `quotRem` by the tail stride
(Coord.hs:184) while unsnoc would be a `quotRem` by the last axis size and a
rebuild of everything above it.

The pattern synonyms `(:|)` and `(:^)` already cover the matching half; this
covers the composing half.

Cost: none, lens is already a direct dependency.
close_reason: Closed

title: CI: tests/Test/Ordinal.hs fails to compile on GHC 9.10.1 -- reifyCoord's result type is untouchable
description:
`cabal build all` fails on GHC 9.10.1 while compiling Test.Ordinal (job runs 372s, so this is a real compile error, not a solver failure). GHC 9.12.3 is green.

Root cause is the single [GHC-83865] at tests/Test/Ordinal.hs:87:29 (and again at 97:19):

    Couldn't match expected type 'a0' with actual type 'Integer'
      'a0' is untouchable
        inside the constraints: (KnownNat m, (m + 1) <= 5)
        bound by a type expected by the context:
          forall (m1 :: Nat) -> (KnownNat m1, (m1 + 1) <= 5) => a0

reifyCoord (Data.Grid.Sized.Coord.Class:58) is

    reifyCoord :: KnownNat n => c n -> (forall m -> (KnownNat m, m + 1 <= n) => x) -> x

so `x` is bound outside an implication that carries givens. On 9.10 OutsideIn treats an unsolved `x` metavariable as untouchable from inside that implication, so `x ~ Integer` (from natVal) cannot be solved there. The three [GHC-39999] ambiguity errors at 84:5, 86:7, 86:8, 92:5 and 94:7 are downstream of that -- the numeric literals have nothing to fix their type to.

Fix: annotate the reifyCoord *application* (`... :: Integer`), which fixes `x` before the continuation is checked. Annotating the continuation body would not work -- that unification still happens inside the implication.

Note the obvious-looking fix of annotating only assertEqual's expected argument ([0 .. 4] :: [Integer]) treats the symptom; the untouchable error is at the reifyCoord call.

Verified: compiles under -Werror and all 49 Ordinal tests pass on 9.12.3.
close_reason: Closed

title: gloss pins GLFW-b < 2, so the HiDPI fix rides a superseded binding
description:
sized-grid-23y3 switched the examples to gloss's GLFW backend to get the HiDPI viewport correction. That works, but gloss.cabal:108 declares

    GLFW-b >= 1.4.1.0 && < 2

and the current release on the index here is GLFW-b 3.3.9.1. So the solver picks GLFW-b 1.4.8.4 -- a whole major line behind -- and the fix the demos now depend on rides an old binding.

Almost certainly a stale bound rather than a real incompatibility: GLFW-b renumbered to track upstream GLFW 3.3 rather than breaking its API wholesale, and gloss's backend uses a small surface (createWindow, getFramebufferSize, getWindowSize, swapBuffers, the callback installers). Worth testing rather than assuming.

Not urgent. Nothing is known to be broken; this is exposure, not a defect. Filed so the pin is on the record rather than discovered again the next time something about the window misbehaves.
design:
TO TEST: add 'allow-newer: gloss:GLFW-b' to cabal.project and see whether gloss compiles against GLFW-b 3.3.9.1 unchanged. If it does, keep the allow-newer with a note (the same shape as the containers entry already there for sized-grid-8hx). If it does not, record what broke and drop it -- 1.4.8.4 is working today.

CONTEXT WORTH KEEPING: this is the second stale bound in the gloss stack. cabal.project already carries an allow-newer block because gloss, gloss-rendering, OpenGL, GLUT and OpenGLRaw all cap containers < 0.8 with no GHC 9.14 release upstream (sized-grid-8hx). gloss's last release is 1.13.2.2 and it is lightly maintained. That is not a reason to leave it -- it is the right altitude for these demos, and dropping to GLFW-b + OpenGL directly would mean writing our own loop, shaders and text rendering for nothing these demos need -- but it does mean the examples' exposure is to gloss's bounds rather than to its behaviour.

Note also that bindings-GLFW vendors the GLFW C source and links the Cocoa frameworks itself, so there is no system library involved and a version bump here is purely a Haskell-side question.

title: grid-atlas can compute orientability now and does not offer it; vertex cycles cannot tell a torus from a Klein bottle
description:
atlas-topology can tell a projective plane from a Klein bottle and cannot tell a Klein bottle from a torus. Its own haddock says so, in vertexCycleLengths: 'a torus and a Klein bottle both report [4], while a projective plane reports [2]'. That is not a defect in the invariant -- vertex cycles are about cone points and the two surfaces genuinely have the same ones -- it is a gap in the set of invariants the package offers.

The missing one is orientability, and sized-grid-lopy.5 just made it computable. rectStep now returns a Crossing saying whether a seam hands the walker's frame back mirrored, and grid-atlas/tests/Test/Frames.hs reads out all four shipped surfaces correctly from tables nobody changed: a cube map never mirrors, a Mobius strip always does on its wrapped seam, a Klein bottle mirrors on Twisted and not on Rolled, a projective plane mirrors on both. A torus, if the package had one, would never mirror -- which is exactly the distinction vertex cycles cannot draw.

Those live in the test suite. They should live in the library, in the shape the package already uses for its other laws:

    seamViolations        :: SeamTable c b -> [HalfEdge c b] -> [HalfEdge c b]
    vertexCycleViolations :: SeamTable c b -> [Corner c b]   -> [Int]

so, alongside them, something like

    mirroringHalfEdges :: (Axis -> Int) -> SeamTable c (Axis, Extremum) -> [HalfEdge c (Axis, Extremum)] -> [HalfEdge c (Axis, Extremum)]
    orientable         :: ... -> Bool

WHERE IT GOES IS THE INTERESTING QUESTION, and the answer is probably not atlas-topology. Whether a crossing mirrors a walker is not a property of the seam table alone: it depends on the heading as well, because a walker's left lies on the increasing side of the shared coordinate for some headings and the decreasing side for others. That is what lopy.5 found out the hard way -- the issue was written believing the table's Bool WAS the walker's answer, and it is not. Deriving it needs leftHandIncreases, which needs to know a chart is a rectangle, which is precisely the half atlas-topology deliberately does not have. So this belongs in Data.Grid.Atlas.Rect, next to the computation, and atlas-topology keeps its combinatorics clean.

Orientability itself is then the parity of mirrorings around closed walks, and for a signed graph on charts that is an ordinary bipartiteness check -- no walking required, and the same shape of answer as vertexCycleLengths gives.

RELATED: sized-grid-oj6z wants stronger seam-table validation. This is a different kind of check -- oj6z asks whether the enumeration is well formed, this asks what surface the table describes -- but they would ship well together and should share a module.

VALUE BEYOND TIDINESS: the package's synopsis is that it is 'the layer for the policies that thesis cannot express (non-separable topologies: a Mobius seam, a cube map)'. Orientability is the property that separates those topologies from the separable ones, and until lopy.5 the package could not state it about its own surfaces.

title: bench gate failed on indexGrid x90000 boxed (41% slower than baseline)
description:
Run 32213722072 (job 95951213763, bench, 2026-08-19T03:53Z) failed the benchmark gate:

    indexGrid x90000           boxed:                      FAIL
      938  us +- 50 us, 280 B allocated, 22 B copied, 79 MB peak memory, 41% more than baseline

--fail-if-slower is 25%, so this tripped it. The unboxed variant of the same benchmark (indexGrid x90000 unboxed) came in "same as baseline" in the same run, which is evidence pointing at shared-runner noise rather than a real regression in indexGrid -- nothing in the boxed-vs-unboxed path was touched recently in a way that would explain a boxed-only slowdown.

ci.yml's own comments (around the bench job) already call out that 25% is a provisional threshold picked before there was real run history on GitHub's shared runners, and say to tighten it "once there is a run history showing what this runner's spread actually is." This failure is a data point for that: worth collecting a few more gate failures/passes before deciding whether to widen the threshold, exclude boxed indexGrid as noisy, or otherwise adjust.

Immediate unblock: rerun the bench job / dispatch with refresh-baseline if this turns out to be a one-off, per the escape hatch documented at the top of ci.yml.
close_reason: CI benchmark outlier not reproducible; focused rerun passed with boxed indexGrid at baseline speed

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text: Focused local rerun on GHC 9.12.3: boxed indexGrid x90000 = 163 us +/- 7.8 us; unboxed = 180 us +/- 14 us. Both passed, and boxed was not slower. The reported 938 us CI result is not reproducible locally; no source change is warranted. Resolved as shared-runner noise.

title: Research: one algorithm, many surfaces -- the abstraction the ant has and Sokoban could not
description:
Research, and honestly framed as such: this is the abstraction the repo keeps almost having, and the one place its two packages would meet.

THE EVIDENCE, from two demos that pulled in opposite directions.

automata/src/Automata/Ant.hs runs the same eleven lines of Langton's ant on Periodic, Clamped and Reflective boards, chosen by a command-line flag. It works because grid-sized's thesis holds: the boundary policy IS the coordinate type, the axes are separable, and stepWalker is the one operation the ant needs.

sokoban cannot do the same thing. Its surface is a Mobius strip, which is not a separable per-axis policy, so the rules are written against Sokoban.Board.stepSpot = mobiusStep and the surface is welded in. When sized-grid-lopy.3 needed to ask 'would this level still be solvable on a cylinder', there was no way to say it: Sokoban.Flat is forty lines of Int arithmetic re-implementing move-and-push on two flat surfaces, because nothing in either library lets one algorithm name the surface it runs on.

That second implementation turned out to be worth having for a different reason -- it is an independent control, and agreement between it and the real rules is evidence rather than tautology -- but it was written for the wrong reason, and nobody should have to.

THE QUESTION. Is there a Surface abstraction that spans both worlds? Something whose whole content is

    step :: pos -> Heading -> f (pos, Heading, Crossing)

with instances for a separable Grid via stepWalker, and for each atlas surface via rectStep. The Applicative f is already how rectStep expresses 'as partial as the gluing it is given', so the partiality is not a new problem.

WHAT MAKES IT HARD, and these are the things to settle before writing any of it:

  1. The two worlds disagree about what a position is. Separable: Coord cs. Atlas: (Ordinal k, Coord cs). sized-grid-3rpp is about the second of those being noise at k = 1, and the answer there changes the answer here.
  2. They disagree about what a heading is. Separable: a Delta, indexed by the difference list, so diagonals are legal. Atlas: a Heading, one axis and one end, so they are not. Reconciling those is not cosmetic -- the ant needs diagonals, a Sokoban does not, and a seam table's boundary label is exactly the atlas kind.
  3. Data.Grid.Atlas.Rect's own header warns against this: 'There is no class here saying what a boundary of an arbitrary chart is, because every atlas that exists is rectangular and a class fitted to instances of one shape would be a guess about the next.' That warning is about chart shape rather than about surfaces, but the reasoning transfers and should be answered rather than ignored.
  4. It might want to be a record rather than a class. Sokoban would pass one around per level; nothing needs instance resolution.

DEPENDS ON sized-grid-pc93 in spirit: if stepWalker learns to report the frame flip, the two worlds already return the same three things and most of the shape question answers itself.

RELATED: sized-grid-lopy.7 is the consumer-side version -- letting sokoban carry a surface so a Klein bottle level can exist. Do that one first. It is smaller, it needs no library change, and it will say whether the record is the right shape before anything is committed to public API.

ALSO RELATED: sized-grid-gyn wants named aliases for separable products (Torus, Cylinder). It calls itself 'pure sugar -- no new capability'. Sokoban.Flat is the counter-evidence: what a caller wants when it says 'cylinder' is to RUN something there, and the alias without the stepper does not give them that.

title: Opt-in parallel mapAxis/scanAxis, if it is wanted at all
description:
Answered by sized-grid-utxm; filed so the decision is recorded rather than re-derived. Read spike/utxm-paraxis/README.md before starting.

The measurements support offering this, but only opt-in and never by silent dispatch (it needs -threaded and changes strictness), and only with these constraints:

- THRESHOLD IS IN FIBRES, NOT CELLS. The unit of parallelism is the fibre and there are len/axisSize of them. A 4x22500 grid has 90,000 cells and four fibres along its inner axis; a cell-count threshold would fork eight workers for four units of work. Crossover measured at ~100 fibres, unambiguous by 200. fibreCount = len/axisSize is known from the type.
- ONE CHUNK PER CAPABILITY. Unlike kb38 and 49hi, granularity matters here because the fibre count bounds it. On 300 fibres at -N8, 32 chunks/capability measured 547.9 us against 65.7 us at 1 -- 8.3x worse. Narrower strips cost even sequentially (70.0 -> 87.4 us at -N1, no threads).
- FOR THE SCAN, THE STRIP SPLIT ONLY. Splitting by fibre reinstates the walk scanAxisStrided deliberately rejected: out of cache it is 7.6x slower sequentially, and parallelising it across four cores is STILL 2.4x slower than the untouched sequential pass. Splitting by a contiguous range of offsets, sweeping row by row, keeps the in-order walk and is the only scan arm that wins on the strided axis (1.61x at -N4).
- mapAxis is the better candidate: its sequential path already walks fibres, so the split is uncontroversial. 2.5x in cache, 3.2x out of it, at -N4.
- Do NOT offer a spark-based variant. It loses on every shape measured except one, where the win belongs to the memory layout (see sized-grid-12sa).

Blocked on the sequential work first: sized-grid-utxm's first follow-up and sized-grid-l63s both move the sequential baseline these thresholds are measured against, so landing them raises the crossover and shrinks what is left for threads to win. Do them before deciding this is worth the API surface at all.

title: Give the offset back: indexed optics for windows, tiles, lowerDim and axisFold
description:
gridWindows returns [Grid small] and throws away where each window came from; tiles, lowerDim and axisFold do the same. Every real windowing consumer -- convolution, template matching, 'which 3x3 sums highest', pattern search -- needs to know which offset produced a window, and today recovers it with zip [0..] and a re-derivation of the stride arithmetic the library just did.

This is the offset-carrying view that sized-grid-d9o9 was reaching for, and it costs no new type: lens already has the vocabulary.

  windows   :: IndexedFold      (Coord '[Ordinal k]) ...
  tiles     :: IndexedTraversal (Coord '[Ordinal k]) ...
  lowerDim  :: IndexedTraversal ...
  axisFold  :: IndexedFold      ...

The strengths do not change -- windows stays read-only because overlapping foci cannot form a lawful Traversal, and axisFold stays a Fold for the retention reason its Haddock gives. Only the index is added.

Rationale in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-26-grid-view-design.md, piece 3.
design:
Index type follows sized-grid-mbh0: offsets are Ordinals, not policy-carrying coordinates. Sequence after mbh0 so the index type is settled once.

Keep the unindexed names working -- an IndexedFold is a Fold, so toListOf windows keeps its current meaning and Test.Windows's existing properties keep passing unchanged.

title: The other IsCoord defaults still read their KnownNat as a run-time Natural
description:
sized-grid-bw8 fixed offsetByPosition with a one-line INLINE: the checked offset went from 56.4 ms / 199 MB to 6.85 ms / 35 MB, and in the Core the per-axis call went from $w$coffsetIsCoord main81 ds3 ww2 to an inline ># x (-# 299# y1). The same shape is still in its siblings in src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs.

WHAT IS LEFT. The Core of SizedGrid.Coord.Class still shows integerToInt# (integerFromNatural ($dKnownNat cast ...)) in:
  1. axisBoundaryByPosition, the default for axisBoundaryIsCoord.
  2. the default axisDistanceIsCoord.
Both read ordinalSize @n out of the method's KnownNat dictionary, for the same structural reason bw8 documents: IsCoord is indexed by c alone, so n arrives on the method rather than through the instance.

A third, different in kind: Periodic's own offsetIsCoord override is 'Just (c .+^ d)'.
