unboxed module) was RE-EXAMINED EMPIRICALLY after option 1 shipped, because the original argument
for option 1 was partly wrong. Option 2 was built as a working prototype against pre-change master
(e7d6340) and compiled. Findings, so the follow-ups do not have to redo this:

OPTION 2 WORKS. Full port of the shape algebra to Data.Vector.Unboxed: 25 top-level functions,
~246 lines, including a second 'ShrinkableUGrid' class carrying the windowFits application.
Nothing was blocked. The copy-paste is mechanical apart from two things:
  - splitGrid/combineGrid need mixed representation (outer boxed, inner unboxed), because a grid
    is never Unbox. Same insight option 1 needed; under option 2 it is hand-written.
  - shrinkGrid needs 'sliceGrid', which is DELIBERATELY WITHHELD from the public Data.Grid.Sized.
    So an option-2 unboxed module cannot be the standalone additive public module the issue
    described -- it must import from the hidden Data.Grid.Sized.Internal.Grid, or live inside it.

PERFORMANCE IS A WASH (300x300 Int, unboxed, both with pragmas):
  operation      option2 mono   option1 generic
  tabulate         1.84 ms         2.02 ms
  map then sum     92.3 us         91.7 us
  foldl'           86.6 us         86.6 us
  transpose        2.12 ms         2.26 ms
  SAT build        13.9 ms         14.3 ms
  index x90000      786 us          788 us
Option 2 is ~5-9% ahead on tabulate/transpose, otherwise identical.

THREE CLAIMS FROM THE ORIGINAL DECISION THAT WERE WRONG OR OVERSTATED:
1. 'Option 2 duplicates the windowFits proof.' No. windowFits lives in Internal.Type and is shared
   either way; option 2 duplicates its 3-line APPLICATION. And the size bounds are type-checked, so
   a copy-paste that gets 'off + len <= m' wrong fails to COMPILE rather than silently producing a
   wrong grid. The dangerous kind of drift is largely prevented by the types. The realistic drift
   is a FEATURE GAP -- the unboxed module quietly lacking an operation the boxed one gained.
2. 'The INLINABLE work is a benefit of parameterising.' No, it is orthogonal. Option 2 needs the
   identical pragmas, because Unbox a is a dictionary too -- without them the prototype was 6-20x
   slower on some rows (uindex 16.8 ms vs 786 us). The 60%/78% boxed speedup on tabulate/fmap was
   available without touching the representation at all.
3. 'Option 1 costs only signature churn.' It also cost the collapseGrid +9% / toJSON +19%
   regression (sized-grid-2g0), AllowAmbiguousTypes, four recursion helpers, and the gridFromList
   annotation. Option 2 touches no existing code, so it would have had NONE of these.

WHERE THE BALANCE ACTUALLY LIES. Option 1's surviving advantage is narrower than originally
claimed: every future shape operation is written once rather than twice, in a repo that is actively
adding them, and Storable / strict-boxed representations come free. Option 2's advantage is no
regression, simpler code, better inference and better error messages. It is a genuine judgment
call, not the clear win the original decision presented. Note also that the u-prefixed names in the
prototype are NOT forced -- a real option 2 would use identical names for qualified import, the
vector-package convention -- so 'option 1 gives one name per operation' is not a real point against
option 2.

The prototype was throwaway and lived in a job tmp dir that is now gone; that is deliberate, per
the lesson of bench-spike. Rebuilding it is about 20 minutes from this description if ever needed.

sized-grid beads export workflow (set up 2026-08-11): auto-export is now OFF. config.yaml carries export.auto=false and export.git-add=false, so bd no longer rewrites or git-adds .beads/issues.jsonl after every write. Two reasons it had to go: bd 1.0.3 defaults those to true (bd 1.1 flipped them to opt-in, calling the JSONL 'not the canonical source of truth, not cross-machine sync, not a full database backup'), and bd export orders the MEMORY lines non-deterministically -- back-to-back exports of an unchanged DB differ, which is what produced the endless phantom 4-add/4-delete diffs and the textual merge conflicts.

EXPORT MANUALLY, SORTED, once at session end -- always sorted, or the phantom churn returns:
  bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl && sort -o .beads/issues.jsonl .beads/issues.jsonl
Sorted output is byte-stable run to run and round-trips (bd import --dry-run reads back all issues + memories).

Merge conflicts on that path are handled by a merge driver: .gitattributes maps it to merge=beads, and LOCAL git config (not committed -- re-run in any fresh clone) defines:
  git config merge.beads.name 'regenerate beads JSONL from Dolt'
  git config merge.beads.driver 'bd export -o %A && sort -o %A %A'
This regenerates from the shared Dolt DB instead of merging text, which also fixes the old worktree problem: every worktree shares the MAIN checkout's .beads, so a worktree branch used to carry a stale issues.jsonl.

STILL TRUE: no Dolt remote is configured and .beads/backup/ is gitignored, so the git-tracked issues.jsonl remains the ONLY off-machine copy. Do not gitignore it. On bd >= 1.1 the export and driver both need --include-memories or the 7 memories silently vanish from the file.

sized-grid: you can RUN an aoc day against a worktree build, not just type-check it, which is how sized-grid-dr1's acceptance was verified without the puzzle input. Extend the scratch-project recipe in memory sized-grid-aoc-cannot-be-cabal-built: (1) aoc day files are an implicit 'module Main' with a main that reads input/YYYY/DD.txt, which is NOT in the repo -- strip main and insert 'module DayNN where' before the first import to make the file importable; (2) compile it with a Runner.hs that calls the day's own doctest example (the '-- >>> solve example' lines give known answers, e.g. 2024/04 = 18 and 9), via 'ghc -O0 -package-env <scratch>/.ghc.environment... -o check Runner.hs DayNN.hs'; (3) for a rewrite, generate BOTH old and new as DayNNOld/DayNNNew and compare them over a few hundred random grids -- that is far stronger evidence the real input still answers the same than one example. Do NOT try 'ghci -ghci-script' for this: it hangs or loses module scope in this environment. Runner needs OverloadedStrings for the attoparsec ByteString literal.

tasty-bench measures CPU time by default (getCPUTime), which its own Haddock says is 'total elapsed CPU time across all cores' for a multithreaded algorithm. So it CANNOT see a parallel speedup: a perfect 4x on four cores measures the same or slightly worse. Any parallel benchmark in sized-grid must pass --time-mode wall (or localOption WallTime). Discovered in sized-grid-kb38, which lost a full round of measurement to it; the tell was +RTS -s reporting 3.0s mutator against 1.25s elapsed on a run tasty-bench had called flat. Note is in bench/README.md. Applies to sized-grid-49hi, sized-grid-0bej, sized-grid-utxm.

The full 'manifolds' package (Data.Manifold.Atlas, Manifold, SemimanifoldWithBoundary, Shade, Web, TreeCover) cannot be built on this project's toolchain and this is not fixable by us. manifolds-0.6.1.0 depends on half-space, which caps base < 4.19 (GHC 9.8). Only two half-space versions exist (0.1.0.0, 0.1.1.0) and both carry that cap. grid-sized requires GHC 9.10+ / base >= 4.20, so cabal cannot produce a build plan at all -- verified by 'cabal build --dry-run -w ghc-9.12.3', which fails resolving base against half-space. Consequence: manifolds' own Atlas class is unavailable for grid-atlas's Mobius/Klein/CubeMap charts. Do not re-investigate that angle without first checking whether half-space has gained a base bound past 4.19. By contrast manifolds-core-0.6.1.1 (Semimanifold, PseudoAffine) builds clean on GHC 9.12.3 with warnings only -- it does not depend on half-space. See sized-grid-8nz.

The maintainer's benchmark machine (aarch64-darwin, the one the checked-in baselines come from) has 10 cores that are NOT alike: hw.perflevel0.logicalcpu is 4 performance cores and hw.perflevel1.logicalcpu is 6 efficiency cores. So +RTS -N4 is roughly 'the fast cores' and -N8 necessarily puts half a static equal split on cores several times slower, where the join then waits for the slowest. Any 'returns stop past four cores' measured here -- sized-grid-kb38 and sized-grid-49hi both saw it -- is partly a fact about this laptop, not only about the algorithm. Say so when quoting the knee.

Type-checker plugins are not transitive, so they cannot fix a constraint that leaks into a consumer's signature. -fplugin applies only to the modules of the package that enables it; a downstream package solves its own wanteds with GHC alone. In sized-grid this means a leak like 'KnownNat (n*n)' escaping through an exported signature is only fixable by an API change (class instead of type family), never by adding ghc-typelits-knownnat here. Corollary for testing: any test of what a consumer must write has to be compiled WITHOUT the plugins -- sized-grid.cabal splits 'common lang-base' from 'common lang' and the 'downstream' test-suite imports the former for exactly this reason.

TypeData (`type data`) has no application in sized-grid, checked 2026-08-12. The extension's whole value is for a data type you promote and never use at the term level; sized-grid has zero such types. Every data/newtype in src is a genuine runtime value (Extremum, Ordinal, Clamped, Periodic, Coord, OffGrid, Grid, FocusedGrid, GridSizeProof), and all type-level indexing comes from builtin kinds (Nat, [], Type) plus the coord types themselves -- which must stay inhabited because Coord cs = Coord (NP I cs) stores an I x per axis, and a type-data constructor has no inhabitants. Extremum is the tempting near-miss (closed AtMin/AtMax tag set) but it is the RESULT of axisBoundaryIsCoord :: c n -> Maybe Extremum, i.e. pure runtime -- exactly inverted. Also verified against GHC 9.12.3: GHC2024 does NOT imply TypeData (error GHC-15013), and type data fields must still have kind Type just like plain data ('type data P = MkP 5' is rejected identically), so type data buys namespace hygiene only, never new expressiveness.

Verifying demo/executable logic in this repo without a GUI: run 'cabal repl <pkg> --repl-options=-v0 -v0 < script.ghci' with the commands on STDIN. Do NOT use --repl-options=-ghci-script=FILE: that script runs before cabal's own :load, so every name is out of scope. Also use ':module + *Some.Module' (with the star) to get a module's full top-level scope, not just its export list -- Main.hs modules are 'module Main (main)' and their internals are otherwise invisible. This is how the glider gun, the Wireworld circuits, Langton's ant and the maze invariants in sized-grid-nnww were checked against reference implementations.
